title: Section 2A.13 Guidance 7 - Standardization of Location
text:
Section 2A.13 Guidance 7 - Standardization of Location
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2A. General
Page: 57

Signs should be located so that they: A. Are outside the clear zone unless placed on a crashworthy (see definition in Section 1C.02) support, B. Optimize nighttime visibility, C. Minimize the effects of mud splatter and debris, D. Do not obscure each other, E. Do not obscure the sight distance to approaching vehicles on the major street for drivers who are stopped on minor-street approaches, and F. Are not hidden from view.

title: Section 2A.13 Guidance 8 - Standardization of Location
text:
Section 2A.13 Guidance 8 - Standardization of Location
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2A. General
Page: 57

Except for STOP, YIELD, DO NOT ENTER, and WRONG WAY signs, or as otherwise provided in this Manual, where a sign on a one-way roadway indicates an action intended exclusively or primarily for a road user in the left-hand lane or at the left-hand side of that roadway, such as LEFT LANE MUST TURN LEFT (R3-7) or LEFT LANE ENDS (W9-1), the sign should be located on the left-hand side of the roadway. In the case of a divided road, the sign should be located in the median.

title: Section 2A.13 Option 9 - Standardization of Location
text:
Section 2A.13 Option 9 - Standardization of Location
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2A. General
Page: 57

Signs located on the left-hand side of a one-way roadway or in the median of a divided road, in accordance with Paragraph 8 of this Section, may be supplemented by an identical sign located on the right-hand side of the roadway.

title: Section 2A.13 Support 10 - Standardization of Location
text:
Section 2A.13 Support 10 - Standardization of Location
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2A. General
Page: 57

The clear zone (see definition in Section 1C.02) is the total roadside border area, starting at the edge of the traveled way, available for an errant driver to stop or regain control of a vehicle. The width of the clear zone is dependent upon traffic volumes, speeds, and roadside geometry. Additional information can be found in the “Roadside Design Guide,” 4th Edition, 2011, AASHTO.

title: Section 2A.13 Guidance 11 - Standardization of Location
text:
Section 2A.13 Guidance 11 - Standardization of Location
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2A. General
Page: 57

With the increase in traffic volumes and the need to provide road users regulatory, warning, and guidance information, an order of priority for sign installation should be established.

title: Section 2A.13 Support 12 - Standardization of Location
text:
Section 2A.13 Support 12 - Standardization of Location
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2A. General
Page: 57

An order of priority is especially critical where space is limited for sign installation and there is a demand for several different types of signs. Overloading road users with too much information is not desirable. Priority according to type of sign will depend on the specific situation and conditions of the site at which the signs are to be installed. For example, in the vicinity of an exit ramp, guide signs and warning signs for the exit ramp might take precedence over regulatory signs that confirm rules of the road, such as a STATE LAW-NO HANDHELD PHONE USE BY DRIVER sign, or a mainline Speed Limit sign where there is no change in the speed zone.

title: Section 2A.13 Guidance 13 - Standardization of Location
text:
Section 2A.13 Guidance 13 - Standardization of Location
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2A. General
Page: 57

Because regulatory and warning information is typically more critical to the road user than guidance information, regulatory and warning signing whose locations are critical should be displayed rather than guide signing in cases where conflicts occur. In such cases, the guide sign should be relocated to another appropriate location where it will still be effective. In other cases, such as at a decision point, the guide sign should take precedence over other signs whose locations are not as critical to an immediate decision or action necessary by the road user. In all cases, careful attention should be given to minimizing sign clutter (see Section 2A.20). Community wayfinding and acknowledgment guide signs should have a lower priority as to placement than other guide signs. Signs conveying information of a less-critical nature should be moved to less-critical locations or omitted.

title: Section 2A.13 Option 14 - Standardization of Location
text:
Section 2A.13 Option 14 - Standardization of Location
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2A. General
Page: 57

Under some circumstances, such as on curves to the right, signs may be placed on median islands or on the left-hand side of the road. A supplementary sign located on the left-hand side of the roadway may be used on a multi-lane road where traffic in a lane to the right might obstruct the view to the right.

title: Section 2A.13 Guidance 15 - Standardization of Location
text:
Section 2A.13 Guidance 15 - Standardization of Location
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2A. General
Page: 58

In urban areas where crosswalks exist, signs should not be placed within 4 feet in advance of the crosswalk (see Drawing D in Figure 2A-3).

title: Section 2A.14 Guidance 1 - Overhead Sign Installations
text:
Section 2A.14 Guidance 1 - Overhead Sign Installations
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2A. General
Page: 58

Overhead signs should be used on freeways and expressways, at locations where some degree of lane-use control is desirable, and at locations where space is not available at the roadside.

title: Section 2A.14 Support 2 - Overhead Sign Installations
text:
Section 2A.14 Support 2 - Overhead Sign Installations
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2A. General
Page: 58

The operational requirements of the present highway system are such that overhead signs have value at many locations. The factors to be considered for the installation of overhead sign displays are not definable in specific numerical terms. In some cases, overhead mounting of a sign might be required by other provisions of this Manual.

title: Section 2A.14 Option 3 - Overhead Sign Installations
text:
Section 2A.14 Option 3 - Overhead Sign Installations
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2A. General
Page: 58

The following conditions (not in priority order) may be considered in an engineering study to determine if overhead signs would be beneficial: A. Traffic volume at or near capacity, B. Complex interchange design, C. Three or more lanes in each direction, D. Restricted sight distance, E. Closely-spaced interchanges, F. Multi-lane exits, G. Large percentage of trucks, H. Street lighting background, I. High-speed traffic, J. Consistency of sign message location through a series of interchanges, K. Insufficient space for post-mounted signs, L. Junction of two freeways, and M. Left-side exit ramps.

title: Section 2A.14 Option 4 - Overhead Sign Installations
text:
Section 2A.14 Option 4 - Overhead Sign Installations
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2A. General
Page: 58

Over-crossing structures may be used to support overhead signs.

title: Section 2A.14 Support 5 - Overhead Sign Installations
text:
Section 2A.14 Support 5 - Overhead Sign Installations
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2A. General
Page: 58

Under some circumstances, the use of over-crossing structures as sign supports might be the only practical solution that will provide adequate viewing distance. The use of such structures as sign supports might eliminate the need for the foundations and sign supports along the roadside.

title: Section 2A.15 Standard 1 - Mounting Height
text:
Section 2A.15 Standard 1 - Mounting Height
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2A. General
Page: 58

The provisions of this Section shall apply unless specifically stated otherwise for a particular sign or object marker elsewhere in this Manual.

title: Section 2A.15 Support 2 - Mounting Height
text:
Section 2A.15 Support 2 - Mounting Height
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2A. General
Page: 58

It might be necessary to use larger minimum mounting heights than those prescribed in this Manual to ensure appropriate crash performance of sign installations that are required to be crashworthy (see Section 1D.11).

title: Section 2A.15 Support 3 - Mounting Height
text:
Section 2A.15 Support 3 - Mounting Height
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2A. General
Page: 58

In addition to the provisions of this Section, information affecting the minimum mounting height of signs as a function of crash performance can be found in the “Roadside Design Guide,” 4th Edition, 2011, AASHTO.

title: Section 2A.15 Standard 4 - Mounting Height
text:
Section 2A.15 Standard 4 - Mounting Height
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2A. General
Page: 58

In rural areas, the minimum height, measured vertically from the bottom of the sign to the elevation of the near edge of the pavement, of signs installed at the side of the road shall be 5 feet (see Figure 2A-2).

title: Section 2A.15 Standard 5 - Mounting Height
text:
Section 2A.15 Standard 5 - Mounting Height
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2A. General
Page: 58

In business, commercial, or residential areas where parking, bicyclist, or pedestrian movements are likely to occur, or where the view of the sign might be obstructed, the minimum height, measured vertically from the bottom of the sign to the top of the curb, or in the absence of curb, measured vertically from the bottom of the sign to the elevation of the near edge of the traveled way, of signs installed at the side of the road shall be 7 feet (see Figure 2A-2).

title: Section 2A.15 Option 6 - Mounting Height
text:
Section 2A.15 Option 6 - Mounting Height
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2A. General
Page: 58

The height to the bottom of a secondary sign mounted below another sign may be 1 foot less than the height specified in Paragraphs 4 and 5 of this Section.

title: Section 2A.15 Standard 7 - Mounting Height
text:
Section 2A.15 Standard 7 - Mounting Height
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2A. General
Page: 59

The minimum height of signs, measured vertically from the bottom of the sign to the sidewalk shall be 7 feet.

title: Section 2A.15 Standard 8 - Mounting Height
text:
Section 2A.15 Standard 8 - Mounting Height
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2A. General
Page: 59

If the bottom of a secondary sign that is mounted below another sign is mounted lower than 7 feet above a pedestrian sidewalk or pathway (see Section 6C.02), the secondary sign shall not project more than 4 inches into the pedestrian facility.

title: Section 2A.16 Standard 1 - Lateral Offset
text:
Section 2A.16 Standard 1 - Lateral Offset
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2A. General
Page: 59

For overhead sign supports, the minimum lateral offset from the edge of the shoulder (or if no shoulder exists, from the edge of the pavement) to the near edge of overhead sign supports (cantilever or sign bridges) shall be 6 feet. Overhead sign supports shall have a barrier or crash cushion to shield them if they are within the clear zone.

title: Section 2A.16 Standard 2 - Lateral Offset
text:
Section 2A.16 Standard 2 - Lateral Offset
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2A. General
Page: 60

Post-mounted sign and object marker supports shall be crashworthy (see Section 1D.11) if within the clear zone.

title: Section 2A.16 Guidance 3 - Lateral Offset
text:
Section 2A.16 Guidance 3 - Lateral Offset
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2A. General
Page: 60

For post-mounted signs, the minimum lateral offset should be 12 feet from the edge of the traveled way. If a shoulder wider than 6 feet exists, the minimum lateral offset for post-mounted signs should be 6 feet from the edge of the shoulder.

title: Section 2A.16 Guidance 4 - Lateral Offset
text:
Section 2A.16 Guidance 4 - Lateral Offset
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2A. General
Page: 60

Supports for signs mounted laterally behind a longitudinal barrier should be placed so that the near edge of the support is located beyond the deflection distance of the longitudinal barrier.

title: Section 2A.16 Support 5 - Lateral Offset
text:
Section 2A.16 Support 5 - Lateral Offset
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2A. General
Page: 60

The minimum lateral offset requirements for object markers are provided in Chapter 2C.

title: Section 2A.16 Support 6 - Lateral Offset
text:
Section 2A.16 Support 6 - Lateral Offset
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2A. General
Page: 60

The minimum lateral offset is intended to keep trucks and cars that use the shoulders from striking the signs or supports. The minimum lateral offset requirements do not supersede the requirement for crashworthiness (see Paragraph 2 of this Section) if the sign is located within the clear zone.

title: Section 2A.16 Guidance 7 - Lateral Offset
text:
Section 2A.16 Guidance 7 - Lateral Offset
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2A. General
Page: 60

All supports should be located as far as practical from the edge of the shoulder. Advantage should be taken to place signs behind existing roadside barriers, on over-crossing structures, or other locations that minimize the exposure of the traffic to sign supports.

title: Section 2A.16 Option 8 - Lateral Offset
text:
Section 2A.16 Option 8 - Lateral Offset
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2A. General
Page: 60

Lesser lateral offsets may be used on connecting roadways or ramps at interchanges, but not less than 6 feet from the edge of the traveled way.

title: Section 2A.16 Option 9 - Lateral Offset
text:
Section 2A.16 Option 9 - Lateral Offset
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2A. General
Page: 60

On conventional, low-volume rural, and special-purpose roads in areas where it is impractical to locate a sign with the lateral offset prescribed by this Section because of roadside features such as terrain or vegetation, a lateral offset of at least 2 feet may be used.

title: Section 2A.16 Option 10 - Lateral Offset
text:
Section 2A.16 Option 10 - Lateral Offset
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2A. General
Page: 60

A lateral offset of at least 1 foot from the face of the curb may be used in business, commercial, or residential areas where sidewalk width is limited or where existing poles are close to the curb.

title: Section 2A.16 Guidance 11 - Lateral Offset
text:
Section 2A.16 Guidance 11 - Lateral Offset
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2A. General
Page: 60

Overhead sign supports and post-mounted sign and object marker supports should not intrude into the usable width of a sidewalk or other pedestrian facility.

title: Section 2A.16 Support 12 - Lateral Offset
text:
Section 2A.16 Support 12 - Lateral Offset
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2A. General
Page: 60

Guidance for maintaining sign shape in laterally-constrained conditions is described in Section 2A.05.

title: Section 2A.16 Support 13 - Lateral Offset
text:
Section 2A.16 Support 13 - Lateral Offset
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2A. General
Page: 60

Figures 2A-2 and 2A-3 illustrate some examples of the lateral offset requirements contained in this Section.

title: Section 2A.17 Guidance 1 - Orientation
text:
Section 2A.17 Guidance 1 - Orientation
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2A. General
Page: 60

Unless otherwise provided in this Manual, signs should be vertically mounted at right angles to the direction of, and facing, the traffic that they are intended to serve.

title: Section 2A.17 Guidance 2 - Orientation
text:
Section 2A.17 Guidance 2 - Orientation
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2A. General
Page: 60

Where mirror reflection from the sign face is encountered to such a degree as to reduce legibility, the sign should be turned slightly away from the road. Signs that are placed 30 feet or more from the pavement edge should be turned toward the road. On curved alignments, the angle of placement should be determined by the direction of approaching traffic rather than by the roadway edge at the point where the sign is located.

title: Section 2A.17 Option 3 - Orientation
text:
Section 2A.17 Option 3 - Orientation
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2A. General
Page: 60

On grades, sign faces may be tilted forward or back from the vertical position to improve the viewing angle.

title: Section 2A.18 Standard 1 - Posts and Mountings
text:
Section 2A.18 Standard 1 - Posts and Mountings
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2A. General
Page: 60

Sign posts, foundations, and mountings shall be so constructed as to hold signs in a proper and permanent position, and to resist swaying in the wind or displacement by vandalism.

title: Section 2A.18 Support 2 - Posts and Mountings
text:
Section 2A.18 Support 2 - Posts and Mountings
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2A. General
Page: 60

The latest edition of AASHTO’s “Specifications for Structural Supports for Highway Signs, Luminaires, and Traffic Signals” contains additional information regarding posts and mounting.

title: Section 2A.18 Option 3 - Posts and Mountings
text:
Section 2A.18 Option 3 - Posts and Mountings
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2A. General
Page: 60

Where permitted, signs may be placed on existing supports used for other purposes, such as highway traffic signal supports, highway lighting supports, and utility poles.

title: Section 2A.19 Guidance 1 - Maintenance
text:
Section 2A.19 Guidance 1 - Maintenance
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2A. General
Page: 61

Maintenance activities should consider proper position, cleanliness, legibility, and daytime and nighttime visibility (see Sections 2A.21 and 2A.22). Damaged or deteriorated signs, gates, or object markers should be replaced.

title: Section 2A.19 Guidance 2 - Maintenance
text:
Section 2A.19 Guidance 2 - Maintenance
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2A. General
Page: 61

To assure adequate maintenance, a schedule for inspecting (both day and night), cleaning, and replacing signs, gates, and object markers should be established. Employees of highway, law enforcement, and other public agencies whose duties require that they travel on the roadways should be encouraged to report any damaged, deteriorated, or obscured signs, gates, or object markers at the first opportunity.

title: Section 2A.19 Guidance 3 - Maintenance
text:
Section 2A.19 Guidance 3 - Maintenance
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2A. General
Page: 61

Steps should be taken to see that weeds, trees, shrubbery, and construction, maintenance, and utility materials and equipment do not obscure the face of any sign or object marker.

title: Section 2A.19 Guidance 4 - Maintenance
text:
Section 2A.19 Guidance 4 - Maintenance
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2A. General
Page: 61

A regular schedule of replacement of lighting elements for illuminated signs should be maintained.

title: Section 2A.20 Guidance 1 - Excessive Use of Signs
text:
Section 2A.20 Guidance 1 - Excessive Use of Signs
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2A. General
Page: 61

Signs should be used and located judiciously, minimizing their proliferation in order to maintain their effectiveness. Regulatory and warning signs should be used conservatively because these signs, if used to excess, tend to lose their effectiveness. Route signs and directional guide signs for primary routes and destinations should be used frequently at strategic locations because their use promotes efficient operations by keeping road users informed of their location. In all cases, however, sign clutter (see Paragraph 2 of this Section) should be avoided and minimized as much as practicable.

title: Section 2A.20 Support 2 - Excessive Use of Signs
text:
Section 2A.20 Support 2 - Excessive Use of Signs
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2A. General
Page: 61

Sign clutter is the proliferation of sign installations or assemblies along the roadway or roadside, either separately or grouped, to such an extent that adequate spacing between installations necessary for orderly processing of the sign messages by the driver cannot be achieved. Sign clutter can reduce the effectiveness of one or more signs in a sequence of signs.

title: Section 2A.20 Support 3 - Excessive Use of Signs
text:
Section 2A.20 Support 3 - Excessive Use of Signs
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2A. General
Page: 61

The basic role of traffic control devices is to provide only as much information to the road user as necessary to promote the safe and efficient operation of streets and highways. Sign clutter can result from the overuse of MUTCD-compliant signs and/or signs that display information unrelated to traffic operation, navigation, or transportation information. Examples of such signs would include, but are not limited to, those displaying the birthplace or home of a noted person, local sports team accomplishments, population information, and self- described qualities of a community such as “friendly” or “open for business.”

title: Section 2A.20 Guidance 4 - Excessive Use of Signs
text:
Section 2A.20 Guidance 4 - Excessive Use of Signs
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2A. General
Page: 61

Signs and other traffic control devices should be installed and maintained from a systematic standpoint rather than individually. When a new sign is installed, the existing signs in the vicinity should be considered for replacement, relocation, or removal as a result of the new sign that is installed. Existing systems of signs should be reviewed periodically for evidence of sign clutter and adjustments should be made accordingly.

title: Section 2A.21 Support 1 - Retroreflection and Illumination
text:
Section 2A.21 Support 1 - Retroreflection and Illumination
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2A. General
Page: 61

There are many materials currently available for retroreflection and various methods currently available for the illumination of signs and object markers. New materials and methods continue to emerge. New materials and methods can be used as long as the signs and object markers meet the standard requirements for color, both by day and by night.

title: Section 2A.21 Support 2 - Retroreflection and Illumination
text:
Section 2A.21 Support 2 - Retroreflection and Illumination
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2A. General
Page: 62

This Section applies to visibility of signs at night or in low-light or adverse weather conditions, whose legends are otherwise visible under typical daytime viewing conditions. December 2025

title: Section 2A.21 Standard 3 - Retroreflection and Illumination
text:
Section 2A.21 Standard 3 - Retroreflection and Illumination
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2A. General
Page: 62

Regulatory, warning, and guide signs (see Section 2A.03), and object markers, shall be retroreflective or illuminated to show the same shape and similar color by both day and night, unless otherwise provided in this Manual for a particular sign or group of signs.

title: Section 2A.21 Standard 4 - Retroreflection and Illumination
text:
Section 2A.21 Standard 4 - Retroreflection and Illumination
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2A. General
Page: 62

Where the color black is specified for the legend or background of a sign, an opaque and non- retroreflective material shall be used.

title: Section 2A.21 Standard 5 - Retroreflection and Illumination
text:
Section 2A.21 Standard 5 - Retroreflection and Illumination
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2A. General
Page: 62

The requirements for sign illumination shall not be considered to be satisfied by street or highway lighting.

title: Section 2A.21 Option 6 - Retroreflection and Illumination
text:
Section 2A.21 Option 6 - Retroreflection and Illumination
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2A. General
Page: 62

Sign elements may be illuminated by the means shown in Table 2A-3. Means of Illumination Sign Element to be Illuminated

title: Section 2A.21 Option 7 - Retroreflection and Illumination
text:
Section 2A.21 Option 7 - Retroreflection and Illumination
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2A. General
Page: 62

Retroreflection of sign elements may be accomplished by the means shown in Table 2A-4.

title: Section 2A.21 Support 8 - Retroreflection and Illumination
text:
Section 2A.21 Support 8 - Retroreflection and Illumination
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2A. General
Page: 62

Information regarding the use of retroreflective material on the sign support is contained in Section 2A.11. Light-emitting diodes (LEDs) • Symbol or word message • Entire sign border Other devices or treatments that highlight the sign shape, color, or message: Luminous tubing Fiber optics Incandescent light bulbs Luminescent panels

title: Section 2A.22 Support 1 - Maintaining Minimum Retroreflectivity
text:
Section 2A.22 Support 1 - Maintaining Minimum Retroreflectivity
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2A. General
Page: 62

Retroreflectivity is one of several factors associated with maintaining nighttime sign visibility (see Section 2A.21).

title: Section 2A.22 Standard 2 - Maintaining Minimum Retroreflectivity
text:
Section 2A.22 Standard 2 - Maintaining Minimum Retroreflectivity
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2A. General
Page: 62

Public agencies or officials having jurisdiction shall use an assessment or management method that is designed to maintain sign retroreflectivity at or above the minimum levels in Table 2A-5.

title: Section 2A.22 Support 3 - Maintaining Minimum Retroreflectivity
text:
Section 2A.22 Support 3 - Maintaining Minimum Retroreflectivity
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2A. General
Page: 62

Compliance with the Standard in Paragraph 2 of this Section is achieved by having a method in place and using the method to maintain the minimum levels established in Table 2A-5. Provided that an assessment or management method is being used, an agency or official having jurisdiction would be in compliance with the Standard in Paragraph 2 of this Section even if there are some individual signs that do not meet the minimum retroreflectivity levels at a particular point in time.

title: Section 2A.22 Guidance 4 - Maintaining Minimum Retroreflectivity
text:
Section 2A.22 Guidance 4 - Maintaining Minimum Retroreflectivity
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2A. General
Page: 62

Except for those signs specifically identified in Paragraph 5 of this Section, one or more of the methods described in “Maintaining Traffic Sign Retroreflectivity,” (FHWA-SA-07-020, Revised 2013), FHWA, or a method developed based on an engineering study, should be used to maintain sign retroreflectivity at or above the minimum levels in Table 2A-5. Signs that are identified through the agency’s method as being below the minimum levels should be replaced.

text:
Section 2A.22 Option 5 - Maintaining Minimum Retroreflectivity
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2A. General
Page: 63

Highway agencies may exclude the following signs from the retroreflectivity maintenance guidelines described in this Section: A. Parking, Standing, and Stopping (R7 and R8 series) signs; B. Walking/Hitchhiking/Crossing (R9 series, R10-1 through R10-4b) signs; C. Acknowledgment signs; and D. Bikeway signs that are intended for exclusive use by bicyclists or pedestrians. title: Section 2A.23 Guidance 1 - Median Opening Treatments for Divided Highways
text:
Section 2A.23 Guidance 1 - Median Opening Treatments for Divided Highways
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2A. General
Page: 63

A divided highway crossing should be signed and marked as separate intersections when both of the following conditions are present: A. The paths of opposing left turns from the divided highway cross each other (see Figure 2A-5), and B. There is adequate storage in the interior approaches for the design vehicles expected to cross the divided highway.

metadata.section_title: Median Opening Treatments for Divided Highways

title: Section 2A.23 Guidance 2 - Median Opening Treatments for Divided Highways
text:
Section 2A.23 Guidance 2 - Median Opening Treatments for Divided Highways
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2A. General
Page: 63

If either one or both of the conditions in Paragraph 1 of this Section do not exist, the divided highway crossing should be signed and marked as a single intersection.

metadata.section_title: Median Opening Treatments for Divided Highways

title: Section 2A.23 Guidance 3 - Median Opening Treatments for Divided Highways
text:
Section 2A.23 Guidance 3 - Median Opening Treatments for Divided Highways
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2A. General
Page: 64

At the crossing of two divided highways, engineering judgment should be used to determine the number of separate intersections. December 2025 Figure 2A-5. Intersection Configuration at a Divided Highway Crossing B - Single intersection (paths of opposing left-turning A - Separate intersections (paths of opposing left-turning vehicles cross) vehicles do not cross)

metadata.section_title: Median Opening Treatments for Divided Highways

title: Section 2A.23 Support 4 - Median Opening Treatments for Divided Highways
text:
Section 2A.23 Support 4 - Median Opening Treatments for Divided Highways
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2A. General
Page: 65

Divided highway crossings with median widths between 30 feet and 85 feet might function as either one or two intersections depending upon the interaction of the opposing left-turn vehicle paths and the available interior storage in the median for a crossing vehicle. Other factors that could determine whether a divided highway crossing is operating as one or two intersections include: A. The geometric design of the divided highway crossing, B. The use of positive offset mainline left-turn lanes, C. The length of the median opening (as measured parallel to the center line of the divided highway), D. The geometric design of the median noses, E. Other roadway geometric considerations such as a skewed side street approach or a variable median width, F. Intersection sight distance, G. The physical characteristics of the design vehicle, and H. The observed prevailing driver behavior with regard to opposing left-turn path interaction.

metadata.section_title: Median Opening Treatments for Divided Highways

title: Section 2B.01 Standard 1 - Application of Regulatory Signs
text:
Section 2B.01 Standard 1 - Application of Regulatory Signs
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2B. Regulatory Signs, Barricades, And Gates
Page: 67

Regulatory signs shall be used to inform road users of selected traffic laws or regulations and to indicate the applicability of the legal requirements.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 2B. Regulatory Signs, Barricades, And Gates

title: Section 2B.01 Standard 2 - Application of Regulatory Signs
text:
Section 2B.01 Standard 2 - Application of Regulatory Signs
Part: Part 2 Signs

text:
Section 2B.05 Support 1 - YIELD Sign (R1-2)
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2B. Regulatory Signs, Barricades, And Gates
Page: 74

Vehicles controlled by a YIELD sign need to slow down to a speed that is reasonable for the existing conditions or stop when necessary to avoid interfering with conflicting traffic.

title: Section 2B.06 Support 1 - General Considerations
text:
Section 2B.06 Support 1 - General Considerations
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2B. Regulatory Signs, Barricades, And Gates
Page: 75

Unsignalized intersections represent the most common form of intersection right-of-way control. Selection of control type might be impacted by specific requirements of State law or local ordinances.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 2B. Regulatory Signs, Barricades, And Gates

title: Section 2B.06 Support 2 - General Considerations
text:
Section 2B.06 Support 2 - General Considerations
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2B. Regulatory Signs, Barricades, And Gates
Page: 75

Roundabouts and traffic circles are circular intersection designs and are not traffic control devices. The decision to convert an intersection from a conventional intersection to a circular intersection is an engineering design decision and not a traffic control device decision. As such, criteria for conversion from a conventional intersection to a circular intersection are not included in the MUTCD.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 2B. Regulatory Signs, Barricades, And Gates

title: Section 2B.06 Guidance 3 - General Considerations
text:
Section 2B.06 Guidance 3 - General Considerations
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2B. Regulatory Signs, Barricades, And Gates
Page: 75

The type of traffic control used at an unsignalized intersection should be the least restrictive that provides appropriate levels of safety and efficiency for all road users.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 2B. Regulatory Signs, Barricades, And Gates

title: Section 2B.06 Support 4 - General Considerations
text:
Section 2B.06 Support 4 - General Considerations
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2B. Regulatory Signs, Barricades, And Gates
Page: 75

Some types of right-of-way control that can exist at an unsignalized intersection in order from the least restrictive to the most restrictive are the following: A. No intersection control (see Section 2B.09): There are no right-of-way traffic control devices on any of the approaches to the intersection. B. Yield control (see Section 2B.10): YIELD signs are placed on all approaches (for a circular intersection), on opposing approaches for a four-leg intersection, on a single approach for a three-leg intersection, or in the median of a divided highway. The YIELD signs are placed on the minor road. C. Minor road stop control (see Section 2B.11): STOP signs are typically placed on opposing approaches (for a four-leg intersection) or on a single approach (for a three-leg intersection). The STOP signs are normally placed on the minor road. Section 2B.07 contains guidance on selecting the minor road. D. All-way stop control (see Section 2B.12): STOP signs are placed on all approaches to the intersection.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 2B. Regulatory Signs, Barricades, And Gates

title: Section 2B.06 Guidance 5 - General Considerations
text:
Section 2B.06 Guidance 5 - General Considerations
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2B. Regulatory Signs, Barricades, And Gates
Page: 75

When selecting a form of intersection control, the following factors should be considered: A. Motor vehicle, bicycle, and pedestrian traffic volumes on all approaches; where the term units/day or units/hour is indicated, it should be the total of motor vehicle, bicycle, and pedestrian volume; B. Driver yielding behavior with regard to all modes of conflicting traffic, including bicyclists and pedestrians; C. Number and angle of approaches; D. Approach speeds; E. Sight distance available on each approach; F. Reported crash experience; and G. The presence of a grade crossing near the intersection.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 2B. Regulatory Signs, Barricades, And Gates

title: Section 2B.06 Standard 6 - General Considerations
text:
Section 2B.06 Standard 6 - General Considerations
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2B. Regulatory Signs, Barricades, And Gates
Page: 75

YIELD or STOP signs shall not be used for speed control.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 2B. Regulatory Signs, Barricades, And Gates

title: Section 2B.06 Support 7 - General Considerations
text:
Section 2B.06 Support 7 - General Considerations
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2B. Regulatory Signs, Barricades, And Gates
Page: 75

Appropriate traffic calming or other speed control measures are available to control vehicle speeds, such as those that do not have the potential to diminish the effectiveness of traffic control devices when used for their specified purpose.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 2B. Regulatory Signs, Barricades, And Gates

title: Section 2B.06 Standard 8 - General Considerations
text:
Section 2B.06 Standard 8 - General Considerations
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2B. Regulatory Signs, Barricades, And Gates
Page: 75

Because the potential for conflicting commands could create driver confusion, YIELD or STOP signs shall not be used in conjunction with any traffic control signal operation, except in the following cases: A. If the signal indication for an approach is a flashing red at all times; B. If a minor street or driveway is located within or adjacent to the area controlled by the traffic control signal, but does not require separate traffic signal control because an extremely low potential for conflict exists; or C. If a channelized turn lane is separated from the adjacent travel lanes by an island and the channelized turn lane is not controlled by a traffic control signal.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 2B. Regulatory Signs, Barricades, And Gates

title: Section 2B.06 Standard 9 - General Considerations
text:
Section 2B.06 Standard 9 - General Considerations
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2B. Regulatory Signs, Barricades, And Gates
Page: 75

STOP signs and YIELD signs shall not be installed on different approaches to the same unsignalized intersection if those approaches conflict with or oppose each other, except as provided for in Items A and B in Paragraph 3 of Section 2B.10.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 2B. Regulatory Signs, Barricades, And Gates

title: Section 2B.06 Standard 10 - General Considerations
text:
Section 2B.06 Standard 10 - General Considerations
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2B. Regulatory Signs, Barricades, And Gates
Page: 76

Portable or part-time STOP or YIELD signs shall not be used except for emergency and temporary traffic control zone purposes.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 2B. Regulatory Signs, Barricades, And Gates

title: Section 2B.06 Standard 11 - General Considerations
text:
Section 2B.06 Standard 11 - General Considerations
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2B. Regulatory Signs, Barricades, And Gates
Page: 76

A portable or part-time (folding) STOP sign that is manually placed into view and manually removed from view shall not be used during a power outage to control a signalized approach unless the maintaining agency establishes that the signal indication that will first be displayed to that approach upon restoration of power is a flashing red signal indication and that the portable STOP sign will be manually removed from view prior to resuming stop-and-go operation of the traffic control signal.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 2B. Regulatory Signs, Barricades, And Gates

title: Section 2B.06 Option 12 - General Considerations
text:
Section 2B.06 Option 12 - General Considerations
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2B. Regulatory Signs, Barricades, And Gates
Page: 76

A portable or part-time (folding) STOP sign that is electrically or mechanically operated such that it only displays the stop message during a power outage and ceases to display the stop message upon restoration of power may be used during a power outage to control a signalized approach.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 2B. Regulatory Signs, Barricades, And Gates

title: Section 2B.06 Support 13 - General Considerations
text:
Section 2B.06 Support 13 - General Considerations
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2B. Regulatory Signs, Barricades, And Gates
Page: 76

The use of STOP signs at grade crossings is described in Sections 8B.04 and 8B.05.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 2B. Regulatory Signs, Barricades, And Gates

title: Section 2B.07 Guidance 1 - Determining the Minor Road for Unsignalized Intersections
text:
Section 2B.07 Guidance 1 - Determining the Minor Road for Unsignalized Intersections
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2B. Regulatory Signs, Barricades, And Gates
Page: 76

The selection of the minor road to be controlled by YIELD or STOP signs should be based on one or more of the following criteria: A. A roadway intersecting a designated through or numbered highway, B. A roadway with the lower functional classification, C. A roadway with the lower traffic volume, D. A roadway with the lower speed limit, and/or E. A roadway that intersects with a roadway that has a higher priority for one or more modes of travel.

metadata.section_title: Determining the Minor Road for Unsignalized Intersections
metadata.chapter: Chapter 2B. Regulatory Signs, Barricades, And Gates

title: Section 2B.07 Guidance 2 - Determining the Minor Road for Unsignalized Intersections
text:
Section 2B.07 Guidance 2 - Determining the Minor Road for Unsignalized Intersections
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2B. Regulatory Signs, Barricades, And Gates
Page: 76

When two roadways that have relatively equal volumes, speeds, and/or other characteristics intersect, the following factors should be considered in selecting the minor road for installation of YIELD or STOP signs: A. Controlling the direction that conflicts the most with established pedestrian crossing activity or school walking routes; B. Controlling the direction that has obscured vision, dips, or bumps that already require drivers to use lower operating speeds; and C. Controlling the direction that has the best sight distance from a controlled position to observe conflicting traffic.

metadata.section_title: Determining the Minor Road for Unsignalized Intersections
metadata.chapter: Chapter 2B. Regulatory Signs, Barricades, And Gates

title: Section 2B.08 Guidance 1 - Right-of-Way Intersection Control Considerations
text:
Section 2B.08 Guidance 1 - Right-of-Way Intersection Control Considerations
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2B. Regulatory Signs, Barricades, And Gates
Page: 77

Before converting to a more restrictive form of right-of-way control at an unsignalized intersection, the following alternative treatments to address safety, operational, or other concerns should be among those to be considered: A. Where yield or stop controlled, installing Yield Ahead or Stop Ahead signs on the appropriate approaches to the intersection; B. Removing parking on one or more approaches; C. Removing sight distance obstructions; D. Installing signs along the major street to warn road users approaching the intersection; E. Relocating the stop line(s) and making other changes to improve the sight distance at the intersection; F. Installing measures designed to reduce speeds on the approaches; G. Installing an Intersection Control Beacon (see Section 4S.02) or Stop Beacon (see Section 4S.05) at the intersection to supplement STOP sign control; H. Installing a Warning Beacon (see Section 4S.03) on warning signs in advance of a stop-controlled intersection on major-street and/or minor-street approaches; I. Adding one or more lanes on a minor-street approach to reduce the number of vehicles per lane on the approach; J. Revising the geometrics at the intersection to channelize vehicular movements and reduce the time required for a vehicle to complete a movement, which could also assist pedestrians; K. Revising the geometrics at the intersection to add pedestrian median refuge islands and/or curb extensions; L. Installing roadway lighting if a disproportionate number of crashes occur at night; M. Restricting one or more turning movements on a full-time or part-time basis if alternate routes are available; MUTCD 11th Edition - Revision 1 N. Installing on the major street a pedestrian-actuated device: Warning Beacon (see Section 4S.03), rectangular rapid-flashing beacon (see Section 4L.01), or In-Roadway Warning Lights (see Chapter 4U), if pedestrian safety is the major concern; O. If the warrant is satisfied, installing all-way stop control; P. Installing a pedestrian hybrid beacon (see Chapter 4J) on the major street to address pedestrian safety; Q. Installing a circular intersection; and R. Employing other alternatives, depending on conditions at the intersection.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 2B. Regulatory Signs, Barricades, And Gates

title: Section 2B.09 Guidance 1 - No Intersection Control
text:
Section 2B.09 Guidance 1 - No Intersection Control
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2B. Regulatory Signs, Barricades, And Gates
Page: 77

The decision not to use intersection control should be based on engineering judgment.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 2B. Regulatory Signs, Barricades, And Gates

title: Section 2B.09 Option 2 - No Intersection Control
text:
Section 2B.09 Option 2 - No Intersection Control
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2B. Regulatory Signs, Barricades, And Gates
Page: 77

The following factors may be considered: A. Intersection sight distance is adequate on all approaches. B. All approaches to the intersection are a single lane and there are no separate turn lanes. C. The combined motor vehicle, bicycle, and pedestrian volume (existing or projected) entering the intersection from all approaches averages less than 1,000 units per day or 80 units in the peak hour. D. There are no marked crosswalks or bicycle lanes on any approach. E. None of the approaches to the intersection are for a through highway, main road, or higher functional classification. F. The angle of intersection is between 90 and 75 degrees. G. The functional classification of the intersecting streets is either the intersection of two local streets or the intersection of a local street with a collector street.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 2B. Regulatory Signs, Barricades, And Gates

title: Section 2B.10 Guidance 1 - Yield Control
text:
Section 2B.10 Guidance 1 - Yield Control
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2B. Regulatory Signs, Barricades, And Gates
Page: 77

At intersections where a full stop is not necessary at all times, consideration should first be given to using less restrictive measures such as YIELD signs.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 2B. Regulatory Signs, Barricades, And Gates

title: Section 2B.10 Guidance 2 - Yield Control
text:
Section 2B.10 Guidance 2 - Yield Control
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2B. Regulatory Signs, Barricades, And Gates
Page: 77

Yield control should be considered when engineering judgment indicates that all of the following conditions exist: A. Intersection sight distance is adequate on the approaches to be controlled by YIELD signs. B. All approaches to the intersection are a single lane and there are no separate turn lanes. C. One of the following crash-related criteria applies: 1. For changing from no intersection control to yield control, there have been two or more reported crashes in the previous 12 months that are susceptible to correction by the installation of a YIELD sign. 2. For changing from minor road stop control to yield control, there have been two or fewer reported crashes in the previous 12 months. D. The combined motor vehicle, bicycle, and pedestrian volume entering the intersection averages less than Rev. 1 1,800 units per day or 140 units in the peak hour. E. The angle of intersection is between 90 and 75 degrees. F. The functional classification of the intersecting streets is either the intersection of two local streets or the intersection of a local street with a collector street.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 2B. Regulatory Signs, Barricades, And Gates

title: Section 2B.10 Option 3 - Yield Control
text:
Section 2B.10 Option 3 - Yield Control
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2B. Regulatory Signs, Barricades, And Gates
Page: 78

YIELD signs may be installed at an intersection when any of the following conditions apply: A. At the second intersection of a divided highway crossing or median break functioning as two separate intersections (see Figure 2B-19). In this case, a YIELD sign may be installed at the entrance to the second intersection. B. For a channelized turn lane that is separated from the adjacent travel lanes by an island, even if the adjacent lanes at the intersection are controlled by a highway traffic control signal or by a STOP sign. C. At an intersection where a special problem exists and where engineering judgment indicates the problem to be susceptible to correction by the use of the YIELD sign. D. Facing the entering roadway for a merge-type movement if engineering judgment indicates that control is needed because acceleration geometry and/or sight distance is not adequate for merging traffic operation. E. On low-volume rural roads if engineering judgment indicates that a YIELD sign would provide adequate control. December 2025

metadata.chapter: Chapter 2B. Regulatory Signs, Barricades, And Gates

title: Section 2B.10 Guidance 4 - Yield Control
text:
Section 2B.10 Guidance 4 - Yield Control
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2B. Regulatory Signs, Barricades, And Gates
Page: 78

The YIELD signs should be installed on opposing minor-street approaches (for a four-leg intersection) or on the minor-street approach (for a three-leg intersection). When two intersecting roadways have relatively equal volumes, speeds, and other characteristics, yield control should be installed on the approach that conflicts the most with established pedestrian crossing activity, school walking routes, or bicycle crossing activity.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 2B. Regulatory Signs, Barricades, And Gates

title: Section 2B.10 Standard 5 - Yield Control
text:
Section 2B.10 Standard 5 - Yield Control
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2B. Regulatory Signs, Barricades, And Gates
Page: 78

A YIELD sign shall be used to require road users to yield the right-of-way to other traffic at the entrance to a roundabout. YIELD signs at roundabouts shall be used to control the approach roadways and shall not be used to control the circulatory roadway.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 2B. Regulatory Signs, Barricades, And Gates

title: Section 2B.10 Standard 6 - Yield Control
text:
Section 2B.10 Standard 6 - Yield Control
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2B. Regulatory Signs, Barricades, And Gates
Page: 78

YIELD signs shall not be placed on all of the approaches to an intersection, except at roundabouts.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 2B. Regulatory Signs, Barricades, And Gates

title: Section 2B.11 Guidance 1 - Minor Road Stop Control
text:
Section 2B.11 Guidance 1 - Minor Road Stop Control
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2B. Regulatory Signs, Barricades, And Gates
Page: 78

Stop control on the minor-road approach or approaches to an intersection should be considered when engineering judgment indicates that one or more of the following conditions exist: A. A restricted view exists that requires road users to stop in order to adequately observe conflicting traffic on the through street or highway. B. Crash records indicate that: 1. For a four-leg intersection, there are three or more reported crashes in a 12-month period or six or more reported crashes in a 36-month period. The crashes should be susceptible to correction by installation of minor-road stop control. 2. For a three-leg intersection, there are three or more reported crashes in a 12-month period or five or more reported crashes in a 36-month period. The crashes should be susceptible to correction by installation of minor-road stop control. C. The intersection is of a lower functional classification road with a higher functional classification road. D. Conditions that previously supported the installation of all-way stop control no longer exist.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 2B. Regulatory Signs, Barricades, And Gates

title: Section 2B.11 Guidance 2 - Minor Road Stop Control
text:
Section 2B.11 Guidance 2 - Minor Road Stop Control
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2B. Regulatory Signs, Barricades, And Gates
Page: 78

On low-volume rural roads, a STOP sign should be considered at an intersection where engineering judgment indicates that Item C in Paragraph 1 of this Section is applicable or where the intersection has inadequate sight distance for the operating vehicle speeds.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 2B. Regulatory Signs, Barricades, And Gates

title: Section 2B.12 Support 1 - All-Way Stop Control
text:
Section 2B.12 Support 1 - All-Way Stop Control
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2B. Regulatory Signs, Barricades, And Gates
Page: 78

The provisions in the following sections describe warrants for the recommended engineering study to determine all-way stop control. Warrants are not a substitute for engineering judgment. The fact that a warrant for a particular traffic control device is met is not conclusive justification to install or not install all-way stop control. Because each intersection will have unique characteristics that affect its operational performance or safety, it is the engineering study for a given intersection that is ultimately the basis for a decision to install or not install all-way stop control.

All-Way Stop Control Warrant A: Crash Experience (see Section 2B.13) B. All-Way Stop Control Warrant B: Sight Distance (see Section 2B.14) C. All-Way Stop Control Warrant C: Transition to Signal Control or Transition to Yield Control at a Circular Intersection (see Section 2B.15) D. All-Way Stop Control Warrant D: 8-Hour Volume (Vehicles, Pedestrians, Bicycles) (see Section 2B.16) E. All-Way Stop Control Warrant E: Other Factors (see Section 2B.17)

In general, the maximum speed limits applicable to rural and urban roads are established: A. Statutorily - a maximum speed limit applicable to a particular class of road, such as freeways or city streets, that is established by State law; or B. As speed zones - based on engineering studies.

title: Section 2B.21 Support 2 - Speed Limit Sign (R2-1)
text:
Section 2B.21 Support 2 - Speed Limit Sign (R2-1)
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2B. Regulatory Signs, Barricades, And Gates
Page: 84

State statutory limits might restrict the maximum speed limit that can be established on a particular road, notwithstanding what an engineering study might indicate.

title: Section 2B.21 Support 3 - Speed Limit Sign (R2-1)
text:
Section 2B.21 Support 3 - Speed Limit Sign (R2-1)
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2B. Regulatory Signs, Barricades, And Gates
Page: 84

Agencies with designated authorities to set speed limits, which include States, and sometimes local jurisdictions, can establish non-statutory speed limits or designate reduced speed zones using an engineering study. Setting appropriate speed limits is especially important to ensure safety for all road users in varying types of contexts, particularly on roadways where adjacent land use suggests that trips could be served by varied modes. These situations include urban and suburban non-freeway arterials or rural arterials that serve as main streets in smaller communities, consistent with the context classifications of urban core, urban, suburban, and rural towns found in “A Policy on Geometric Design of Highways and Streets,” 2018 Edition, AASHTO. When setting a speed limit, a range of factors such as land-use context, pedestrian and bicyclist activity, crash history, intersection spacing, driveway density, roadway geometry, roadside conditions, roadway functional classification, traffic volume, and observed speeds can influence the speed limit determined in the engineering study. The engineering study will determine which of the recommended factors will prevail in setting the speed limit.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 2B. Regulatory Signs, Barricades, And Gates

title: Section 2B.21 Support 4 - Speed Limit Sign (R2-1)
text:
Section 2B.21 Support 4 - Speed Limit Sign (R2-1)
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2B. Regulatory Signs, Barricades, And Gates
Page: 84

Jurisdictions can use speed limit setting tools and methods such as expert systems and those consistent with the safe system approach as part of the required engineering study for a non-statutory speed limit. As speed limit setting tools vary, jurisdictions need to be aware of their limitations and advantages, possible variation between the tools and the need to explore gaps or weaknesses of tools, and weigh the output accordingly in consideration of setting speed limits.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 2B. Regulatory Signs, Barricades, And Gates

title: Section 2B.21 Support 5 - Speed Limit Sign (R2-1)
text:
Section 2B.21 Support 5 - Speed Limit Sign (R2-1)
Part: Part 2 Signs

Page: 84

metadata.chapter: Chapter 2B. Regulatory Signs, Barricades, And Gates

title: Section 2B.21 Guidance 7 - Speed Limit Sign (R2-1)
text:
Section 2B.21 Guidance 7 - Speed Limit Sign (R2-1)
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2B. Regulatory Signs, Barricades, And Gates
Page: 84

Among the factors that should be considered when conducting an engineering study for establishing or reevaluating speed limits within speed zones are the following: A. Roadway environment (such as roadside development, number and frequency of driveways and access points, and land use), functional classification, public transit volume and location or frequency of stops, parking practices, and pedestrian and bicycle facilities and activity; B. Roadway characteristics (such as lane widths, shoulder condition, grade, alignment, median type, and sight distance); C. Geographic context (such as an urban district, rural town center, non-urbanized rural area, or suburban area), and multi-modal trip generation; D. Reported crash experience for at least a 12-month period; E. Speed distribution of free-flowing vehicles including the pace, median (50th-percentile), and Rev. 1 85th-percentile speeds; and F. A review of past speed studies to identify any trends in operating speeds.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 2B. Regulatory Signs, Barricades, And Gates

title: Section 2B.21 Guidance 8 - Speed Limit Sign (R2-1)
text:
Section 2B.21 Guidance 8 - Speed Limit Sign (R2-1)
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2B. Regulatory Signs, Barricades, And Gates
Page: 84

When the 85th-percentile speed is appreciably greater than the posted speed limit, and the roadway context does not support setting a higher speed limit, the engineering study should consider whether changes to geometric features, enforcement, and/or other speed-reduction countermeasures might improve compliance with the posted speed limit. A similar approach should be used if the results of past speed studies indicate that the 85th-percentile speed has consistently increased.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 2B. Regulatory Signs, Barricades, And Gates

title: Section 2B.21 Guidance 9 - Speed Limit Sign (R2-1)
text:
Section 2B.21 Guidance 9 - Speed Limit Sign (R2-1)
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2B. Regulatory Signs, Barricades, And Gates
Page: 85

On urban and suburban arterials, and on rural arterials that serve as main streets through developed areas of communities, the 85th-percentile speed should not be used to set speed limits without consideration of all factors described in Paragraph 7 of this Section. December 2025 MUTCD 11th Edition - Revision 1

metadata.chapter: Chapter 2B. Regulatory Signs, Barricades, And Gates

title: Section 2B.21 Guidance 10 - Speed Limit Sign (R2-1)
text:
Section 2B.21 Guidance 10 - Speed Limit Sign (R2-1)
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2B. Regulatory Signs, Barricades, And Gates
Page: 85

On a freeway, expressway, or rural highway (outside urbanized locations or conditions), the speed limit that is posted within a speed zone should be within 5 mph of the 85th-percentile speed of free-flowing motor-vehicle traffic under the following conditions: A. All factors described in Paragraph 7 of this Section have been considered and determined to be non- mitigating, and B. The measures described in Paragraph 8 of this Section have been considered to the extent practicable.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 2B. Regulatory Signs, Barricades, And Gates

title: Section 2B.21 Guidance 11 - Speed Limit Sign (R2-1)
text:
Section 2B.21 Guidance 11 - Speed Limit Sign (R2-1)
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2B. Regulatory Signs, Barricades, And Gates
Page: 85

State and local agencies should conduct engineering studies to reevaluate non-statutory speed limits on segments of their roadways that have undergone significant changes since the last review (such as changes to roadway context, the addition or elimination of parking or driveways, changes in the number of travel lanes, changes in the configuration of bicycle lanes, changes to road geometrics, changes in traffic control signal coordination, or significant changes in traffic volumes).

metadata.chapter: Chapter 2B. Regulatory Signs, Barricades, And Gates

title: Section 2B.21 Guidance 12 - Speed Limit Sign (R2-1)
text:
Section 2B.21 Guidance 12 - Speed Limit Sign (R2-1)
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2B. Regulatory Signs, Barricades, And Gates
Page: 85

Speed studies for signalized intersection approaches should be taken outside the influence area of the traffic control signal, which is generally considered to be approximately 1/2 mile, to avoid obtaining skewed results for the speed distribution. If the signal spacing is less than 1 mile, the speed study should be at approximately the middle of the segment.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 2B. Regulatory Signs, Barricades, And Gates

title: Section 2B.21 Standard 13 - Speed Limit Sign (R2-1)
text:
Section 2B.21 Standard 13 - Speed Limit Sign (R2-1)
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2B. Regulatory Signs, Barricades, And Gates
Page: 85

The Speed Limit (R2-1) sign (see Figure 2B-3) shall display the limit established by law, ordinance, regulation, or as adopted by the authorized agency based on an engineering study. The speed limits displayed shall be in multiples of 5 mph.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 2B. Regulatory Signs, Barricades, And Gates

title: Section 2B.21 Standard 14 - Speed Limit Sign (R2-1)
text:
Section 2B.21 Standard 14 - Speed Limit Sign (R2-1)
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2B. Regulatory Signs, Barricades, And Gates
Page: 85

Speed Limit (R2-1) signs, indicating speed limits for which posting is required by law, shall be located at the points of change from one speed limit to another.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 2B. Regulatory Signs, Barricades, And Gates

title: Section 2B.21 Standard 15 - Speed Limit Sign (R2-1)
text:
Section 2B.21 Standard 15 - Speed Limit Sign (R2-1)
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2B. Regulatory Signs, Barricades, And Gates
Page: 85

At the downstream end of the section to which a particular speed limit applies, a Speed Limit sign showing the next speed limit shall be installed.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 2B. Regulatory Signs, Barricades, And Gates

title: Section 2B.21 Standard 16 - Speed Limit Sign (R2-1)
text:
Section 2B.21 Standard 16 - Speed Limit Sign (R2-1)
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2B. Regulatory Signs, Barricades, And Gates
Page: 85

Speed Limit signs indicating the statutory speed limits shall be installed at entrances to the State and, where appropriate, at jurisdictional boundaries in urban areas.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 2B. Regulatory Signs, Barricades, And Gates

title: Section 2B.21 Guidance 17 - Speed Limit Sign (R2-1)
text:
Section 2B.21 Guidance 17 - Speed Limit Sign (R2-1)
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2B. Regulatory Signs, Barricades, And Gates
Page: 85

Additional Speed Limit signs should be installed beyond interchanges and major intersections and at other locations where it is necessary to remind road users of the speed limit that is applicable.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 2B. Regulatory Signs, Barricades, And Gates

title: Section 2B.21 Support 18 - Speed Limit Sign (R2-1)
text:
Section 2B.21 Support 18 - Speed Limit Sign (R2-1)
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2B. Regulatory Signs, Barricades, And Gates
Page: 85

The 2nd Edition of the “Traffic Control Devices Handbook,” 2013, Institute of Transportation Engineers” contains suggested criteria on the spacing of speed limit signs.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 2B. Regulatory Signs, Barricades, And Gates

title: Section 2B.21 Option 19 - Speed Limit Sign (R2-1)
text:
Section 2B.21 Option 19 - Speed Limit Sign (R2-1)
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2B. Regulatory Signs, Barricades, And Gates
Page: 85

If a jurisdiction has a policy of installing Speed Limit signs in accordance with statutory requirements only on the streets that enter a city, neighborhood, or residential area to indicate the speed limit that is applicable to the entire city, neighborhood, or residential area unless otherwise posted, a CITYWIDE (R2-5aP), NEIGHBORHOOD (R2-5bP), or RESIDENTIAL (R2-5cP) plaque may be mounted above the Speed Limit sign and an UNLESS OTHERWISE POSTED (R2-5P) plaque may be mounted below the Speed Limit sign (see Figure 2B-3).

metadata.chapter: Chapter 2B. Regulatory Signs, Barricades, And Gates

title: Section 2B.22 Standard 1 - Vehicle Speed Limit Plaques (R2-2P Series)
text:
Section 2B.22 Standard 1 - Vehicle Speed Limit Plaques (R2-2P Series)
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2B. Regulatory Signs, Barricades, And Gates
Page: 87

Where a special speed limit applies to certain classes of vehicles, the Truck Speed Limit (R2-2P) plaque, Bus Speed Limit (R2-2aP) plaque, Truck-Bus Speed Limit (R2-2bP) plaque, or Vehicles over X Tons Speed Limit (R2-2cP) plaque (see Figure 2B-3) shall be displayed below the Speed Limit (R2-1) sign, except as provided in Paragraph 2 of this Section.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 2B. Regulatory Signs, Barricades, And Gates

title: Section 2B.22 Option 2 - Vehicle Speed Limit Plaques (R2-2P Series)
text:
Section 2B.22 Option 2 - Vehicle Speed Limit Plaques (R2-2P Series)
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2B. Regulatory Signs, Barricades, And Gates
Page: 87

The legend of a Vehicle Speed Limit (R2-2P series) plaque may be combined in a single sign and displayed below the SPEED LIMIT XX legend, similar to the Combined Maximum and Minimum Speed Limits (R2-4a) sign (see Section 2B.24).

metadata.chapter: Chapter 2B. Regulatory Signs, Barricades, And Gates

title: Section 2B.22 Option 3 - Vehicle Speed Limit Plaques (R2-2P Series)
text:
Section 2B.22 Option 3 - Vehicle Speed Limit Plaques (R2-2P Series)
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2B. Regulatory Signs, Barricades, And Gates
Page: 87

A different vehicle class legend may be substituted on the R2-2P series plaque for other classes of vehicles not included in Paragraph 1 of this Section.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 2B. Regulatory Signs, Barricades, And Gates

title: Section 2B.23 Standard 1 - Night Speed Limit Plaque (R2-3P)
text:
Section 2B.23 Standard 1 - Night Speed Limit Plaque (R2-3P)
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2B. Regulatory Signs, Barricades, And Gates
Page: 87

Where different speed limits are prescribed for day and night, both limits shall be posted.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 2B. Regulatory Signs, Barricades, And Gates

text:
Section 2B.23 Guidance 2 - Night Speed Limit Plaque (R2-3P)
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2B. Regulatory Signs, Barricades, And Gates
Page: 87

A Night Speed Limit (R2-3P) plaque (see Figure 2B-3) should be reversed using a white retroreflective legend and border on a black background.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 2B. Regulatory Signs, Barricades, And Gates

title: Section 2B.23 Option 3 - Night Speed Limit Plaque (R2-3P)
text:
Section 2B.23 Option 3 - Night Speed Limit Plaque (R2-3P)
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2B. Regulatory Signs, Barricades, And Gates
Page: 87

A Night Speed Limit plaque may be combined with or installed below the standard Speed Limit (R2-1) sign.

title: Section 2B.24 Standard 1 - Minimum Speed Limit Plaque (R2-4P) and Combined Maximum and Minimum Speed Limits Sign (R2-4a)
text:
Section 2B.24 Standard 1 - Minimum Speed Limit Plaque (R2-4P) and Combined Maximum and Minimum Speed Limits Sign (R2-4a)
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2B. Regulatory Signs, Barricades, And Gates
Page: 87

A Minimum Speed Limit (R2-4P) plaque (see Figure 2B-3) shall be displayed only in combination with a Speed Limit sign. Where used, the R2-4P plaque shall be mounted below a Speed Limit (R2-1) sign.

metadata.section_title: Minimum Speed Limit Plaque (R2-4P) and Combined Maximum and Minimum Speed Limits Sign (R2-4a)
metadata.chapter: Chapter 2B. Regulatory Signs, Barricades, And Gates

title: Section 2B.24 Option 2 - Minimum Speed Limit Plaque (R2-4P) and Combined Maximum and Minimum Speed Limits Sign (R2-4a)
text:
Section 2B.24 Option 2 - Minimum Speed Limit Plaque (R2-4P) and Combined Maximum and Minimum Speed Limits Sign (R2-4a)
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2B. Regulatory Signs, Barricades, And Gates
Page: 87

Where engineering judgment determines that slow speeds on a highway might impede the normal and reasonable movement of traffic, the Minimum Speed Limit (R2-4P) plaque may be installed below a Speed Limit (R2-1) sign to indicate the minimum legal speed. In lieu of a sign assembly with the R2-1 sign and R2-4P plaque, the Combined Maximum and Minimum Speed Limits (R2-4a) sign may be used.

metadata.section_title: Minimum Speed Limit Plaque (R2-4P) and Combined Maximum and Minimum Speed Limits Sign (R2-4a)

title: Section 2B.25 Standard 1 - Higher Fines Signs and Plaque (R2-6P, R2-10, and R2-11)
text:
Section 2B.25 Standard 1 - Higher Fines Signs and Plaque (R2-6P, R2-10, and R2-11)
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2B. Regulatory Signs, Barricades, And Gates
Page: 87

Except as provided in Paragraph 3 of this Section, if increased fines are imposed for traffic violations within a designated zone of a roadway, a BEGIN HIGHER FINES ZONE (R2-10) sign (see Figure 2B-3) or a FINES HIGHER (R2-6P) plaque (see Figure 2B-3) shall be used to provide notice to road users.

metadata.section_title: Higher Fines Signs and Plaque (R2-6P, R2-10, and R2-11)
metadata.chapter: Chapter 2B. Regulatory Signs, Barricades, And Gates

text:
Section 2B.25 Standard 2 - Higher Fines Signs and Plaque (R2-6P, R2-10, and R2-11)
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2B. Regulatory Signs, Barricades, And Gates
Page: 87

If an R2-10 sign or an R2-6P plaque is posted to provide notice of increased fines for traffic violations, an END HIGHER FINES ZONE (R2-11) sign (see Figure 2B-3) shall be installed at the downstream end of the zone to provide notice to road users of the termination of the increased fines zone.

metadata.section_title: Higher Fines Signs and Plaque (R2-6P, R2-10, and R2-11)
metadata.chapter: Chapter 2B. Regulatory Signs, Barricades, And Gates

text:
Section 2B.25 Option 3 - Higher Fines Signs and Plaque (R2-6P, R2-10, and R2-11)
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2B. Regulatory Signs, Barricades, And Gates
Page: 87

The BEGIN HIGHER FINES ZONE (R2-10) sign or FINES HIGHER (R2-6P) plaque may be omitted where the higher fines zone is established by statute.

metadata.section_title: Higher Fines Signs and Plaque (R2-6P, R2-10, and R2-11)
metadata.chapter: Chapter 2B. Regulatory Signs, Barricades, And Gates

title: Section 2B.25 Guidance 4 - Higher Fines Signs and Plaque (R2-6P, R2-10, and R2-11)
text:
Section 2B.25 Guidance 4 - Higher Fines Signs and Plaque (R2-6P, R2-10, and R2-11)
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2B. Regulatory Signs, Barricades, And Gates
Page: 88

The BEGIN HIGHER FINES ZONE sign or FINES HIGHER plaque should be located at the beginning of the temporary traffic control zone, school zone, or other applicable designated zone and just beyond any interchanges, major intersections, or other major traffic generators.

metadata.section_title: Higher Fines Signs and Plaque (R2-6P, R2-10, and R2-11)
metadata.chapter: Chapter 2B. Regulatory Signs, Barricades, And Gates

title: Section 2B.25 Guidance 5 - Higher Fines Signs and Plaque (R2-6P, R2-10, and R2-11)
text:
Section 2B.25 Guidance 5 - Higher Fines Signs and Plaque (R2-6P, R2-10, and R2-11)
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2B. Regulatory Signs, Barricades, And Gates
Page: 88

Agencies should limit the use of the Higher Fines signs and plaque to locations where work is actually underway, or to locations where the roadway, shoulder, or other conditions, including the presence of a school zone and/or a reduced school speed limit zone, require a speed reduction or extra caution on the part of the road user.

metadata.section_title: Higher Fines Signs and Plaque (R2-6P, R2-10, and R2-11)
metadata.chapter: Chapter 2B. Regulatory Signs, Barricades, And Gates

text:
Section 2B.25 Standard 6 - Higher Fines Signs and Plaque (R2-6P, R2-10, and R2-11)
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2B. Regulatory Signs, Barricades, And Gates
Page: 88

The Higher Fines signs and plaque shall have a black legend and border on a white rectangular background. All supplemental plaques mounted below the Higher Fines signs and plaque shall have a black legend and border on a white rectangular background.

metadata.section_title: Higher Fines Signs and Plaque (R2-6P, R2-10, and R2-11)
metadata.chapter: Chapter 2B. Regulatory Signs, Barricades, And Gates

Section 2B.25 Standard 7 - Higher Fines Signs and Plaque (R2-6P, R2-10, and R2-11)
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2B. Regulatory Signs, Barricades, And Gates
Page: 88

The FINES HIGHER plaque shall be mounted below an applicable regulatory or warning sign in a temporary traffic control zone (see Section 6G.08), a school zone (see Section 7B.06), or other applicable designated zone.

metadata.section_title: Higher Fines Signs and Plaque (R2-6P, R2-10, and R2-11)
metadata.chapter: Chapter 2B. Regulatory Signs, Barricades, And Gates

Section 2B.25 Option 8 - Higher Fines Signs and Plaque (R2-6P, R2-10, and R2-11)

Page: 88

Alternate legends such as BEGIN (or END) DOUBLE FINES ZONE may also be used for the R2-10 and R2-11 signs.

metadata.section_title: Higher Fines Signs and Plaque (R2-6P, R2-10, and R2-11)
metadata.chapter: Chapter 2B. Regulatory Signs, Barricades, And Gates

Section 2B.25 Option 9 - Higher Fines Signs and Plaque (R2-6P, R2-10, and R2-11)

Page: 88

The legend FINES HIGHER on the R2-6P plaque may be replaced by FINES DOUBLE (R2-6aP), $XX FINE (R2-6bP), or another legend appropriate to the specific regulation (see Figure 2B-3).

metadata.section_title: Higher Fines Signs and Plaque (R2-6P, R2-10, and R2-11)
metadata.chapter: Chapter 2B. Regulatory Signs, Barricades, And Gates

The following may be mounted below an R2-10 sign or R2-6P plaque: A. A supplemental plaque specifying the times that the higher fines are in effect (similar to the S4-1P plaque shown in Figure 7B-1), B. A supplemental plaque WHEN CHILDREN (WORKERS) ARE PRESENT, or C. A supplemental plaque WHEN FLASHING (similar to the S4-4P plaque shown in Figure 7B-1) if used in conjunction with a Speed Limit Sign Beacon (see Section 4S.04). MOVEMENT AND LANE CONTROL SIGNS AND PLAQUES

title: Section 2B.26 Standard 1 - Movement Prohibition Signs (R3-1 through R3-4, R3-18, and R3-27)

Section 2B.26 Standard 1 - Movement Prohibition Signs (R3-1 through R3-4, R3-18, and R3-27)

Chapter: Chapter 2B. Regulatory Signs, Barricades, And Gates
Page: 89

Movement Prohibition signs (see Figure 2B-4) shall be installed where specific movements are prohibited at an intersection approach except as provided in Paragraphs 13 and 17 of this Section.

metadata.section_title: Movement Prohibition Signs (R3-1 through R3-4, R3-18, and R3-27)
metadata.chapter: Chapter 2B. Regulatory Signs, Barricades, And Gates

text:
Section 2B.26 Guidance 2 - Movement Prohibition Signs (R3-1 through R3-4, R3-18, and R3-27)
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2B. Regulatory Signs, Barricades, And Gates
Page: 89

Movement Prohibition signs should only be used to prohibit a turn or through movement from an entire approach and should not be used to designate movements that are required or permitted from a specific lane or lanes on a multi-lane approach.

metadata.section_title: Movement Prohibition Signs (R3-1 through R3-4, R3-18, and R3-27)
metadata.chapter: Chapter 2B. Regulatory Signs, Barricades, And Gates

text:
Section 2B.26 Guidance 3 - Movement Prohibition Signs (R3-1 through R3-4, R3-18, and R3-27)
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2B. Regulatory Signs, Barricades, And Gates
Page: 89

Movement Prohibition signs should be placed where they will be most easily seen by road users who might be intending to make the movement.

metadata.section_title: Movement Prohibition Signs (R3-1 through R3-4, R3-18, and R3-27)
metadata.chapter: Chapter 2B. Regulatory Signs, Barricades, And Gates

Section 2B.26 Guidance 4 - Movement Prohibition Signs (R3-1 through R3-4, R3-18, and R3-27)
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2B. Regulatory Signs, Barricades, And Gates
Page: 89

If a No Right Turn (R3-1) sign (see Figure 2B-4) is used, at least one should be placed either over the roadway or at a right-hand corner of the intersection.

metadata.section_title: Movement Prohibition Signs (R3-1 through R3-4, R3-18, and R3-27)
metadata.chapter: Chapter 2B. Regulatory Signs, Barricades, And Gates

text:
Section 2B.26 Guidance 5 - Movement Prohibition Signs (R3-1 through R3-4, R3-18, and R3-27)
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2B. Regulatory Signs, Barricades, And Gates
Page: 89

If a No Left Turn (R3-2) sign (see Figure 2B-4) is used, at least one should be placed over the roadway, at the far left corner of the intersection, on a median, or in conjunction with the STOP sign or YIELD sign located on the near right corner.

metadata.section_title: Movement Prohibition Signs (R3-1 through R3-4, R3-18, and R3-27)
metadata.chapter: Chapter 2B. Regulatory Signs, Barricades, And Gates

title: Section 2B.26 Guidance 6 - Movement Prohibition Signs (R3-1 through R3-4, R3-18, and R3-27)
text:
Section 2B.26 Guidance 6 - Movement Prohibition Signs (R3-1 through R3-4, R3-18, and R3-27)
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2B. Regulatory Signs, Barricades, And Gates
Page: 89

Except as provided in Item C in Paragraph 11 of this Section for signalized locations, if a NO TURNS (R3-3) sign (see Figure 2B-4) is used, two signs should be used, one at a location specified for a No Right Turn sign and one at a location specified for a No Left Turn sign.

metadata.section_title: Movement Prohibition Signs (R3-1 through R3-4, R3-18, and R3-27)
metadata.chapter: Chapter 2B. Regulatory Signs, Barricades, And Gates

Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2B. Regulatory Signs, Barricades, And Gates
Page: 89

If a No U-Turn (R3-4) sign (see Figure 2B-4) or a combination No U or Left Turn (R3-18) sign (see Figure 2B-4) is used, at least one should be used at a location specified for a No Left Turn sign.

metadata.section_title: Movement Prohibition Signs (R3-1 through R3-4, R3-18, and R3-27)
metadata.chapter: Chapter 2B. Regulatory Signs, Barricades, And Gates

text:
Section 2B.26 Guidance 8 - Movement Prohibition Signs (R3-1 through R3-4, R3-18, and R3-27)
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2B. Regulatory Signs, Barricades, And Gates
Page: 89

If both left turns and U-turns are prohibited, the combination No U or Left Turn (R3-18) sign should be used instead of separate R3-2 and R3-4 signs.

Section 2B.26 Support 9 - Movement Prohibition Signs (R3-1 through R3-4, R3-18, and R3-27)
Part: Part 2 Signs

Sections 2B.27 through 2B.30 contain information regarding lane control signs that indicate the required or permitted movements from individual lanes.

Section 2B.26 Guidance 10 - Movement Prohibition Signs (R3-1 through R3-4, R3-18, and R3-27)
