text:
Section 2N.02 Standard 6 - Design and Use of Emergency Management Signs
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2N. Emergency Management Signs
Page: 532

Except as provided in Section 2A.07, the sizes for Emergency Management signs shall be as shown in Table 2N-1.

metadata.section_title: Design and Use of Emergency Management Signs

title: Section 2N.03 Standard 1 - Evacuation Route Signs (EM1 Series)
text:
Section 2N.03 Standard 1 - Evacuation Route Signs (EM1 Series)
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2N. Emergency Management Signs
Page: 532

An Advance Turn Arrow (M5 series) or Directional Arrow (M6 series) auxiliary plaque (see Figure 2D-6) shall be installed below the EM1-2 sign. The Advance Turn Arrow or Directional Arrow auxiliary plaque shall have a white arrow and border on a blue background when used with an EM1-2 sign.

title: Section 2N.03 Option 2 - Evacuation Route Signs (EM1 Series)
text:
Section 2N.03 Option 2 - Evacuation Route Signs (EM1 Series)
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2N. Emergency Management Signs
Page: 532

Where different evacuation conditions use different evacuation routes in the same area, the word HURRICANE, or a word that describes some other type of evacuation route, may be added above the EVACUATION ROUTE legend within the blue circular symbol on the EM1-1a sign.

title: Section 2N.03 Standard 3 - Evacuation Route Signs (EM1 Series)
text:
Section 2N.03 Standard 3 - Evacuation Route Signs (EM1 Series)
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2N. Emergency Management Signs
Page: 532

The EM1-1 series signs shall include a white directional arrow. The arrow designs on the EM1-1 series signs shall include a straight, vertical arrow pointing upward, a straight horizontal arrow pointing to the left or right, or a bent arrow pointing to the left or right for advance warning of a turn.

title: Section 2N.03 Guidance 4 - Evacuation Route Signs (EM1 Series)
text:
Section 2N.03 Guidance 4 - Evacuation Route Signs (EM1 Series)
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2N. Emergency Management Signs
Page: 532

If used, the Evacuation Route sign, with the appropriate arrow, should be installed 150 to 300 feet in advance of, and at, any turn in an approved evacuation route. The sign should also be installed elsewhere for straight- ahead confirmation where needed.

title: Section 2N.03 Standard 5 - Evacuation Route Signs (EM1 Series)
text:
Section 2N.03 Standard 5 - Evacuation Route Signs (EM1 Series)
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2N. Emergency Management Signs
Page: 533

If used in urban areas, the Evacuation Route sign shall be mounted at the right-hand side of the roadway, not less than 7 feet above the top of the curb, and at least 1 foot back from the face of the curb. If used in rural areas, the Evacuation Route sign shall be mounted at the right-hand side of the roadway, not less than 7 feet above the near edge of the pavement and not less than 6 feet or more than 10 feet to the right of the right-hand roadway edge. Table 2N-1. Emergency Management Sign Sizes Sign or Plaque Sign Designation Section Minimum Size Evacuation Route EM1-1, EM-1a, EM1-2 2N.03 24 x 24* Area Closed EM2-1 2N.04 30 x 24 Traffic Control Point EM2-2 2N.05 30 x 24 Maintain Top Safe Speed EM2-3 2N.06 24 x 30 Permit Required EM2-4 2N.07 24 x 30 Emergency Aid Center EM3-1, EM3-1a, EM3-1b, EM3-1c 2N.08 30 x 24 Shelter Directional EM4-1, EM4-1a, EM4-1b, EM4-1c 2N.09 30 x 24 * A minimum size of 18 x 18 may be used on low-volume roadways or roadways with speeds of 25 mph or less Notes: 1. Larger signs may be used when appropriate 2. Dimensions are shown as width x height, in inches December 2025

title: Section 2N.03 Standard 6 - Evacuation Route Signs (EM1 Series)
text:
Section 2N.03 Standard 6 - Evacuation Route Signs (EM1 Series)
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2N. Emergency Management Signs
Page: 533

Evacuation Route signs shall not be placed where they will conflict with other signs. Where a conflict in placement would occur between the Evacuation Route sign and a standard regulatory sign, the regulatory sign shall take precedence.

title: Section 2N.03 Option 7 - Evacuation Route Signs (EM1 Series)
text:
Section 2N.03 Option 7 - Evacuation Route Signs (EM1 Series)
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2N. Emergency Management Signs
Page: 533

In case of a conflict with guide or warning signs, the Evacuation Route sign may take precedence.

title: Section 2N.03 Guidance 8 - Evacuation Route Signs (EM1 Series)
text:
Section 2N.03 Guidance 8 - Evacuation Route Signs (EM1 Series)
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2N. Emergency Management Signs
Page: 533

Placement of Evacuation Route signs should be made under the supervision of the officials having jurisdiction over the placement of other traffic signs. Coordination with Emergency Management authorities and agreement between contiguous political entities should occur to assure continuity of routes.

title: Section 2N.03 Guidance 9 - Evacuation Route Signs (EM1 Series)
text:
Section 2N.03 Guidance 9 - Evacuation Route Signs (EM1 Series)
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2N. Emergency Management Signs
Page: 533

Use of the specific Evacuation Route (EM1-1a and EM1-2) signs should be limited to areas where different evacuation conditions use different evacuation routes.

title: Section 2N.04 Guidance 1 - AREA CLOSED Sign (EM2-1)
text:
Section 2N.04 Guidance 1 - AREA CLOSED Sign (EM2-1)
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2N. Emergency Management Signs
Page: 533

The AREA CLOSED (EM2-1) sign (see Figure 2N-1) should be used to close a roadway in order to prohibit traffic from entering the area. It should be installed on the shoulder as near as practical to the right-hand edge of the roadway, or preferably, on a portable mounting or barricade partly or entirely in the roadway.

title: Section 2N.04 Guidance 2 - AREA CLOSED Sign (EM2-1)
text:
Section 2N.04 Guidance 2 - AREA CLOSED Sign (EM2-1)
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2N. Emergency Management Signs
Page: 533

For best visibility, particularly at night, the sign height should not exceed 4 feet measured vertically from the pavement to the bottom of the sign. Unless adequate advance warning signs are used, it should not be placed to create a complete and unavoidable blocked route. Where feasible, the sign should be located at an intersection that provides a detour route.

title: Section 2N.05 Guidance 1 - TRAFFIC CONTROL POINT Sign (EM2-2)
text:
Section 2N.05 Guidance 1 - TRAFFIC CONTROL POINT Sign (EM2-2)
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2N. Emergency Management Signs
Page: 533

The TRAFFIC CONTROL POINT (EM2-2) sign (see Figure 2N-1) should be used to designate a location where an official traffic control point has been set up to impose such controls as are necessary to limit congestion, expedite emergency traffic, exclude unauthorized vehicles, or protect the public.

title: Section 2N.05 Guidance 2 - TRAFFIC CONTROL POINT Sign (EM2-2)
text:
Section 2N.05 Guidance 2 - TRAFFIC CONTROL POINT Sign (EM2-2)
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2N. Emergency Management Signs
Page: 533

The sign should be installed in the same manner as the AREA CLOSED sign (see Section 2N.04), and at the point where traffic must stop to be checked.

title: Section 2N.05 Guidance 3 - TRAFFIC CONTROL POINT Sign (EM2-2)
text:
Section 2N.05 Guidance 3 - TRAFFIC CONTROL POINT Sign (EM2-2)
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2N. Emergency Management Signs
Page: 533

A STOP (R1-1) sign (see Section 2B.04) should be used in conjunction with the TRAFFIC CONTROL POINT sign.

title: Section 2N.05 Guidance 4 - TRAFFIC CONTROL POINT Sign (EM2-2)
text:
Section 2N.05 Guidance 4 - TRAFFIC CONTROL POINT Sign (EM2-2)
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2N. Emergency Management Signs
Page: 533

The TRAFFIC CONTROL POINT sign should be mounted directly below the STOP sign.

title: Section 2N.06 Option 1 - MAINTAIN TOP SAFE SPEED Sign (EM2-3)
text:
Section 2N.06 Option 1 - MAINTAIN TOP SAFE SPEED Sign (EM2-3)
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2N. Emergency Management Signs
Page: 533

The MAINTAIN TOP SAFE SPEED (EM2-3) sign (see Figure 2N-1) may be used on highways where conditions are such that it is prudent to evacuate or traverse an area as quickly as possible.

title: Section 2N.06 Option 2 - MAINTAIN TOP SAFE SPEED Sign (EM2-3)
text:
Section 2N.06 Option 2 - MAINTAIN TOP SAFE SPEED Sign (EM2-3)
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2N. Emergency Management Signs
Page: 533

Where an existing Speed Limit (R2-1) sign is in a suitable location, the MAINTAIN TOP SAFE SPEED sign may be mounted directly over the face of the speed limit sign that it supersedes.

title: Section 2N.06 Support 3 - MAINTAIN TOP SAFE SPEED Sign (EM2-3)
text:
Section 2N.06 Support 3 - MAINTAIN TOP SAFE SPEED Sign (EM2-3)
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2N. Emergency Management Signs
Page: 533

Since any speed zoning would be impractical under such emergency conditions, no minimum speed limit can be prescribed by the MAINTAIN TOP SAFE SPEED sign in numerical terms. Where traffic is supervised by a traffic control point, official instructions will usually be given verbally, and the sign will serve as an occasional reminder of the urgent need for maintaining the proper speed.

title: Section 2N.06 Guidance 4 - MAINTAIN TOP SAFE SPEED Sign (EM2-3)
text:
Section 2N.06 Guidance 4 - MAINTAIN TOP SAFE SPEED Sign (EM2-3)
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2N. Emergency Management Signs
Page: 533

The sign should be installed as needed, in the same manner as other standard speed signs.

title: Section 2N.06 Standard 5 - MAINTAIN TOP SAFE SPEED Sign (EM2-3)
text:
Section 2N.06 Standard 5 - MAINTAIN TOP SAFE SPEED Sign (EM2-3)
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2N. Emergency Management Signs
Page: 534

If used in rural areas, the MAINTAIN TOP SAFE SPEED sign shall be mounted on the right-hand side of the road at a horizontal distance of not less than 6 feet or more than 10 feet from the roadway edge, and at a minimum height, measured vertically from the bottom of the sign to the elevation of the near edge of the traveled way, of 5 feet. If used in urban areas, the minimum height, measured vertically from the bottom of the sign to the top of the curb, or in the absence of curb, measured vertically from the bottom of the sign to the elevation of the near edge of the traveled way, shall be 7 feet, and the nearest edge of the sign shall be not less than 1 foot back from the face of the curb.

title: Section 2N.07 Support 1 - Permit Required Sign (EM2-4)
text:
Section 2N.07 Support 1 - Permit Required Sign (EM2-4)
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2N. Emergency Management Signs
Page: 534

The intent of the Permit Required (EM2-4) sign (see Figure 2N-1) is to notify road users of the presence of the traffic control point so that those who do not have priority permits issued by designated authorities can take another route, or turn back, without making a needless trip and without adding to the screening load at the post. Local traffic, without permits, can proceed as far as the traffic control post.

title: Section 2N.07 Standard 2 - Permit Required Sign (EM2-4)
text:
Section 2N.07 Standard 2 - Permit Required Sign (EM2-4)
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2N. Emergency Management Signs
Page: 534

If used, the Permit Required (EM2-4) sign shall be used at an intersection that is an entrance to a route on which a traffic control point is located.

title: Section 2N.07 Standard 3 - Permit Required Sign (EM2-4)
text:
Section 2N.07 Standard 3 - Permit Required Sign (EM2-4)
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2N. Emergency Management Signs
Page: 534

If used, the EM2-4 sign shall be installed in a manner similar to that of the MAINTAIN TOP SAFE SPEED sign (see Section 2N.06).

title: Section 2N.08 Standard 1 - Emergency Aid Center Signs (EM3-1 Series)
text:
Section 2N.08 Standard 1 - Emergency Aid Center Signs (EM3-1 Series)
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2N. Emergency Management Signs
Page: 534

In the event of emergency, State and local authorities shall establish various centers for civilian relief, communication, medical service, and similar purposes. To guide the public to such centers a series of directional signs shall be used.

title: Section 2N.08 Standard 2 - Emergency Aid Center Signs (EM3-1 Series)
text:
Section 2N.08 Standard 2 - Emergency Aid Center Signs (EM3-1 Series)
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2N. Emergency Management Signs
Page: 534

Emergency Aid Center (EM3-1 series) signs (see Figure 2N-1) shall display the designation of the center and an arrow indicating the direction to the center. They shall be installed as needed, at intersections and elsewhere, on the right-hand side of the roadway, in urban areas at a minimum height, measured vertically from the bottom of the sign to the top of the curb, or in the absence of curb, measured vertically from the bottom of the sign to the elevation of the near edge of the traveled way, of 7 feet, and not less than 1 foot back from the face of the curb, and in rural areas at a minimum height, measured vertically from the bottom of the sign to the elevation of the near edge of the traveled way, of 5 feet, and at a horizontal distance of not less than 6 feet or more than 10 feet from the roadway edge.

title: Section 2N.08 Standard 3 - Emergency Aid Center Signs (EM3-1 Series)
text:
Section 2N.08 Standard 3 - Emergency Aid Center Signs (EM3-1 Series)
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2N. Emergency Management Signs
Page: 534

Emergency Aid Center signs shall display one of the following legends, as appropriate, or others designating similar emergency facilities: A. MEDICAL CENTER (EM3-1), B. WELFARE CENTER (EM3-1a), C. REGISTRATION CENTER (EM3-1b), or D. DECONTAMINATION CENTER (EM3-1c).

title: Section 2N.08 Standard 4 - Emergency Aid Center Signs (EM3-1 Series)
text:
Section 2N.08 Standard 4 - Emergency Aid Center Signs (EM3-1 Series)
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2N. Emergency Management Signs
Page: 534

The Emergency Aid Center sign shall be a horizontally-oriented rectangle. Except as provided in Paragraph 5 of this Section, the Emergency Aid Center signs shall have a black legend and border on a white background.

title: Section 2N.08 Option 5 - Emergency Aid Center Signs (EM3-1 Series)
text:
Section 2N.08 Option 5 - Emergency Aid Center Signs (EM3-1 Series)
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2N. Emergency Management Signs
Page: 534

When Emergency Aid Center signs are used in an incident situation, such as during the aftermath of a nuclear or biological attack, the background color may be fluorescent pink (see Chapter 6O).

title: Section 2N.09 Standard 1 - Shelter Directional Signs (EM4-1 Series)
text:
Section 2N.09 Standard 1 - Shelter Directional Signs (EM4-1 Series)
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2N. Emergency Management Signs
Page: 534

Shelter Directional (EM4-1 series) signs (see Figure 2N-1) shall be used to direct the public to selected shelters that have been licensed and marked for emergency use.

title: Section 2N.09 Standard 2 - Shelter Directional Signs (EM4-1 Series)
text:
Section 2N.09 Standard 2 - Shelter Directional Signs (EM4-1 Series)
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2N. Emergency Management Signs
Page: 534

The installation of Shelter Directional signs shall comply with established signing standards. Where used, the signs shall not be installed in competition with other necessary highway regulatory, guide, and warning signs.

title: Section 2N.09 Standard 3 - Shelter Directional Signs (EM4-1 Series)
text:
Section 2N.09 Standard 3 - Shelter Directional Signs (EM4-1 Series)
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2N. Emergency Management Signs
Page: 534

The Shelter Directional sign shall be a horizontally-oriented rectangle. Except as provided in Paragraph 4 of this Section, the Shelter Directional signs shall have a black legend and border on a white background.

title: Section 2N.09 Option 4 - Shelter Directional Signs (EM4-1 Series)
text:
Section 2N.09 Option 4 - Shelter Directional Signs (EM4-1 Series)
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2N. Emergency Management Signs
Page: 534

When Shelter Directional signs are used in an incident situation, such as during the aftermath of a nuclear or biological attack, the background color may be fluorescent pink (see Chapter 6O).

title: Section 2N.09 Option 5 - Shelter Directional Signs (EM4-1 Series)
text:
Section 2N.09 Option 5 - Shelter Directional Signs (EM4-1 Series)
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2N. Emergency Management Signs
Page: 534

The distance to the shelter may be omitted from the sign when appropriate.

title: Section 2N.09 Option 6 - Shelter Directional Signs (EM4-1 Series)
text:
Section 2N.09 Option 6 - Shelter Directional Signs (EM4-1 Series)
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2N. Emergency Management Signs
Page: 535

Shelter Directional signs may display one of the following legends, or others designating similar emergency facilities: A. EMERGENCY (EM4-1), B. HURRICANE (EM4-1a), C. FALLOUT (EM4-1b), or D. CHEMICAL (EM4-1c).

title: Section 2N.09 Option 7 - Shelter Directional Signs (EM4-1 Series)
text:
Section 2N.09 Option 7 - Shelter Directional Signs (EM4-1 Series)
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2N. Emergency Management Signs
Page: 535

If appropriate, the name of the facility may be used.

title: Section 2N.09 Option 8 - Shelter Directional Signs (EM4-1 Series)
text:
Section 2N.09 Option 8 - Shelter Directional Signs (EM4-1 Series)
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2N. Emergency Management Signs
Page: 535

The Shelter Directional signs may be installed on the Interstate Highway System or any other major highway system when it has been determined that a need exists for such signs as part of a State or local shelter plan.

title: Section 2N.09 Option 9 - Shelter Directional Signs (EM4-1 Series)
text:
Section 2N.09 Option 9 - Shelter Directional Signs (EM4-1 Series)
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2N. Emergency Management Signs
Page: 535

The Shelter Directional signs may be used to identify different routes to a shelter to provide for rapid movement of large numbers of persons.

title: Section 2N.09 Guidance 10 - Shelter Directional Signs (EM4-1 Series)
text:
Section 2N.09 Guidance 10 - Shelter Directional Signs (EM4-1 Series)
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2N. Emergency Management Signs
Page: 535

The Shelter Directional sign should be used sparingly and only in conjunction with approved plans of State and local authorities.

title: Section 2N.09 Guidance 11 - Shelter Directional Signs (EM4-1 Series)
text:
Section 2N.09 Guidance 11 - Shelter Directional Signs (EM4-1 Series)
Part: Part 2 Signs
Chapter: Chapter 2N. Emergency Management Signs
Page: 537

The Shelter Directional sign should not be posted more than 5 miles from a shelter. (This page intentionally left blank)

title: Section 3A.01 Support 1 - Standardization of Application
text:
Section 3A.01 Support 1 - Standardization of Application
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3A. General
Page: 537

Markings are used to supplement other traffic control devices such as signs, signals, and other markings. In other instances, markings are used alone to effectively convey regulations, warnings, or guidance in ways not obtainable by the use of other devices.

title: Section 3A.01 Support 2 - Standardization of Application
text:
Section 3A.01 Support 2 - Standardization of Application
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3A. General
Page: 537

Markings can take many forms including road surface markings, curb markings, delineators, colored pavements, and channelizing devices.

title: Section 3A.01 Standard 3 - Standardization of Application
text:
Section 3A.01 Standard 3 - Standardization of Application
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3A. General
Page: 537

Each standard marking shall be used only to convey the meaning prescribed for that marking in this Manual, including when used for applications not described in this Manual.

title: Section 3A.01 Standard 4 - Standardization of Application
text:
Section 3A.01 Standard 4 - Standardization of Application
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3A. General
Page: 537

Except as provided in Chapter 3H, markings that must be visible at night shall be retroreflective unless the markings are adequately visible under street or highway lighting. All markings on Interstate highways shall be retroreflective.

title: Section 3A.01 Standard 5 - Standardization of Application
text:
Section 3A.01 Standard 5 - Standardization of Application
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3A. General
Page: 537

Markings that are no longer applicable for roadway conditions or restrictions and that might cause confusion for the road user shall be removed or obliterated to be unidentifiable as a marking as soon as practicable.

title: Section 3A.01 Option 6 - Standardization of Application
text:
Section 3A.01 Option 6 - Standardization of Application
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3A. General
Page: 537

Until they can be removed or obliterated, markings that are no longer applicable for roadway conditions or restrictions may be temporarily masked with non-reflective, preformed tape that is approximately the same color as the pavement surface.

title: Section 3A.02 Guidance 1 - Materials
text:
Section 3A.02 Guidance 1 - Materials
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3A. General
Page: 537

The materials used for markings should provide the specified color throughout their useful life.

title: Section 3A.02 Guidance 2 - Materials
text:
Section 3A.02 Guidance 2 - Materials
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3A. General
Page: 537

Consideration should be given to selecting pavement marking materials that will minimize tripping or loss of traction for road users, including pedestrians, bicyclists, and motorcyclists.

title: Section 3A.02 Option 3 - Materials
text:
Section 3A.02 Option 3 - Materials
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3A. General
Page: 537

Marking systems that consist of clumps or droplets of material with visible open spaces of bare pavement between the material droplets, which can function in a manner that is similar to the marking systems that completely cover the pavement surface, may be used as pavement markings if they meet the other pavement marking requirements of the highway agency.

title: Section 3A.04 Standard 1 - Functions, Widths, and Patterns of Longitudinal Pavement Markings
text:
Section 3A.04 Standard 1 - Functions, Widths, and Patterns of Longitudinal Pavement Markings
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3A. General
Page: 538

The general functions of longitudinal lines shall be as follows: A. A double line indicates maximum or special restrictions. B. A solid line discourages or prohibits crossing (depending on the specific application). C. A broken line indicates a permissive condition. D. A dotted lane line provides warning of a downstream change in lane function. E. A dotted line used as a lane line or edge line extension guides vehicles through an intersection, a taper area, or an interchange ramp area.

metadata.section_title: Functions, Widths, and Patterns of Longitudinal Pavement Markings

title: Section 3A.04 Standard 2 - Functions, Widths, and Patterns of Longitudinal Pavement Markings
text:
Section 3A.04 Standard 2 - Functions, Widths, and Patterns of Longitudinal Pavement Markings
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3A. General
Page: 538

The widths and patterns of longitudinal lines shall be as follows: A. Normal line-4 to 6 inches wide. B. Wide line-at least twice the width of a normal line. C. Double line-two parallel lines separated by a discernible space. The pavement surface shall be visible between the lines in the same way that it is visible outside the lines, except where contrast markings are used in combination with the double line (see Section 3A.03). D. Broken line-normal width line segments separated by gaps. E. Dotted line-noticeably shorter line segments separated by shorter gaps than used for a broken line. The width of a dotted line extension shall be at least the same as the width of the line it extends.

metadata.section_title: Functions, Widths, and Patterns of Longitudinal Pavement Markings

title: Section 3A.04 Guidance 3 - Functions, Widths, and Patterns of Longitudinal Pavement Markings
text:
Section 3A.04 Guidance 3 - Functions, Widths, and Patterns of Longitudinal Pavement Markings
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3A. General
Page: 538

To be recognized as a double line rather than two separate, disassociated single lines, the discernible space separating the parallel lines of a double line should not exceed two times the line width of a single line.

metadata.section_title: Functions, Widths, and Patterns of Longitudinal Pavement Markings

title: Section 3A.04 Support 4 - Functions, Widths, and Patterns of Longitudinal Pavement Markings
text:
Section 3A.04 Support 4 - Functions, Widths, and Patterns of Longitudinal Pavement Markings
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3A. General
Page: 538

The width of the line indicates the degree of emphasis.

metadata.section_title: Functions, Widths, and Patterns of Longitudinal Pavement Markings

title: Section 3A.04 Support 5 - Functions, Widths, and Patterns of Longitudinal Pavement Markings
text:
Section 3A.04 Support 5 - Functions, Widths, and Patterns of Longitudinal Pavement Markings
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3A. General
Page: 538

Increasing edge line width from 4 inches to 6 inches has been shown to be a beneficial countermeasure to enhance safety at locations with a history of run-off-the-road crashes (see Section 3B.09). Wider normal lines with a 6-inch width instead of the minimum 4-inch width can be beneficial to both human drivers and driving automation systems (see Section 5B.02).

metadata.section_title: Functions, Widths, and Patterns of Longitudinal Pavement Markings

title: Section 3A.04 Guidance 6 - Functions, Widths, and Patterns of Longitudinal Pavement Markings
text:
Section 3A.04 Guidance 6 - Functions, Widths, and Patterns of Longitudinal Pavement Markings
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3A. General
Page: 538

Broken lines should consist of 10-foot line segments and 30-foot gaps, or dimensions in a similar ratio of line segments to gaps as appropriate for traffic speeds and the need for delineation.

metadata.section_title: Functions, Widths, and Patterns of Longitudinal Pavement Markings

title: Section 3A.04 Guidance 7 - Functions, Widths, and Patterns of Longitudinal Pavement Markings
text:
Section 3A.04 Guidance 7 - Functions, Widths, and Patterns of Longitudinal Pavement Markings
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3A. General
Page: 538

A dotted line used as a lane line (see Section 3B.07) should consist of 3-foot line segments and 9-foot gaps. A dotted line for line extensions within an intersection, taper area, or interchange ramp area (see Section 3B.11) should consist of 2-foot line segments and 2-foot to 6-foot gaps.

metadata.section_title: Functions, Widths, and Patterns of Longitudinal Pavement Markings

title: Section 3A.05 Standard 1 - Maintaining Minimum Pavement Marking Retroreflectivity
text:
Section 3A.05 Standard 1 - Maintaining Minimum Pavement Marking Retroreflectivity
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3A. General
Page: 539

Except as provided in Paragraph 5 of this Section, a method designed to maintain retroreflectivity at or above 50 mcd/m2/lx under dry conditions shall be used for longitudinal markings on roadways with speed limits of 35 mph or greater.

title: Section 3A.05 Guidance 2 - Maintaining Minimum Pavement Marking Retroreflectivity
text:
Section 3A.05 Guidance 2 - Maintaining Minimum Pavement Marking Retroreflectivity
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3A. General
Page: 539

Except as provided in Paragraph 5 of this Section, a method designed to maintain retroreflectivity at or above 100 mcd/m2/lx under dry conditions should be used for longitudinal markings on roadways with speed limits of 70 mph or greater.

title: Section 3A.05 Guidance 3 - Maintaining Minimum Pavement Marking Retroreflectivity
text:
Section 3A.05 Guidance 3 - Maintaining Minimum Pavement Marking Retroreflectivity
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3A. General
Page: 539

The method used to maintain retroreflectivity should be one or more of those described in “Methods for Maintaining Pavement Marking Retroreflectivity” (FHWA-SA-22-028), 2022 Edition, FHWA or developed from an engineering study based on the values in Paragraphs 1 and 2 of this Section.

title: Section 3A.05 Support 4 - Maintaining Minimum Pavement Marking Retroreflectivity
text:
Section 3A.05 Support 4 - Maintaining Minimum Pavement Marking Retroreflectivity
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3A. General
Page: 539

Retroreflectivity levels for pavement markings are measured with an entrance angle of 88.76 degrees and an observation angle of 1.05 degrees. This geometry is also referred to as 30-meter geometry. The units of pavement marking retroreflectivity are reported in mcd/m2/lx, which means millicandelas per square meter per lux.

title: Section 3A.05 Option 5 - Maintaining Minimum Pavement Marking Retroreflectivity
text:
Section 3A.05 Option 5 - Maintaining Minimum Pavement Marking Retroreflectivity
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3A. General
Page: 539

The following markings may be excluded from the provisions established in Paragraphs 1 and 2 of this Section: A. Markings where ambient illumination assures that the markings are adequately visible; B. Markings on streets or highways that have an ADT of less than 6,000 vehicles per day; C. Dotted extension lines that extend a longitudinal line through an intersection, major driveway, or interchange area (see Section 3B.11); D. Curb markings; E. Parking space markings; and F. Shared-use path markings.

title: Section 3A.05 Support 6 - Maintaining Minimum Pavement Marking Retroreflectivity
text:
Section 3A.05 Support 6 - Maintaining Minimum Pavement Marking Retroreflectivity
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3A. General
Page: 539

The provisions of this Section do not apply to non-longitudinal pavement markings including, but not limited to, the following: A. Transverse markings; B. Word, symbol, and arrow markings; C. Crosswalk markings; and D. Chevron, diagonal, and crosshatch markings.

title: Section 3A.05 Support 7 - Maintaining Minimum Pavement Marking Retroreflectivity
text:
Section 3A.05 Support 7 - Maintaining Minimum Pavement Marking Retroreflectivity
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3A. General
Page: 539

Special circumstances will periodically cause pavement marking retroreflectivity to be below the minimum levels. These circumstances include, but are not limited to, the following: A. Isolated locations of abnormal degradation; B. Periods preceding imminent resurfacing or reconstruction; C. Unanticipated events such as equipment breakdowns, material shortages, and contracting problems; and D. Loss of retroreflectivity resulting from snow maintenance operations.

title: Section 3A.05 Support 8 - Maintaining Minimum Pavement Marking Retroreflectivity
text:
Section 3A.05 Support 8 - Maintaining Minimum Pavement Marking Retroreflectivity
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3A. General
Page: 540

When such circumstances occur, compliance with Paragraphs 1 and 2 of this Section is still considered to be achieved if a reasonable course of action is taken to resume maintenance of minimum retroreflectivity in a timely manner according to the maintaining agency’s method(s), policies, and procedures. MUTCD 11th Edition - Revision 1

title: Section 3B.01 Standard 1 - Yellow Center Line Pavement Markings
text:
Section 3B.01 Standard 1 - Yellow Center Line Pavement Markings
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 540

Center line pavement markings, when used, shall be the pavement markings used to delineate the separation of traffic lanes that have opposite directions of travel on a roadway and shall be yellow.

title: Section 3B.01 Option 2 - Yellow Center Line Pavement Markings
text:
Section 3B.01 Option 2 - Yellow Center Line Pavement Markings
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 540

Center line pavement markings may be placed at a location that is not the geometric center of the roadway.

title: Section 3B.01 Option 3 - Yellow Center Line Pavement Markings
text:
Section 3B.01 Option 3 - Yellow Center Line Pavement Markings
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 540

On roadways without continuous center line pavement markings, short sections may be marked with center line pavement markings to control the position of traffic at specific locations, such as around curves, over hills, on approaches to grade crossings, at grade crossings, and at bridges.

title: Section 3B.01 Standard 4 - Yellow Center Line Pavement Markings
text:
Section 3B.01 Standard 4 - Yellow Center Line Pavement Markings
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 540

The center line markings on two-lane, two-way roadways shall be one of the following as shown in Figure 3B-1: A. Two-direction passing zone markings consisting of a normal width broken yellow line where crossing the center line markings for passing with care is permitted for traffic traveling in either direction; B. One-direction no-passing zone markings consisting of a double yellow line, one of which is a normal width broken yellow line and the other is a normal width solid yellow line, where crossing the center line markings for passing with care is permitted for the traffic traveling adjacent to the broken line, but is prohibited for traffic traveling adjacent to the solid line; or C. Two-direction no-passing zone markings consisting of two normal width solid yellow lines where crossing the center line markings for passing is prohibited for traffic traveling in either direction.

title: Section 3B.01 Standard 5 - Yellow Center Line Pavement Markings
text:
Section 3B.01 Standard 5 - Yellow Center Line Pavement Markings
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 540

A single solid yellow line shall not be used as a center line marking on a two-way roadway.

title: Section 3B.01 Standard 6 - Yellow Center Line Pavement Markings
text:
Section 3B.01 Standard 6 - Yellow Center Line Pavement Markings
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 540

Except where a reversible lane (see Section 3B.04) or a two-way left-turn lane (see Section 3B.05) is present, the center line markings on undivided two-way roadways with four or more lanes for moving motor vehicle traffic always available shall be the two-direction no-passing zone markings consisting of normal width double solid yellow lines as shown in Figure 3B-2.

title: Section 3B.02 Standard 1 - Warrants for Yellow Center Lines
text:
Section 3B.02 Standard 1 - Warrants for Yellow Center Lines
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 542

Center line markings shall be placed on all paved undivided two-way urban arterials and collectors that have a traveled way of 20 feet or more in width and an ADT of 6,000 vehicles per day or greater. Center line markings shall also be placed on all paved undivided two-way streets or highways that have three or more lanes for moving motor vehicle traffic.

title: Section 3B.02 Guidance 2 - Warrants for Yellow Center Lines
text:
Section 3B.02 Guidance 2 - Warrants for Yellow Center Lines
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 542

Center line markings should be placed on paved urban arterials and collectors that have a traveled way of 20 feet or more in width and an ADT of 4,000 vehicles per day or greater. Center line markings should also be placed on all rural arterials and collectors that have a traveled way of 18 feet or more in width and an ADT of 3,000 vehicles per day or greater. Center line markings should also be placed on other traveled ways where an engineering study indicates such a need.

title: Section 3B.02 Guidance 3 - Warrants for Yellow Center Lines
text:
Section 3B.02 Guidance 3 - Warrants for Yellow Center Lines
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 542

Engineering judgment should be used in determining whether to place center line markings on traveled ways that are less than 16 feet wide because of the potential for traffic encroaching on the pavement edges, traffic being affected by parked vehicles, and traffic encroaching into the opposing traffic lane.

title: Section 3B.02 Option 4 - Warrants for Yellow Center Lines
text:
Section 3B.02 Option 4 - Warrants for Yellow Center Lines
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 542

Center line markings may be placed on other paved two-way traveled ways that are 16 feet or more in width.

title: Section 3B.02 Option 5 - Warrants for Yellow Center Lines
text:
Section 3B.02 Option 5 - Warrants for Yellow Center Lines
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 542

If a traffic count is not available, the ADTs described in this Section may be estimates that are based on engineering judgment.

title: Section 3B.03 Standard 1 - No-Passing Zone Pavement Markings
text:
Section 3B.03 Standard 1 - No-Passing Zone Pavement Markings
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 542

No-passing zones shall be marked by either the one-direction no-passing zone pavement markings or the two-direction no-passing zone pavement markings described in Section 3B.01 and shown in Figures 3B-1 and 3B-3.

title: Section 3B.03 Standard 2 - No-Passing Zone Pavement Markings
text:
Section 3B.03 Standard 2 - No-Passing Zone Pavement Markings
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 542

No-passing zone markings shall be used on: A. Two-way roadways at lane-reduction transitions (see Section 3B.12), B. Approaches to obstructions that must be passed on the right (see Section 3B.13), C. Approaches to grade crossings (see Section 8C.02), and D. Approaches to crosswalks.

title: Section 3B.03 Standard 3 - No-Passing Zone Pavement Markings
text:
Section 3B.03 Standard 3 - No-Passing Zone Pavement Markings
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 543

On two-way, two-lane or three-lane roadways where center line markings are installed, no-passing zones shall be established at vertical and horizontal curves and other locations where an engineering study indicates that passing must be prohibited because of inadequate sight distances or other special conditions.

title: Section 3B.03 Standard 4 - No-Passing Zone Pavement Markings
text:
Section 3B.03 Standard 4 - No-Passing Zone Pavement Markings
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 543

On roadways with center line markings, no-passing zone markings shall be used at horizontal or vertical curves where the passing sight distance is less than the minimum shown in Table 3B-1 for the 85th-percentile speed or the speed limit.

title: Section 3B.03 Support 5 - No-Passing Zone Pavement Markings
text:
Section 3B.03 Support 5 - No-Passing Zone Pavement Markings
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 543

The passing sight distance on a vertical curve is the distance at which an object 3.5 feet above the pavement surface can be seen from a point 3.5 feet above the pavement (see Figure 3B-4). Similarly, the passing sight distance on a horizontal curve is the distance measured along the center line (or right- hand lane line of a three-lane roadway) between two points 3.5 feet above the pavement on a line tangent to the embankment or other obstruction that cuts off the view on the inside of the curve (see Figure 3B-4). 35 mph 550 feet 40 mph 600 feet 45 mph 700 feet 50 mph 800 feet 55 mph 900 feet 60 mph 1,000 feet 65 mph 1,100 feet 70 mph 1,200 feet

title: Section 3B.03 Support 6 - No-Passing Zone Pavement Markings
text:
Section 3B.03 Support 6 - No-Passing Zone Pavement Markings
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 543

The upstream end of a no-passing zone at point “a” in Figure 3B-4 is that point where the sight distance first becomes less than that specified in Table 3B-1. The downstream end of the no-passing zone at point “b” in Figure 3B-4 is that point at which the sight distance again becomes greater than the minimum specified.

title: Section 3B.03 Guidance 7 - No-Passing Zone Pavement Markings
text:
Section 3B.03 Guidance 7 - No-Passing Zone Pavement Markings
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 543

Where the distance between successive no-passing zones is less than 400 feet, no-passing zone markings should connect the zones.

title: Section 3B.03 Support 8 - No-Passing Zone Pavement Markings
text:
Section 3B.03 Support 8 - No-Passing Zone Pavement Markings
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 543

No-passing zone signs (see Sections 2B.36, 2B.37, and 2C.53) are sometimes used to emphasize the existence and extent of a no-passing zone.

title: Section 3B.03 Standard 9 - No-Passing Zone Pavement Markings
text:
Section 3B.03 Standard 9 - No-Passing Zone Pavement Markings
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 543

On three-lane roadways where the direction of travel in the center lane transitions from one direction to the other, a no-passing buffer zone, consisting of a flush median island (see Section 3J.03) at least 50 feet in length, shall be provided in the center lane as shown in Figure 3B-5. A lane-reduction transition (see Section 3B.12) shall be provided approaching each end of the buffer zone.

title: Section 3B.04 Standard 1 - Yellow Pavement Markings for Reversible Lanes
text:
Section 3B.04 Standard 1 - Yellow Pavement Markings for Reversible Lanes
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 543

If reversible lanes are used, the lane line pavement markings on each side of reversible lanes shall consist of a normal width broken double yellow line to delineate the edge of a lane in which the direction of travel is reversed from time to time, such that each of these markings serve as the center line markings of the roadway during some period (see Figure 3B-6).

metadata.section_title: Yellow Pavement Markings for Reversible Lanes

title: Section 3B.04 Standard 2 - Yellow Pavement Markings for Reversible Lanes
text:
Section 3B.04 Standard 2 - Yellow Pavement Markings for Reversible Lanes
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 543

Signs (see Section 2B.34), lane-use control signals (see Chapter 4T), or both shall be used to supplement reversible lane pavement markings.

metadata.section_title: Yellow Pavement Markings for Reversible Lanes

title: Section 3B.05 Standard 1 - Pavement Markings for Two-Way Left-Turn Lanes
text:
Section 3B.05 Standard 1 - Pavement Markings for Two-Way Left-Turn Lanes
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 543

If a two-way left-turn lane that is never operated as a reversible lane is used, the lane line pavement markings on each side of the two-way left-turn lane shall consist of a normal width broken yellow line and a normal width solid yellow line to delineate the edges of a lane that can be used by traffic in either direction as part of a left-turn maneuver. These markings shall be placed with the broken line toward the two-way left-turn lane and the solid line toward the adjacent traffic lane as shown in Figure 3B-7.

metadata.section_title: Pavement Markings for Two-Way Left-Turn Lanes

title: Section 3B.05 Guidance 2 - Pavement Markings for Two-Way Left-Turn Lanes
text:
Section 3B.05 Guidance 2 - Pavement Markings for Two-Way Left-Turn Lanes
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 546

White two-way left-turn lane-use arrows should be used at or just downstream from the beginning of a two- way left-turn lane. Figure 3B-4. Method of Locating and Determining the Limits of No-Passing Zones at Curves A - No-passing zone at VERTICAL CURVE Profile View Note: No-passing zones in opposite directions might or might not overlap, depending on alignment B - No-passing zone at HORIZONTAL CURVE Plan View Note: No-passing zones in opposite directions might or might not overlap, depending on alignment Figure 3B-5. Application of Three-Lane, Two-Way Markings for Changing the Direction of the Center Lane Notes: 1. See Section 3B.03 for determining the minimum length of the buffer zone 2. See Section 3B.12 for lane-reduction transition markings and determination of taper length L 3. See Section 3J.03 for the design of the flush median island Figure 3B-6. Example of Yellow Pavement Markings for Reversible Lanes

metadata.section_title: Pavement Markings for Two-Way Left-Turn Lanes

title: Section 3B.05 Option 3 - Pavement Markings for Two-Way Left-Turn Lanes
text:
Section 3B.05 Option 3 - Pavement Markings for Two-Way Left-Turn Lanes
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 546

Additional two-way left-turn lane-use arrow markings may be used at other locations along a two-way left-turn lane where engineering judgment determines that such additional markings are needed to emphasize the proper use of the lane.

metadata.section_title: Pavement Markings for Two-Way Left-Turn Lanes

title: Section 3B.05 Standard 4 - Pavement Markings for Two-Way Left-Turn Lanes
text:
Section 3B.05 Standard 4 - Pavement Markings for Two-Way Left-Turn Lanes
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 546

A single-direction lane-use arrow shall not be used in a lane bordered on both sides by yellow two-way left-turn lane longitudinal markings.

metadata.section_title: Pavement Markings for Two-Way Left-Turn Lanes

title: Section 3B.05 Guidance 5 - Pavement Markings for Two-Way Left-Turn Lanes
text:
Section 3B.05 Guidance 5 - Pavement Markings for Two-Way Left-Turn Lanes
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 546

Signs should be used in conjunction with the two-way left-turn markings (see Section 2B.32).

metadata.section_title: Pavement Markings for Two-Way Left-Turn Lanes

title: Section 3B.05 Guidance 6 - Pavement Markings for Two-Way Left-Turn Lanes
text:
Section 3B.05 Guidance 6 - Pavement Markings for Two-Way Left-Turn Lanes
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 546

Two-way left-turn lane markings should not extend to intersections (see definition in Section 1C.02).

metadata.section_title: Pavement Markings for Two-Way Left-Turn Lanes

title: Section 3B.05 Option 7 - Pavement Markings for Two-Way Left-Turn Lanes
text:
Section 3B.05 Option 7 - Pavement Markings for Two-Way Left-Turn Lanes
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 546

Two-way left-turn lanes may be transitioned to mandatory left-turn lanes as shown in Figure 3B-7 or painted median islands where they approach an intersection.

metadata.section_title: Pavement Markings for Two-Way Left-Turn Lanes

title: Section 3B.06 Standard 1 - White Lane Line Pavement Markings
text:
Section 3B.06 Standard 1 - White Lane Line Pavement Markings
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 546

When used, lane line pavement markings delineating the separation of traffic lanes that have the same direction of travel shall be white.

title: Section 3B.06 Standard 2 - White Lane Line Pavement Markings
text:
Section 3B.06 Standard 2 - White Lane Line Pavement Markings
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 546

Lane line markings shall be used on all freeways and Interstate highways.

title: Section 3B.06 Guidance 3 - White Lane Line Pavement Markings
text:
Section 3B.06 Guidance 3 - White Lane Line Pavement Markings
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 546

Lane line markings should be used: A. On all roadways that are intended to operate with two or more adjacent traffic lanes in the same direction of travel, except as otherwise required for reversible lanes. B. At congested locations where the roadway will accommodate more traffic lanes with lane line markings than without the markings.

title: Section 3B.06 Support 4 - White Lane Line Pavement Markings
text:
Section 3B.06 Support 4 - White Lane Line Pavement Markings
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 546

Examples of lane line markings are shown in Figures 3B-2, 3B-3, and 3B-7 through 3B-13.

title: Section 3B.06 Standard 5 - White Lane Line Pavement Markings
text:
Section 3B.06 Standard 5 - White Lane Line Pavement Markings
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 546

Except as provided in Paragraph 1 of Section 3B.07, where crossing the lane line markings with care is not discouraged or prohibited, the lane line markings shall consist of a normal width broken white line.

title: Section 3B.06 Standard 6 - White Lane Line Pavement Markings
text:
Section 3B.06 Standard 6 - White Lane Line Pavement Markings
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 546

Where crossing the lane line markings is discouraged, the lane line markings shall consist of a normal width solid white line.

title: Section 3B.06 Guidance 7 - White Lane Line Pavement Markings
text:
Section 3B.06 Guidance 7 - White Lane Line Pavement Markings
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 548

A solid white lane line marking should be used on approaches to: A. Intersections to separate a through lane from a mandatory turn lane. B. Intersections to separate contiguous mandatory turn lanes from each other. C. Toll collection points to separate toll lanes, payment methods, channelized movements, or obstructions. Figure 3B-7. Examples of Two-Way Left-Turn Lane Marking Applications A - Intersecting Cross Streets B - Intersecting Driveways MUTCD 11th Edition - Revision 1

title: Section 3B.06 Option 8 - White Lane Line Pavement Markings
text:
Section 3B.06 Option 8 - White Lane Line Pavement Markings
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 548

Solid white lane line markings may be used: A. On approaches to intersections to separate contiguous through lanes. B. To separate through traffic lanes from auxiliary lanes, such as an added uphill truck lane. C. On approaches to crosswalks across multi-lane roadways.

title: Section 3B.06 Option 9 - White Lane Line Pavement Markings
text:
Section 3B.06 Option 9 - White Lane Line Pavement Markings
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 548

Wide solid lane line markings may be used for greater emphasis.

title: Section 3B.06 Option 10 - White Lane Line Pavement Markings
text:
Section 3B.06 Option 10 - White Lane Line Pavement Markings
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 548

A curved transition may be used where a lane line changes direction.

title: Section 3B.06 Support 11 - White Lane Line Pavement Markings
text:
Section 3B.06 Support 11 - White Lane Line Pavement Markings
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 548

Examples of locations where a curved transition can have value include freeway exit and entrance ramps.

title: Section 3B.06 Standard 12 - White Lane Line Pavement Markings
text:
Section 3B.06 Standard 12 - White Lane Line Pavement Markings
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 548

Where crossing the lane line markings is prohibited, the lane line markings shall consist of a double solid white line (see Figure 3B-8).

title: Section 3B.07 Standard 1 - White Lane Line Markings for Non-Continuing Lanes
text:
Section 3B.07 Standard 1 - White Lane Line Markings for Non-Continuing Lanes
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 548

A normal width dotted white line marking shall be used as the lane line to separate a through lane that continues beyond the interchange or intersection from an adjacent deceleration or acceleration lane.

metadata.section_title: White Lane Line Markings for Non-Continuing Lanes

title: Section 3B.07 Standard 2 - White Lane Line Markings for Non-Continuing Lanes
text:
Section 3B.07 Standard 2 - White Lane Line Markings for Non-Continuing Lanes
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 548

For exit ramps with a parallel deceleration lane, a normal width dotted white lane line extension shall be installed from the upstream end of the taper to the theoretical gore or to the upstream end of a solid white lane line, if used, that extends upstream from the theoretical gore as shown in Drawings A and C in Figure 3B-9.

metadata.section_title: White Lane Line Markings for Non-Continuing Lanes

title: Section 3B.07 Standard 3 - White Lane Line Markings for Non-Continuing Lanes
text:
Section 3B.07 Standard 3 - White Lane Line Markings for Non-Continuing Lanes
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 548

For an exit ramp with a tapered deceleration lane, a normal width dotted white line extension shall be installed from the theoretical gore through the taper area such that it meets the edge line at the upstream end of the taper as shown in Drawing B in Figure 3B-9.

metadata.section_title: White Lane Line Markings for Non-Continuing Lanes

title: Section 3B.07 Standard 4 - White Lane Line Markings for Non-Continuing Lanes
text:
Section 3B.07 Standard 4 - White Lane Line Markings for Non-Continuing Lanes
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 548

For entrance ramps with a parallel acceleration lane, a normal width dotted white lane line shall be installed from the theoretical gore or from the downstream end of a solid white lane line, if used, that extends downstream from the theoretical gore, to a point at least one-half the distance from the theoretical gore to the downstream end of the acceleration taper, as shown in Drawing A in Figure 3B-10.

metadata.section_title: White Lane Line Markings for Non-Continuing Lanes

title: Section 3B.07 Option 5 - White Lane Line Markings for Non-Continuing Lanes
text:
Section 3B.07 Option 5 - White Lane Line Markings for Non-Continuing Lanes
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 553

For entrance ramps with a parallel acceleration lane, a normal width dotted white line extension may be installed from the downstream end of the dotted white lane line to the downstream end of the acceleration taper, as shown in Drawing A in Figure 3B-10. Figure 3B-8. Example of a Double Solid White Line Used to Prohibit Lane Changing December 2025 MUTCD 11th Edition - Revision 1 Figure 3B-9. Examples of Dotted Line and Channelizing Line Applications for Exit Ramp Markings (Sheet 1 of 2) A - Parallel deceleration lane B - Tapered deceleration lane Rev. 1 December 2025 MUTCD 11th Edition - Revision 1 Figure 3B-9. metadata.section_title: White Lane Line Markings for Non-Continuing Lanes

title: Section 3B.07 Option 6 - White Lane Line Markings for Non-Continuing Lanes
text:
Section 3B.07 Option 6 - White Lane Line Markings for Non-Continuing Lanes
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 553

For entrance ramps with a tapered acceleration lane, a normal width dotted white line extension may be installed from the downstream end of the channelizing line adjacent to the through lane to the downstream end of the acceleration taper, as shown in Drawings B and C in Figure 3B-10.

metadata.section_title: White Lane Line Markings for Non-Continuing Lanes

title: Section 3B.07 Standard 7 - White Lane Line Markings for Non-Continuing Lanes
text:
Section 3B.07 Standard 7 - White Lane Line Markings for Non-Continuing Lanes
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 553

A wide dotted white lane line shall be used: A. As a lane drop marking in advance of lane drops at exit ramps to distinguish a lane drop from a normal exit ramp (see Drawings A, B, and C in Figure 3B-11), B. In advance of freeway route splits with dedicated lanes (see Drawing D in Figure 3B-11), C. In advance of freeway route splits with an option lane (see Drawing E in Figure 3B-11), D. To separate a through lane that continues beyond an interchange from an adjacent continuous auxiliary lane between an entrance ramp and an exit ramp (see Drawing F in Figure 3B-11), E. As a lane drop marking in advance of lane drops at intersections to distinguish a lane drop from an intersection through lane (see Drawing A in Figure 3B-12), and F. To separate a through lane that continues beyond an intersection from an adjacent auxiliary lane between two intersections (see Drawing B in Figure 3B-12).

metadata.section_title: White Lane Line Markings for Non-Continuing Lanes

title: Section 3B.07 Guidance 8 - White Lane Line Markings for Non-Continuing Lanes
text:
Section 3B.07 Guidance 8 - White Lane Line Markings for Non-Continuing Lanes
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 553

Lane drop markings used in advance of lane drops at freeway and expressway exit ramps should begin at least ½ mile in advance of the theoretical gore.

metadata.section_title: White Lane Line Markings for Non-Continuing Lanes

title: Section 3B.07 Guidance 9 - White Lane Line Markings for Non-Continuing Lanes
text:
Section 3B.07 Guidance 9 - White Lane Line Markings for Non-Continuing Lanes
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 553

On the approach to a multi-lane exit ramp having an optional exit lane that also carries through traffic, lane line markings should be used as illustrated in Drawing B in Figure 3B-11.

metadata.section_title: White Lane Line Markings for Non-Continuing Lanes

title: Section 3B.07 Guidance 10 - White Lane Line Markings for Non-Continuing Lanes
text:
Section 3B.07 Guidance 10 - White Lane Line Markings for Non-Continuing Lanes
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 553

Lane drop markings used in advance of lane drops at intersections should begin a distance in advance of the intersection that is determined by engineering judgment as suitable to enable drivers who do not desire to make the mandatory turn to move out of the lane being dropped prior to reaching the queue of vehicles that are waiting to make the turn. The lane drop markings should begin no closer to the intersection than the most upstream regulatory or warning sign associated with the lane drop.

metadata.section_title: White Lane Line Markings for Non-Continuing Lanes

title: Section 3B.07 Guidance 11 - White Lane Line Markings for Non-Continuing Lanes
text:
Section 3B.07 Guidance 11 - White Lane Line Markings for Non-Continuing Lanes
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 553

The dotted white lane lines that are used for lane drop markings and that are used as a lane line separating through lanes from auxiliary lanes should consist of line segments that are 3 feet in length separated by 9-foot gaps.

metadata.section_title: White Lane Line Markings for Non-Continuing Lanes

title: Section 3B.07 Support 12 - White Lane Line Markings for Non-Continuing Lanes
text:
Section 3B.07 Support 12 - White Lane Line Markings for Non-Continuing Lanes
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 553

Sections 3B.21 and 3B.23 contain information regarding other markings that are associated with lane drops, such as ONLY word pavement markings and lane-use arrows.

metadata.section_title: White Lane Line Markings for Non-Continuing Lanes

title: Section 3B.08 Support 1 - Channelizing Lines
text:
Section 3B.08 Support 1 - Channelizing Lines
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 553

Channelizing lines are used to form neutral areas where traffic traveling in the same general direction is permitted on both sides including entrance and exit ramps, access and egress points to and from managed lanes, toll-plaza bypasses, and left-turn lanes separated from through lanes. Channelizing lines are also sometimes used to alter travel paths for speed management or other purposes.

title: Section 3B.08 Support 2 - Channelizing Lines
text:
Section 3B.08 Support 2 - Channelizing Lines
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 553

Chapter 3J contains information for the application of channelizing lines used in conjunction with islands.

title: Section 3B.08 Standard 3 - Channelizing Lines
text:
Section 3B.08 Standard 3 - Channelizing Lines
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 553

Except as provided in Section 3E.04 and Paragraph 6 of Section 3J.05, a channelizing line shall be a solid wide or double solid white line.

title: Section 3B.08 Support 4 - Channelizing Lines
text:
Section 3B.08 Support 4 - Channelizing Lines
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 553

Examples of channelizing line applications are shown in Figures 3B-9, 3B-10, 3B-11, Drawing C in Figure 3B-15, Figures 3J-1 through 3J-5, and Drawing B in Figure 3J-6.

title: Section 3B.08 Standard 5 - Channelizing Lines
text:
Section 3B.08 Standard 5 - Channelizing Lines
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 562

For all exit ramps and for entrance ramps with parallel acceleration lanes, channelizing lines shall be placed on both sides of the neutral area (see Figures 3B-9 and 3B-11 and Drawing A in Figure 3B-10). Figure 3B-12. Examples of Applications of Conventional Road Lane-Drop Markings (Sheet 2 of 2) B - Auxiliary lane between intersections Note: See Section 3B.20 for the spacing of pavement markings grouped together to formulate one message. MUTCD 11th Edition - Revision 1

title: Section 3B.08 Standard 6 - Channelizing Lines
text:
Section 3B.08 Standard 6 - Channelizing Lines
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 562

For entrance ramps with tapered acceleration lanes, channelizing lines shall be placed along both sides of the neutral area to a point at least one-half of the distance to the theoretical gore (see Drawing C in Figure 3B-10).

title: Section 3B.08 Standard 7 - Channelizing Lines
text:
Section 3B.08 Standard 7 - Channelizing Lines
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 562

Channelizing lines shall be placed on both sides of the neutral area for bifurcations created from open- road tolling lanes that bypass a conventional toll plaza.

title: Section 3B.08 Standard 8 - Channelizing Lines
text:
Section 3B.08 Standard 8 - Channelizing Lines
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 562

Where neutral areas are formed at access and egress points to and from a managed-lane facility, channelizing lines shall be placed on both sides of the neutral area (see Figures 2G-8, 2G-10, 2G-13, 2G-16, 2G-22, 2G-23, 2G-27, and 2G-28).

title: Section 3B.08 Option 9 - Channelizing Lines
text:
Section 3B.08 Option 9 - Channelizing Lines
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 562

For entrance ramps with tapered acceleration lanes, the channelizing lines may extend to the theoretical gore as shown in Drawing B in Figure 3B-10.

title: Section 3B.08 Standard 10 - Channelizing Lines
text:
Section 3B.08 Standard 10 - Channelizing Lines
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 562

Other pavement markings in the neutral area shall be white.

title: Section 3B.08 Support 11 - Channelizing Lines
text:
Section 3B.08 Support 11 - Channelizing Lines
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 562

Pavement markings within the neutral area include chevron markings (see Section 3B.25), retroreflective raised pavement markers (see Section 3B.16), and internally illuminated raised pavement markers (see Section 3B.16).

title: Section 3B.08 Option 12 - Channelizing Lines
text:
Section 3B.08 Option 12 - Channelizing Lines
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 562

A curved transition may be used where a channelizing line changes direction.

title: Section 3B.08 Support 13 - Channelizing Lines
text:
Section 3B.08 Support 13 - Channelizing Lines
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 562

Examples of locations where a curved transition can have value include freeway exit and entrance ramps and separated turn lanes.

title: Section 3B.09 Standard 1 - Edge Line Pavement Markings
text:
Section 3B.09 Standard 1 - Edge Line Pavement Markings
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 562

If used, edge line pavement markings shall delineate the right or left edges of a roadway.

title: Section 3B.09 Standard 2 - Edge Line Pavement Markings
text:
Section 3B.09 Standard 2 - Edge Line Pavement Markings
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 562

Except as provided in Section 3E.04, right edge line pavement markings, if used, shall consist of a normal width solid white line to delineate the right-hand edge of the roadway.

title: Section 3B.09 Standard 3 - Edge Line Pavement Markings
text:
Section 3B.09 Standard 3 - Edge Line Pavement Markings
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 562

If used on the roadways of divided highways or one-way streets, or on any ramp in the direction of travel, left edge line pavement markings shall consist of a normal width solid yellow line to delineate the left-hand edge of a roadway or to indicate driving or passing restrictions left of these markings, except as provided in Section 3E.04.

title: Section 3B.09 Support 4 - Edge Line Pavement Markings
text:
Section 3B.09 Support 4 - Edge Line Pavement Markings
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 562

Edge line markings provide visual references to guide road users during adverse weather and visibility conditions.

title: Section 3B.09 Option 5 - Edge Line Pavement Markings
text:
Section 3B.09 Option 5 - Edge Line Pavement Markings
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 562

Wide solid edge line markings may be used for greater emphasis.

title: Section 3B.09 Support 6 - Edge Line Pavement Markings
text:
Section 3B.09 Support 6 - Edge Line Pavement Markings
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 562

Increasing edge line width from 4 inches to at least 6 inches can be a beneficial countermeasure on all facility types in both urban and rural areas.

title: Section 3B.09 Guidance 7 - Edge Line Pavement Markings
text:
Section 3B.09 Guidance 7 - Edge Line Pavement Markings
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 562

Edge line markings should not be continued through intersections, except for the following situations: A. Dotted edge line extensions (see Section 3B.11), or B. Through that part of an intersection with no intersection approach (such as the far side of a T-intersection).

title: Section 3B.10 Standard 1 - Warrants for Use of Edge Lines
text:
Section 3B.10 Standard 1 - Warrants for Use of Edge Lines
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 563

Edge line markings shall be placed on paved streets or highways with the following characteristics: A. Freeways, B. Expressways, and C. Rural arterials with a traveled way of 20 feet or more in width and an ADT of 6,000 vehicles per day or greater. December 2025 MUTCD 11th Edition - Revision 1

metadata.section_title: Warrants for Use of Edge Lines

title: Section 3B.10 Guidance 2 - Warrants for Use of Edge Lines
text:
Section 3B.10 Guidance 2 - Warrants for Use of Edge Lines
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 563

Edge line markings should be placed on paved streets or highways with the following characteristics: A. Rural arterials and collectors with a traveled way of 20 feet or more in width and an ADT of 3,000 vehicles per day or greater. B. On other paved streets and highways where an engineering study indicates a need for edge line markings.

metadata.section_title: Warrants for Use of Edge Lines

title: Section 3B.10 Guidance 3 - Warrants for Use of Edge Lines
text:
Section 3B.10 Guidance 3 - Warrants for Use of Edge Lines
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 563

Edge line markings should not be placed where an engineering study or engineering judgment indicates that providing them is likely to decrease safety for all road users.

metadata.section_title: Warrants for Use of Edge Lines

title: Section 3B.10 Option 4 - Warrants for Use of Edge Lines
text:
Section 3B.10 Option 4 - Warrants for Use of Edge Lines
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 563

Edge line markings may be placed on streets and highways with or without center line markings.

metadata.section_title: Warrants for Use of Edge Lines

title: Section 3B.10 Option 5 - Warrants for Use of Edge Lines
text:
Section 3B.10 Option 5 - Warrants for Use of Edge Lines
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 563

Edge line markings may be excluded, based on engineering judgment, for reasons such as if the traveled way edges are delineated by curbs, parking, or other markings.

metadata.section_title: Warrants for Use of Edge Lines

title: Section 3B.10 Option 6 - Warrants for Use of Edge Lines
text:
Section 3B.10 Option 6 - Warrants for Use of Edge Lines
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 563

If a bicycle lane is marked on the outside portion of the traveled way, the edge line that would mark the outside edge of the bicycle lane may be omitted.

metadata.section_title: Warrants for Use of Edge Lines

title: Section 3B.10 Option 7 - Warrants for Use of Edge Lines
text:
Section 3B.10 Option 7 - Warrants for Use of Edge Lines
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 563

Edge line markings may be used where edge delineation is desirable to minimize unnecessary driving on paved shoulders or on refuge areas that have lesser structural pavement strength than the adjacent roadway.

metadata.section_title: Warrants for Use of Edge Lines

title: Section 3B.11 Standard 1 - Application of Pavement Markings through Intersections or Interchanges
text:
Section 3B.11 Standard 1 - Application of Pavement Markings through Intersections or Interchanges
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 563

Pavement markings extended into or continued through an intersection or interchange area shall be the same color as the line markings they extend (see Figure 3B-13).

metadata.section_title: Application of Pavement Markings through Intersections or Interchanges

title: Section 3B.11 Guidance 2 - Application of Pavement Markings through Intersections or Interchanges
text:
Section 3B.11 Guidance 2 - Application of Pavement Markings through Intersections or Interchanges
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 563

Pavement markings extended into or continued through an intersection or interchange area should be at least the same width as the line markings they extend.

metadata.section_title: Application of Pavement Markings through Intersections or Interchanges

title: Section 3B.11 Guidance 3 - Application of Pavement Markings through Intersections or Interchanges
text:
Section 3B.11 Guidance 3 - Application of Pavement Markings through Intersections or Interchanges
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 563

Where highway design or reduced visibility conditions make it desirable to provide control or to guide vehicles through an intersection or interchange, such as at offset, skewed, complex, or multi-leg intersections, on curved roadways, where multiple turn lanes are used, or where offset left-turn lanes might cause driver confusion, dotted lane line extension markings consisting of 2-foot line segments and 2-foot to 6-foot gaps should be used to extend longitudinal line markings through an intersection or interchange area.

metadata.section_title: Application of Pavement Markings through Intersections or Interchanges

title: Section 3B.11 Guidance 4 - Application of Pavement Markings through Intersections or Interchanges
text:
Section 3B.11 Guidance 4 - Application of Pavement Markings through Intersections or Interchanges
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 563

Where greater restriction is preferred, solid lane lines or channelizing lines should be extended into or continued through intersections.

metadata.section_title: Application of Pavement Markings through Intersections or Interchanges

title: Section 3B.11 Standard 5 - Application of Pavement Markings through Intersections or Interchanges
text:
Section 3B.11 Standard 5 - Application of Pavement Markings through Intersections or Interchanges
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 563

Extensions of center lines through intersections shall be dotted lines.

metadata.section_title: Application of Pavement Markings through Intersections or Interchanges

title: Section 3B.11 Guidance 6 - Application of Pavement Markings through Intersections or Interchanges
text:
Section 3B.11 Guidance 6 - Application of Pavement Markings through Intersections or Interchanges
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 563

Where a double line is extended through an intersection, a single line of equal width to one of the lines of the double line should be used.

metadata.section_title: Application of Pavement Markings through Intersections or Interchanges

title: Section 3B.11 Standard 7 - Application of Pavement Markings through Intersections or Interchanges
text:
Section 3B.11 Standard 7 - Application of Pavement Markings through Intersections or Interchanges
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 563

Solid lines shall not be used to extend edge lines into or through intersections except through that part of an intersection with no intersecting approach (such as at the far side of a T-intersection).

metadata.section_title: Application of Pavement Markings through Intersections or Interchanges

title: Section 3B.11 Guidance 8 - Application of Pavement Markings through Intersections or Interchanges
text:
Section 3B.11 Guidance 8 - Application of Pavement Markings through Intersections or Interchanges
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 563

Edge line markings should be discontinued across intersecting approaches at intersections or interchanges.

metadata.section_title: Application of Pavement Markings through Intersections or Interchanges

title: Section 3B.11 Guidance 9 - Application of Pavement Markings through Intersections or Interchanges
text:
Section 3B.11 Guidance 9 - Application of Pavement Markings through Intersections or Interchanges
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 563

Driveways that do not meet the definition of an intersection (see Section 1C.02) should have edge line markings maintained across the intersecting approach of the driveway.

metadata.section_title: Application of Pavement Markings through Intersections or Interchanges

title: Section 3B.11 Option 10 - Application of Pavement Markings through Intersections or Interchanges
text:
Section 3B.11 Option 10 - Application of Pavement Markings through Intersections or Interchanges
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 563

Dotted edge line extensions may be placed through intersections.

metadata.section_title: Application of Pavement Markings through Intersections or Interchanges

title: Section 3B.12 Support 1 - Lane-Reduction Transitions
text:
Section 3B.12 Support 1 - Lane-Reduction Transitions
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 566

A lane-reduction is where the number of through lanes is reduced at a location that is not at an interchange or intersection because of narrowing of the roadway or because of a section of on-street parking in what would otherwise be a through lane.

title: Section 3B.13 Standard 1 - Approach Markings for Obstructions
text:
Section 3B.13 Standard 1 - Approach Markings for Obstructions
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 568

Pavement markings shall be used to guide traffic away from fixed obstructions within a paved roadway. Approach markings for bridge supports, refuge islands, median islands, toll plaza islands, and raised channelization islands shall consist of a tapered line or lines extending from the center line or the lane line to a point 1 to 2 feet to the right-hand side, or to both sides, of the approach end of the obstruction (see Figure 3B-15).

title: Section 3B.13 Guidance 2 - Approach Markings for Obstructions
text:
Section 3B.13 Guidance 2 - Approach Markings for Obstructions
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 568

For roadways having a speed limit of 45 mph or greater, the taper length of the tapered line markings should be computed by the formula L = WS, where L equals the taper length in feet, W equals the width of the offset distance in feet, and S equals the 85th-percentile speed or the speed limit, whichever is higher. For roadways where the speed limit is less than 45 mph, the formula L = WS2/60 should be used to compute the taper length.

title: Section 3B.13 Guidance 3 - Approach Markings for Obstructions
text:
Section 3B.13 Guidance 3 - Approach Markings for Obstructions
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 568

The minimum taper length should be 100 feet in urban areas and 200 feet in rural areas.

title: Section 3B.13 Option 4 - Approach Markings for Obstructions
text:
Section 3B.13 Option 4 - Approach Markings for Obstructions
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 568

The minimum taper length may be less than 100 feet on roadways where the operating speed is less than 25 mph.

title: Section 3B.13 Standard 5 - Approach Markings for Obstructions
text:
Section 3B.13 Standard 5 - Approach Markings for Obstructions
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 568

If traffic is required to pass only to the right of the obstruction, the markings shall consist of a two- direction no-passing zone marking at least twice the length of the diagonal portion as determined by the appropriate taper formula (see Drawing A in Figure 3B-15).

title: Section 3B.13 Option 6 - Approach Markings for Obstructions
text:
