Section 3B.13 Option 6 - Approach Markings for Obstructions
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 568

If traffic is required to pass only to the right of the obstruction, yellow diagonal markings (see Section 3B.25) may be placed in the flush median islands (see Section 3J.03) between the no-passing zone markings as shown in Drawings A and B in Figure 3B-15.

title: Section 3B.13 Standard 7 - Approach Markings for Obstructions
text:
Section 3B.13 Standard 7 - Approach Markings for Obstructions
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 568

If traffic can pass either to the right or left of the obstruction, the markings shall consist of two channelizing lines diverging from the lane line, one to each side of the obstruction. In advance of the point of divergence, a wide solid white line or normal width double solid white line shall be extended in place of the broken lane line for a distance equal to the length of the diverging lines (see Drawing C in Figure 3B-15).

title: Section 3B.13 Option 8 - Approach Markings for Obstructions
text:
Section 3B.13 Option 8 - Approach Markings for Obstructions
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 568

If traffic can pass either to the right or left of the obstruction, additional white chevron markings (see Section 3B.25) may be placed in the flush neutral area between the channelizing lines as shown in Drawing C in Figure 3B-15. Other markings, such as white delineators, white channelizing devices, white raised pavement markers, and white crosswalk markings may also be placed in the flush neutral area.

title: Section 3B.14 Standard 1 - Raised Pavement Markers – General
text:
Section 3B.14 Standard 1 - Raised Pavement Markers – General
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 568

The color of raised pavement markers under both daylight and nighttime conditions shall conform to the color of the marking for which they serve as a positioning guide, or for which they supplement or substitute.

title: Section 3B.14 Option 2 - Raised Pavement Markers – General
text:
Section 3B.14 Option 2 - Raised Pavement Markers – General
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 568

The side of a raised pavement marker that is visible to traffic proceeding in the wrong direction may be red (see Section 3A.03).

title: Section 3B.14 Option 3 - Raised Pavement Markers – General
text:
Section 3B.14 Option 3 - Raised Pavement Markers – General
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 568

Retroreflective or internally illuminated raised pavement markers may be used in the roadway immediately adjacent to curbed approach ends of raised medians and curbs of islands, or on top of such curbs (see Section 3J.06).

title: Section 3B.14 Standard 4 - Raised Pavement Markers – General
text:
Section 3B.14 Standard 4 - Raised Pavement Markers – General
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 568

When used, internally illuminated raised pavement markers shall be steadily illuminated and shall not be flashed.

title: Section 3B.14 Support 5 - Raised Pavement Markers – General
text:
Section 3B.14 Support 5 - Raised Pavement Markers – General
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 568

Flashing raised pavement markers are considered to be In-Roadway Warning Lights (see Chapter 4U).

title: Section 3B.14 Guidance 6 - Raised Pavement Markers – General
text:
Section 3B.14 Guidance 6 - Raised Pavement Markers – General
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 571

The spacing of raised pavement markers used to supplement or substitute for other types of longitudinal markings should correspond with the pattern of broken lines for which the markers supplement or substitute. December 2025 Figure 3B-15. Examples of Applications of Markings for Obstructions in the Roadway (Sheet 1 of 2) A - Center of a two-lane road B - Center of a four-lane road For speeds 45 mph or more: L = WS For speeds less than 45 mph: L = WS2/60 S = 85th-percentile speed or the speed limit in mph, whichever is higher W = Offset distance in feet Minimum length of : L = 100 feet in urban areas L = 200 feet in rural areas Length “L” should be extended as required by sight distance conditions Figure 3B-15. Examples of Applications of Markings for Obstructions in the Roadway (Sheet 2 of 2) C - Traffic passing in the same direction on both sides of an obstruction For speeds of 45 mph or more: L = WS For speeds of less than 45 mph: L = WS2/60 S = 85th-percentile speed or the speed limit in mph, whichever is higher W = Offset distance in feet Minimum length of: L = 100 feet in urban areas L = 200 feet in rural areas Length “L” should be extended as required by sight distance conditions

title: Section 3B.14 Standard 7 - Raised Pavement Markers – General
text:
Section 3B.14 Standard 7 - Raised Pavement Markers – General
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 571

The value of N cited in Sections 3B.15 through 3B.17 for the spacing of raised pavement markers shall equal the length of one line segment plus one gap of the broken lines used on the highway.

title: Section 3B.14 Option 8 - Raised Pavement Markers – General
text:
Section 3B.14 Option 8 - Raised Pavement Markers – General
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 571

For additional emphasis, retroreflective raised pavement markers may be spaced closer than described in Sections 3B.15 through 3B.17, as determined by engineering judgment or engineering study.

title: Section 3B.15 Option 1 - Raised Pavement Markers as Vehicle Positioning Guides with Other Longitudinal Markings
text:
Section 3B.15 Option 1 - Raised Pavement Markers as Vehicle Positioning Guides with Other Longitudinal Markings
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 571

Retroreflective or internally illuminated raised pavement markers may be used as positioning guides with longitudinal line markings without necessarily conveying information to the road user about passing or lane-use restrictions. In such applications, markers may be positioned in line with or immediately adjacent to a single line marking, or positioned between the two lines of a double center line or double lane line marking.

metadata.section_title: Raised Pavement Markers as Vehicle Positioning Guides with Other Longitudinal Markings

title: Section 3B.15 Guidance 2 - Raised Pavement Markers as Vehicle Positioning Guides with Other Longitudinal Markings
text:
Section 3B.15 Guidance 2 - Raised Pavement Markers as Vehicle Positioning Guides with Other Longitudinal Markings
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 571

Except as otherwise provided in Paragraphs 3 and 4 of this Section, the spacing for such applications should be 2N (see Section 3B.14).

metadata.section_title: Raised Pavement Markers as Vehicle Positioning Guides with Other Longitudinal Markings

title: Section 3B.15 Option 3 - Raised Pavement Markers as Vehicle Positioning Guides with Other Longitudinal Markings
text:
Section 3B.15 Option 3 - Raised Pavement Markers as Vehicle Positioning Guides with Other Longitudinal Markings
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 571

Where it is desired to alert the road user to changes in the travel path, such as on sharp curves or on transitions that reduce the number of lanes or that shift traffic laterally, the spacing may be reduced to N or less.

metadata.section_title: Raised Pavement Markers as Vehicle Positioning Guides with Other Longitudinal Markings

title: Section 3B.15 Option 4 - Raised Pavement Markers as Vehicle Positioning Guides with Other Longitudinal Markings
text:
Section 3B.15 Option 4 - Raised Pavement Markers as Vehicle Positioning Guides with Other Longitudinal Markings
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 571

On freeways and expressways, the spacing may be increased to 3N for relatively straight and level roadway segments where engineering judgment indicates that such spacing will provide adequate delineation under wet night conditions.

metadata.section_title: Raised Pavement Markers as Vehicle Positioning Guides with Other Longitudinal Markings

title: Section 3B.16 Guidance 1 - Raised Pavement Markers Supplementing Other Markings
text:
Section 3B.16 Guidance 1 - Raised Pavement Markers Supplementing Other Markings
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 571

The use of retroreflective or internally illuminated raised pavement markers for supplementing longitudinal line markings should comply with the following: A. Lateral Positioning 1. When supplementing double line markings, pairs of raised pavement markers placed laterally in line with or immediately outside of the two lines should be used. 2. When supplementing wide line markings, pairs of raised pavement markers placed laterally adjacent to each other should be used. B. Longitudinal Spacing 1. When supplementing solid line markings, raised pavement markers at a spacing no greater than N (see Section 3B.14) should be used, except that when supplementing channelizing lines or edge line markings, a spacing of no greater than N/2 should be used. 2. When supplementing broken line markings, a spacing no greater than 3N should be used. However, when supplementing broken line markings identifying reversible lanes, a spacing of no greater than N should be used. 3. When supplementing dotted lane line markings, a spacing appropriate for the application should be used. 4. When supplementing longitudinal line extension markings through at-grade intersections, one raised pavement marker for each short line segment should be used. 5. When supplementing line extensions through freeway interchanges, a spacing of no greater than N should be used.

metadata.section_title: Raised Pavement Markers Supplementing Other Markings

title: Section 3B.16 Guidance 2 - Raised Pavement Markers Supplementing Other Markings
text:
Section 3B.16 Guidance 2 - Raised Pavement Markers Supplementing Other Markings
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 571

Raised pavement markers should not supplement right-hand edge lines unless an engineering study or engineering judgment indicates the benefits of enhanced delineation of a curve or other location would outweigh possible impacts on bicyclists using the shoulder, and the spacing of raised pavement markers on the right-hand edge does not simulate a broken line during wet night conditions.

metadata.section_title: Raised Pavement Markers Supplementing Other Markings

title: Section 3B.16 Option 3 - Raised Pavement Markers Supplementing Other Markings
text:
Section 3B.16 Option 3 - Raised Pavement Markers Supplementing Other Markings
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 571

Raised pavement markers also may be used to supplement other markings such as channelizing islands, gore areas, approaches to obstructions, or wrong-way arrows.

metadata.section_title: Raised Pavement Markers Supplementing Other Markings

title: Section 3B.16 Option 4 - Raised Pavement Markers Supplementing Other Markings
text:
Section 3B.16 Option 4 - Raised Pavement Markers Supplementing Other Markings
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 572

To improve the visibility of horizontal curves, center lines may be supplemented with retroreflective or internally illuminated raised pavement markers for the entire curved section as well as for a distance in advance of the curve that approximates 5 seconds of travel time. MUTCD 11th Edition - Revision 1

metadata.section_title: Raised Pavement Markers Supplementing Other Markings

title: Section 3B.17 Option 1 - Raised Pavement Markers Substituting for Pavement Markings
text:
Section 3B.17 Option 1 - Raised Pavement Markers Substituting for Pavement Markings
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 572

Retroreflective or internally illuminated raised pavement markers, or non-retroreflective raised pavement markers supplemented by retroreflective or internally illuminated markers, may be substituted for markings of other types.

metadata.section_title: Raised Pavement Markers Substituting for Pavement Markings

title: Section 3B.17 Guidance 2 - Raised Pavement Markers Substituting for Pavement Markings
text:
Section 3B.17 Guidance 2 - Raised Pavement Markers Substituting for Pavement Markings
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 572

If used, the pattern of the raised pavement markers should simulate the pattern of the markings for which they substitute.

metadata.section_title: Raised Pavement Markers Substituting for Pavement Markings

title: Section 3B.17 Standard 3 - Raised Pavement Markers Substituting for Pavement Markings
text:
Section 3B.17 Standard 3 - Raised Pavement Markers Substituting for Pavement Markings
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 572

Non-retroreflective raised pavement markers shall not be used alone, without supplemental retroreflective or internally illuminated markers, as a substitute for other types of pavement markings.

metadata.section_title: Raised Pavement Markers Substituting for Pavement Markings

title: Section 3B.18 Guidance 1 - Curb Markings for Parking Regulations
text:
Section 3B.18 Guidance 1 - Curb Markings for Parking Regulations
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 572

Except as provided in Paragraph 3 of this Section, since yellow and white curb markings are frequently used for curb delineation and visibility, parking regulations should be established through the installation of standard signs (see Sections 2B.53 and 2B.54), especially in areas where curb markings are frequently obscured by snow and ice accumulation.

title: Section 3B.18 Guidance 2 - Curb Markings for Parking Regulations
text:
Section 3B.18 Guidance 2 - Curb Markings for Parking Regulations
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 572

Except as provided in Paragraph 3 of this Section, when curb markings are used without signs to convey parking regulations, a legible word marking regarding the regulation (such as “No Parking” or “No Standing”) should be placed on the curb.

title: Section 3B.18 Option 3 - Curb Markings for Parking Regulations
text:
Section 3B.18 Option 3 - Curb Markings for Parking Regulations
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 572

Curb markings without word markings or signs may be used to convey a general prohibition by statute of parking within a specified distance of a STOP sign, YIELD sign, driveway, fire hydrant, or crosswalk.

title: Section 3B.18 Option 4 - Curb Markings for Parking Regulations
text:
Section 3B.18 Option 4 - Curb Markings for Parking Regulations
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 573

Local highway agencies may prescribe special colors for curb markings to supplement standard signs for parking regulation. December 2025

title: Section 3B.19 Option 1 - Stop and Yield Lines
text:
Section 3B.19 Option 1 - Stop and Yield Lines
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 573

Stop lines may be used to indicate the point behind which vehicles are required to stop in compliance with a STOP (R1-1) sign, a Stop Here for Pedestrians (R1-5b) sign, a Stop Here for School Crossing (R1-5c) sign, a Stop Here for Trail Crossing (R-5e) sign, or some other traffic control device that requires vehicles to stop, except YIELD signs that are not associated with passive grade crossings.

title: Section 3B.19 Standard 2 - Stop and Yield Lines
text:
Section 3B.19 Standard 2 - Stop and Yield Lines
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 573

Stop lines shall consist of solid white lines extending across approach lanes to indicate the point at which the stop is intended or required to be made.

title: Section 3B.19 Standard 3 - Stop and Yield Lines
text:
Section 3B.19 Standard 3 - Stop and Yield Lines
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 573

Except as provided in Section 8C.03, stop lines shall not be used at locations where drivers are required to yield in compliance with a YIELD (R1-2) sign, a Yield Here to Pedestrians (R1-5) sign, a Yield Here to School Crossings (R1-5a) sign, a Yield Here to Trail Crossings (R1-5d) sign, or at locations on uncontrolled approaches where drivers or bicyclists are required by State law to yield to pedestrians.

title: Section 3B.19 Guidance 4 - Stop and Yield Lines
text:
Section 3B.19 Guidance 4 - Stop and Yield Lines
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 573

Stop lines should be used to indicate the point behind which vehicles are required to stop in compliance with a traffic control signal (see Section 4D.08).

title: Section 3B.19 Guidance 5 - Stop and Yield Lines
text:
Section 3B.19 Guidance 5 - Stop and Yield Lines
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 573

Stop lines should be 12 to 24 inches wide.

title: Section 3B.19 Option 6 - Stop and Yield Lines
text:
Section 3B.19 Option 6 - Stop and Yield Lines
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 573

Stop lines may be omitted at ramp control signals.

title: Section 3B.20 Support 1 - Word, Symbol, and Arrow Pavement Markings – General
text:
Section 3B.20 Support 1 - Word, Symbol, and Arrow Pavement Markings – General
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 575

Word, symbol, and arrow markings on the pavement are used for the purpose of regulating, warning, or guiding traffic. These pavement markings can be helpful to road users in some locations by supplementing signs and providing additional emphasis for important regulatory, warning, or guidance messages, because the markings do not require diversion of the road user’s attention from the roadway surface. Symbol messages are preferable to word messages. Examples of standard word and arrow pavement markings are shown in Figures 3B-17 and 3B-21, respectively.

metadata.section_title: Word, Symbol, and Arrow Pavement Markings – General

title: Section 3B.20 Option 2 - Word, Symbol, and Arrow Pavement Markings – General
text:
Section 3B.20 Option 2 - Word, Symbol, and Arrow Pavement Markings – General
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 575

Word, symbol, and arrow pavement markings may be used as determined by engineering judgment to supplement signs and/or to provide additional emphasis for regulatory, warning, or guidance messages provided by other devices.

metadata.section_title: Word, Symbol, and Arrow Pavement Markings – General

title: Section 3B.21 Guidance 1 - Word Pavement Markings
text:
Section 3B.21 Guidance 1 - Word Pavement Markings
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 575

Letters and numerals should be 6 feet or more in height, except as provided in Section 9E.01 for the BIKE LANE word pavement marking and in Section 9E.15 for a bicycle detector symbol and WAIT HERE FOR GREEN word pavement marking.

title: Section 3B.21 Guidance 2 - Word Pavement Markings
text:
Section 3B.21 Guidance 2 - Word Pavement Markings
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 575

If a pavement marking word message consists of more than one line of information, it should read in the direction of travel. The first word of the message should be nearest to the road user.

title: Section 3B.21 Standard 3 - Word Pavement Markings
text:
Section 3B.21 Standard 3 - Word Pavement Markings
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 576

The word STOP shall not be placed on the pavement in advance of a stop line, unless every vehicle is required to stop at all times. December 2025

title: Section 3B.21 Guidance 4 - Word Pavement Markings
text:
Section 3B.21 Guidance 4 - Word Pavement Markings
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 576

Where through lanes approaching an intersection become mandatory turn lanes, ONLY word pavement markings (see Figure 3B-17) should be used in addition to signs (see Sections 2B.27 and 2B.28) and the required lane-use arrow markings (see Section 3B.23).

title: Section 3B.21 Option 5 - Word Pavement Markings
text:
Section 3B.21 Option 5 - Word Pavement Markings
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 576

The ONLY word marking may be used to supplement the lane-use arrow markings in lanes that are designated for the exclusive use of a single movement such as turn bays.

title: Section 3B.21 Option 6 - Word Pavement Markings
text:
Section 3B.21 Option 6 - Word Pavement Markings
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 576

The ONLY word marking may be used to supplement a preferential lane word or symbol marking (see Section 3E.03).

title: Section 3B.21 Option 7 - Word Pavement Markings
text:
Section 3B.21 Option 7 - Word Pavement Markings
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 576

On roadways where the operating speed is less than 25 mph, word markings may be proportionally reduced by 25 percent.

title: Section 3B.21 Standard 8 - Word Pavement Markings
text:
Section 3B.21 Standard 8 - Word Pavement Markings
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 576

The ONLY word marking shall not be used in a lane that is shared by more than one movement.

title: Section 3B.23 Support 1 - Lane-Use Arrows
text:
Section 3B.23 Support 1 - Lane-Use Arrows
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 578

Lane-use arrow markings (see Figure 3B-21) are used to indicate the mandatory or permissible movements in certain lanes (see Figure 3B-22) and in two-way left-turn lanes (see Figure 3B-7).

title: Section 3B.24 Guidance 1 - Wrong-Way Arrows
text:
Section 3B.24 Guidance 1 - Wrong-Way Arrows
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 578

Where crossroad channelization or ramp geometrics do not make wrong-way movements difficult, the appropriate lane-use arrow should be placed in each lane of an exit ramp near the crossroad terminal where it will be clearly visible to a potential wrong-way road user (see Figure 2B-15).

title: Section 3B.24 Option 2 - Wrong-Way Arrows
text:
Section 3B.24 Option 2 - Wrong-Way Arrows
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 578

The wrong-way arrow markings shown in Drawing G in Figure 3B-21 may be placed near the downstream terminus of a ramp as shown in Figure 2B-15 and in Drawing A in Figure 2B-16, or at other locations where lane- use arrows are not appropriate, to indicate the correct direction of traffic flow and to discourage drivers from traveling in the wrong direction.

title: Section 3B.25 Support 1 - Chevron and Diagonal Markings
text:
Section 3B.25 Support 1 - Chevron and Diagonal Markings
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 580

Chevron or diagonal markings are used to discourage travel on certain paved areas, such as shoulders, neutral areas, and flush median islands. MUTCD 11th Edition - Revision 1 Figure 3B-21. Examples of Standard Arrows for Pavement Markings A - Through lane-use arrow C - Turn and through lane-use arrow B - Turn lane-use arrow D - U-Turn lane-use arrow E - U-Turn and turn lane-use arrow Rev. 1 F - Curved-stem lane-use arrows G - Wrong-way arrow H - Wrong-way arrow using retroreflective I - Lane-reduction arrow raised pavement markers Notes: 1. See the "Standard Highway Signs" publication for sizes and details 2. Refer to Section 3B.20 for guidance and options for proportionally scaling the arrows December 2025 MUTCD 11th Edition - Revision 1 Figure 3B-22. Examples of Lane-Use Control Word and Arrow Pavement Markings Rev. 1 Rev. 1

title: Section 3B.25 Option 2 - Chevron and Diagonal Markings
text:
Section 3B.25 Option 2 - Chevron and Diagonal Markings
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 581

Chevron and diagonal markings may be used: A. On approaches to obstructions in the roadway (see Sheet 2 of Figure 3B-15), B. For channelized travel paths on approaches to intersections, C. In buffer spaces between preferential lanes and general-purpose lanes (see Drawing A in Figure 3E-2), D. In the neutral area gores (see Figures 3B-9 through 3B-11), E. In the neutral area of bifurcations created from open-road tolling lanes that bypass a conventional toll plaza, F. In the neutral areas at access and egress points to and from a managed-lane facility (see Figures 2G-8, 2G-10, 2G-22, and 2G-23), and G. In the neutral areas of islands. December 2025 MUTCD 11th Edition - Revision 1

title: Section 3B.25 Option 3 - Chevron and Diagonal Markings
text:
Section 3B.25 Option 3 - Chevron and Diagonal Markings
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 581

Chevron markings may be supplemented with white retroreflective or internally illuminated raised pavement markers (see Section 3B.16) for enhanced nighttime visibility.

title: Section 3B.26 Option 1 - Do Not Block Intersection Markings
text:
Section 3B.26 Option 1 - Do Not Block Intersection Markings
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 581

Do Not Block Intersection markings may be used to mark the edges of an intersection area that is in close proximity to a signalized intersection, railroad crossing, or other nearby traffic control that might cause vehicles to stop within the intersection and impede other traffic entering the intersection. If authorized by law, Do Not Block Intersection markings with appropriate signs may also be used at other locations.

title: Section 3B.26 Standard 2 - Do Not Block Intersection Markings
text:
Section 3B.26 Standard 2 - Do Not Block Intersection Markings
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 581

If used, Do Not Block Intersection markings (see Figure 3B-24) shall consist of one of the following alternatives: A. Wide solid white lines that outline the intersection area that vehicles must not block; B. Wide solid white lines that outline the intersection area that vehicles must not block and a white word message such as DO NOT BLOCK or KEEP CLEAR; C. Wide solid white lines that outline the intersection area that vehicles must not block and white cross-hatching within the intersection area; or D. A white word message, such as DO NOT BLOCK or KEEP CLEAR, within the intersection area that vehicles must not block.

title: Section 3B.26 Standard 3 - Do Not Block Intersection Markings
text:
Section 3B.26 Standard 3 - Do Not Block Intersection Markings
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 581

DO NOT BLOCK INTERSECTION markings shall be accompanied by one or more DO NOT BLOCK INTERSECTION (DRIVEWAY) (CROSSING) (R10-7) signs (see Section 2B.59), one or more DO NOT STOP ON TRACKS (R8-8) signs (see Section 8B.07), or one or more similar signs.

title: Section 3B.27 Standard 1 - Parking Space Markings
text:
Section 3B.27 Standard 1 - Parking Space Markings
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 581

On-street parking space markings shall be white.

title: Section 3B.27 Support 2 - Parking Space Markings
text:
Section 3B.27 Support 2 - Parking Space Markings
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 583

Examples of on-street parking space markings are shown in Figure 3B-23. December 2025 Figure 3B-23. Examples of Parking Space Markings Figure 3B-24. Do Not Block Intersection Markings Note: Align the edges of the outline to define the specific area that is not to be blocked. The outline does not have to be rectangular in shape.

title: Section 3B.27 Option 3 - Parking Space Markings
text:
Section 3B.27 Option 3 - Parking Space Markings
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 583

Blue lines may supplement white parking space markings of each parking space designated for use only by persons with disabilities (see Figure 3B-23).

title: Section 3B.27 Support 4 - Parking Space Markings
text:
Section 3B.27 Support 4 - Parking Space Markings
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 583

Additional parking space markings for the purpose of designating spaces for use only by persons with disabilities are discussed in Section 3B.22 and illustrated in Figure 3B-19.

title: Section 3B.28 Support 1 - Speed Reduction Markings
text:
Section 3B.28 Support 1 - Speed Reduction Markings
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 583

Speed reduction markings (see Figure 3B-25) are transverse markings that are placed on the roadway within a lane (along both edges of the lane) in a pattern of progressively reduced spacing to give drivers the impression that their speed is increasing.

title: Section 3B.28 Support 2 - Speed Reduction Markings
text:
Section 3B.28 Support 2 - Speed Reduction Markings
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 583

Speed reduction markings have been shown to enhance safety around curves and locations with a history of run-off-the-road crashes when applied in combination with horizontal alignment warning signs (see Section 2C.05).

title: Section 3B.28 Option 3 - Speed Reduction Markings
text:
Section 3B.28 Option 3 - Speed Reduction Markings
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 584

Speed reduction markings may be placed in advance of an unexpectedly severe horizontal or vertical curve or other roadway feature where drivers need to decelerate prior to reaching the feature and where the desired reduction in speeds has not been achieved by the installation of warning signs and/or other traffic control devices. Figure 3B-25. Example of the Application of Speed Reduction Markings A - Recommended dimensions B - Example of placement

title: Section 3B.28 Guidance 4 - Speed Reduction Markings
text:
Section 3B.28 Guidance 4 - Speed Reduction Markings
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 584

If used, speed reduction markings should be reserved for unexpected curves or other usages based on engineering judgment. Speed reduction markings should not be used on long tangent sections of roadway or in areas frequented mainly by local or familiar drivers, such as school zones. If used, speed reduction markings should supplement the appropriate warning signs and other traffic control devices and should not substitute for these devices.

title: Section 3B.28 Standard 5 - Speed Reduction Markings
text:
Section 3B.28 Standard 5 - Speed Reduction Markings
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 584

Speed reduction markings shall be a series of white transverse lines on both sides of the lane that are perpendicular to the center line, edge line, or lane line.

title: Section 3B.28 Guidance 6 - Speed Reduction Markings
text:
Section 3B.28 Guidance 6 - Speed Reduction Markings
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 584

The longitudinal spacing between the markings should be progressively reduced from the upstream to the downstream end of the marked portion of the lane.

title: Section 3B.28 Guidance 7 - Speed Reduction Markings
text:
Section 3B.28 Guidance 7 - Speed Reduction Markings
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 584

Speed reduction markings should not be greater than 12 inches in width, and should not extend more than 18 inches into the lane.

title: Section 3B.28 Standard 8 - Speed Reduction Markings
text:
Section 3B.28 Standard 8 - Speed Reduction Markings
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 584

Speed reduction markings shall be used only in lanes that have a longitudinal line (center line, edge line, or lane line) on both sides of the lane.

title: Section 3B.29 Standard 1 - Speed Hump and Speed Table Markings
text:
Section 3B.29 Standard 1 - Speed Hump and Speed Table Markings
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 584

If speed hump markings are used, they shall be a series of white markings placed on a speed hump to identify its location. If markings are used for a speed hump that does not also function as a crosswalk or speed table, the markings shall comply with Option A, B, or C shown in Figure 3B-26. If markings are used for a speed hump that also functions as a crosswalk or speed table, the markings shall comply with Option A or B shown in Figure 3B-27.

metadata.section_title: Speed Hump and Speed Table Markings

title: Section 3B.29 Option 2 - Speed Hump and Speed Table Markings
text:
Section 3B.29 Option 2 - Speed Hump and Speed Table Markings
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 584

Where used, center line markings, lane line markings, and edge lines may be discontinued on the profile of the speed hump.

metadata.section_title: Speed Hump and Speed Table Markings

title: Section 3B.29 Standard 3 - Speed Hump and Speed Table Markings
text:
Section 3B.29 Standard 3 - Speed Hump and Speed Table Markings
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 585

Where a speed hump or a speed table specifically incorporates a crossing movement for pedestrians, bicyclists, or equestrians, and functions as a raised crosswalk, crosswalk markings (see Chapter 3C) shall be provided. Figure 3B-26. Pavement Markings for Speed Humps without Crosswalks OPTION A OPTION B OPTION C

metadata.section_title: Speed Hump and Speed Table Markings

title: Section 3B.30 Option 1 - Advance Speed Hump and Speed Table Markings
text:
Section 3B.30 Option 1 - Advance Speed Hump and Speed Table Markings
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 585

Advance speed hump markings (see Figure 3B-28) may be used in advance of speed humps or other engineered vertical roadway deflections such as dips where added visibility is desired or where such deflection is not expected.

metadata.section_title: Advance Speed Hump and Speed Table Markings

title: Section 3B.30 Option 2 - Advance Speed Hump and Speed Table Markings
text:
Section 3B.30 Option 2 - Advance Speed Hump and Speed Table Markings
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 585

Advance word pavement markings such as BUMP or HUMP (see Section 3B.20) may be used on the approach to a speed hump either alone or in conjunction with advance speed hump markings. Appropriate advance warning signs may be used in compliance with Section 2C.27.

metadata.section_title: Advance Speed Hump and Speed Table Markings

title: Section 3B.30 Standard 3 - Advance Speed Hump and Speed Table Markings
text:
Section 3B.30 Standard 3 - Advance Speed Hump and Speed Table Markings
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 585

If advance speed hump or speed table markings are used, they shall be a series of eight white 12-inch transverse lines that become longer and are spaced closer together as the vehicle approaches the speed hump or other deflection. If advance markings are used, they shall comply with the detailed design shown in Figure 3B-28.

metadata.section_title: Advance Speed Hump and Speed Table Markings

title: Section 3B.30 Guidance 4 - Advance Speed Hump and Speed Table Markings
text:
Section 3B.30 Guidance 4 - Advance Speed Hump and Speed Table Markings
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 586

If used, advance speed hump markings should be installed in each approach lane. MUTCD 11th Edition - Revision 1 Figure 3B-27. Pavement Markings for Speed Tables or Speed Humps with Crosswalks OPTION A OPTION B Note: Crosswalk lines are not shown

metadata.section_title: Advance Speed Hump and Speed Table Markings

title: Section 3B.31 Support 1 - Markings for a Diamond Interchange with a Transposed Alignment Crossroad
text:
Section 3B.31 Support 1 - Markings for a Diamond Interchange with a Transposed Alignment Crossroad
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 586

Markings used in a diamond interchange with a transposed alignment crossroad can be advantageous for minimizing wrong-way movements. The potential for wrong-way movements is greatest at the crossover intersections where the alignment becomes transposed.

metadata.section_title: Markings for a Diamond Interchange with a Transposed Alignment Crossroad

title: Section 3B.31 Standard 2 - Markings for a Diamond Interchange with a Transposed Alignment Crossroad
text:
Section 3B.31 Standard 2 - Markings for a Diamond Interchange with a Transposed Alignment Crossroad
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 586

On the transposed alignment, each direction shall be considered a one-way roadway whereas the edge line convention shall be in accordance with Section 3B.09. Both yellow and white edge lines shall be used.

metadata.section_title: Markings for a Diamond Interchange with a Transposed Alignment Crossroad

title: Section 3B.31 Standard 3 - Markings for a Diamond Interchange with a Transposed Alignment Crossroad
text:
Section 3B.31 Standard 3 - Markings for a Diamond Interchange with a Transposed Alignment Crossroad
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3B. Pavement And Curb Markings
Page: 586

A lane-use arrow (see Section 3B.23) shall be used in each approach lane at the crossover intersection.

metadata.section_title: Markings for a Diamond Interchange with a Transposed Alignment Crossroad

title: Section 3C.01 Support 1 - General
text:
Section 3C.01 Support 1 - General
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3C. Crosswalk Markings
Page: 589

Crosswalk markings provide guidance for pedestrians who are crossing roadways by defining and delineating paths on approaches to and within signalized intersections, and on approaches to other intersections where traffic stops.

title: Section 3C.01 Support 2 - General
text:
Section 3C.01 Support 2 - General
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3C. Crosswalk Markings
Page: 589

In conjunction with signs and other measures, crosswalk markings help to alert road users of a designated pedestrian crossing point across roadways at locations that are not controlled by traffic control signals or STOP or YIELD signs.

title: Section 3C.01 Support 3 - General
text:
Section 3C.01 Support 3 - General
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3C. Crosswalk Markings
Page: 589

At non-intersection locations, crosswalk markings legally establish the crosswalk.

title: Section 3C.01 Support 4 - General
text:
Section 3C.01 Support 4 - General
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3C. Crosswalk Markings
Page: 589

Detectable warning surfaces mark boundaries between pedestrian and vehicular ways where there is no raised curb. Detectable warning surfaces are typically installed where curb ramps are constructed at the junction of sidewalks and the roadway or shoulder, for marked and unmarked crosswalks. Detectable warning surfaces contrast visually with adjacent walking surfaces, either light-on-dark, or dark-on-light. The U.S. Department of Justice 2010 ADA Standards for Accessible Design, September 15, 2010, 28 CFR 35 and 36, Americans with Disabilities Act of 1990 contains specifications for the design of detectable warning surfaces.

title: Section 3C.02 Guidance 1 - Application of Crosswalk Markings
text:
Section 3C.02 Guidance 1 - Application of Crosswalk Markings
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3C. Crosswalk Markings
Page: 589

At locations controlled by traffic control signals, crosswalk markings should be installed.

title: Section 3C.02 Option 2 - Application of Crosswalk Markings
text:
Section 3C.02 Option 2 - Application of Crosswalk Markings
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3C. Crosswalk Markings
Page: 589

Crosswalk markings may be omitted if engineering judgment indicates they are not needed to direct pedestrians to the proper crossing path(s).

title: Section 3C.02 Guidance 3 - Application of Crosswalk Markings
text:
Section 3C.02 Guidance 3 - Application of Crosswalk Markings
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3C. Crosswalk Markings
Page: 589

On approaches controlled by STOP or YIELD signs, crosswalk markings should be installed where engineering judgment indicates they are needed to direct pedestrians to the proper crossing path(s).

title: Section 3C.02 Guidance 4 - Application of Crosswalk Markings
text:
Section 3C.02 Guidance 4 - Application of Crosswalk Markings
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3C. Crosswalk Markings
Page: 589

At uncontrolled approaches, an engineering study should be performed before a marked crosswalk is installed. The following criteria should be considered: A. Total number of approach lanes, B. The presence of a median, C. The distance from adjacent signalized intersections or other controlled crossings, D. Projected pedestrian and bicyclist volumes, E. Pedestrian and bicyclist paths of travel, F. Pedestrian ages and abilities, G. Pedestrian and bicyclist delays, H. Location or frequency of public transit stops, I. Average daily traffic (ADT), J. Speed limit or the 85th-percentile speed, K. The horizontal and vertical geometry of the crossing location, L. The possible consolidation of multiple crossing points, M. The availability of street lighting, and N. Other appropriate factors.

title: Section 3C.02 Standard 5 - Application of Crosswalk Markings
text:
Section 3C.02 Standard 5 - Application of Crosswalk Markings
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3C. Crosswalk Markings
Page: 589

Crosswalk markings shall be provided at legally established crosswalks at non-intersection locations.

title: Section 3C.02 Guidance 6 - Application of Crosswalk Markings
text:
Section 3C.02 Guidance 6 - Application of Crosswalk Markings
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3C. Crosswalk Markings
Page: 590

The installation of other traffic control devices and other measures designed to reduce traffic speeds, shorten crossing distances, enhance driver awareness of the crossing, and/or provide active warning of pedestrian presence, should be considered in addition to a new marked crosswalk and signs across an uncontrolled approach to an intersection or midblock crossing location where any of the following conditions exist: Rev. 1 A. The roadway has four or more lanes of travel without a raised median or pedestrian refuge island and an ADT of 12,000 vehicles per day or greater; or B. The roadway has four or more lanes of travel with a raised median or pedestrian refuge island and an ADT of 15,000 vehicles per day or greater, or C. The posted speed limit is 40 mph or greater, or D. A crash study reveals that multiple-threat crashes are the predominant crash type on a multi-lane approach, or E. When adequate visibility cannot be provided by parking prohibitions. December 2025

title: Section 3C.02 Support 7 - Application of Crosswalk Markings
text:
Section 3C.02 Support 7 - Application of Crosswalk Markings
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3C. Crosswalk Markings
Page: 590

Chapter 4J contains information on pedestrian hybrid beacons.

title: Section 3C.02 Support 8 - Application of Crosswalk Markings
text:
Section 3C.02 Support 8 - Application of Crosswalk Markings
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3C. Crosswalk Markings
Page: 590

Chapter 4L contains information on rectangular rapid flashing beacons.

title: Section 3C.04 Guidance 1 - Transverse Line Crosswalks
text:
Section 3C.04 Guidance 1 - Transverse Line Crosswalks
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3C. Crosswalk Markings
Page: 591

Transverse line crosswalk markings should be limited to locations controlled by traffic control signals or on approaches controlled by STOP or YIELD signs.

title: Section 3C.04 Support 2 - Transverse Line Crosswalks
text:
Section 3C.04 Support 2 - Transverse Line Crosswalks
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3C. Crosswalk Markings
Page: 591

Transverse line crosswalk marking design consists of two parallel transverse lines (see Figure 3C-1).

title: Section 3C.04 Support 3 - Transverse Line Crosswalks
text:
Section 3C.04 Support 3 - Transverse Line Crosswalks
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3C. Crosswalk Markings
Page: 591

Transverse line crosswalk markings can provide benefits to crosswalk operations including: A. Define where the channelization of pedestrians or other non-motorized users is necessary to facilitate crossing the roadway. B. Alert motorists to the location of where pedestrians and other non-motorized users might be expected when crossing the roadway. C. Emphasize a crosswalk at a controlled intersection. D. Fulfill a legal need to mark the crosswalk.

title: Section 3C.05 Option 1 - High-Visibility Crosswalks
text:
Section 3C.05 Option 1 - High-Visibility Crosswalks
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3C. Crosswalk Markings
Page: 591

High-visibility crosswalk markings may be used where additional conspicuity is desired for a crosswalk over transverse line crosswalk markings.

title: Section 3C.05 Support 2 - High-Visibility Crosswalks
text:
Section 3C.05 Support 2 - High-Visibility Crosswalks
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3C. Crosswalk Markings
Page: 591

High-visibility crosswalk markings include the longitudinal bar, ladder, and bar pair designs (see Figure 3C-1).

title: Section 3C.05 Support 3 - High-Visibility Crosswalks
text:
Section 3C.05 Support 3 - High-Visibility Crosswalks
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3C. Crosswalk Markings
Page: 591

High-visibility crosswalk markings can provide benefits to crosswalk operations including: A. Providing greater detection distances for the approaching motorist. B. Emphasizing a crosswalk where substantial numbers of pedestrians cross without any other traffic control device. C. Emphasizing a crosswalk at an uncontrolled approach. D. Emphasizing the location where a high number of conflicts between turning motorists and users of the crosswalk are expected. E. Improving visibility of the crosswalk location for otherwise difficult-to-detect pedestrians or other non- motorized users of the crosswalk. F. Emphasizing a school crossing.

title: Section 3C.05 Standard 4 - High-Visibility Crosswalks
text:
Section 3C.05 Standard 4 - High-Visibility Crosswalks
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3C. Crosswalk Markings
Page: 592

The minimum number of individual longitudinal elements to establish a high-visibility crosswalk shall be three. For the bar pair crosswalk design (see Section 3C.08), a coupling set of two longitudinal bars shall be considered to be one individual longitudinal element. December 2025 MUTCD 11th Edition - Revision 1

title: Section 3C.05 Guidance 5 - High-Visibility Crosswalks
text:
Section 3C.05 Guidance 5 - High-Visibility Crosswalks
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3C. Crosswalk Markings
Page: 592

The dimensions of the individual longitudinal element and the lateral spacing between subsequent individual longitudinal elements for a high-visibility crosswalk should be uniform when establishing the crosswalk.

title: Section 3C.05 Guidance 6 - High-Visibility Crosswalks
text:
Section 3C.05 Guidance 6 - High-Visibility Crosswalks
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3C. Crosswalk Markings
Page: 592

The dimensions of the individual longitudinal element and the lateral spacing between subsequent individual longitudinal elements for a high-visibility crosswalk should be uniform when establishing separate crosswalks on multiple approaches to the same intersection and on both sides of a median refuge if one is present.

title: Section 3C.05 Guidance 7 - High-Visibility Crosswalks
text:
Section 3C.05 Guidance 7 - High-Visibility Crosswalks
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3C. Crosswalk Markings
Page: 592

The individual longitudinal elements of a high-visibility crosswalk should be angled such that they are parallel to the travel path of approaching traffic.

title: Section 3C.05 Option 8 - High-Visibility Crosswalks
text:
Section 3C.05 Option 8 - High-Visibility Crosswalks
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3C. Crosswalk Markings
Page: 592

The lateral spacing between longitudinal elements may be staggered to avoid wheel paths, center lines, and lane lines.

title: Section 3C.06 Support 1 - Longitudinal Bar Crosswalks
text:
Section 3C.06 Support 1 - Longitudinal Bar Crosswalks
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3C. Crosswalk Markings
Page: 592

The longitudinal bar crosswalk marking design (see Figure 3C-1) provides for improved detection and recognition over the transverse line crosswalk for people with low vision and cognitive impairments.

title: Section 3C.06 Standard 2 - Longitudinal Bar Crosswalks
text:
Section 3C.06 Standard 2 - Longitudinal Bar Crosswalks
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3C. Crosswalk Markings
Page: 592

The width of an individual longitudinal bar shall not be less than 12 inches or greater than 24 inches.

title: Section 3C.06 Standard 3 - Longitudinal Bar Crosswalks
text:
Section 3C.06 Standard 3 - Longitudinal Bar Crosswalks
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3C. Crosswalk Markings
Page: 592

The lateral spacing between subsequent longitudinal bars shall not be less than 12 inches or greater than 60 inches. The lateral spacing of the longitudinal bars shall not exceed 2.5 times the width of a longitudinal bar.

title: Section 3C.07 Support 1 - Ladder Crosswalks
text:
Section 3C.07 Support 1 - Ladder Crosswalks
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3C. Crosswalk Markings
Page: 592

Ladder crosswalks (see Figure 3C-1) implement a design where longitudinal bars are used in the interior portion of the crosswalk between the transverse lines that define the limits of the crosswalk. Rev. 1

title: Section 3C.07 Support 2 - Ladder Crosswalks
text:
Section 3C.07 Support 2 - Ladder Crosswalks
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3C. Crosswalk Markings
Page: 592

The ladder crosswalk marking design provides for improved detection and recognition over the transverse crosswalk for people with low vision and cognitive impairments.

title: Section 3C.07 Support 3 - Ladder Crosswalks
text:
Section 3C.07 Support 3 - Ladder Crosswalks
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3C. Crosswalk Markings
Page: 592

Since the longitudinal component of the ladder crosswalk marking design is similar to the benefits provided by the longitudinal bar crosswalk design, the ladder crosswalk design is normally used to discourage or prohibit diagonal walking between crosswalks.

title: Section 3C.07 Standard 4 - Ladder Crosswalks
text:
Section 3C.07 Standard 4 - Ladder Crosswalks
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3C. Crosswalk Markings
Page: 592

The transverse lines used to establish the limits of the ladder crosswalk shall not be less than 6 inches or greater than 24 inches in width.

title: Section 3C.07 Standard 5 - Ladder Crosswalks
text:
Section 3C.07 Standard 5 - Ladder Crosswalks
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3C. Crosswalk Markings
Page: 592

The width of an individual interior longitudinal bar shall not be less than 12 inches or greater than 24 inches.

title: Section 3C.07 Standard 6 - Ladder Crosswalks
text:
Section 3C.07 Standard 6 - Ladder Crosswalks
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3C. Crosswalk Markings
Page: 592

The lateral spacing between subsequent interior longitudinal bars shall not be less than 12 inches or greater than 60 inches. The lateral spacing of the interior longitudinal bars shall not exceed 2.5 times the width of an interior longitudinal bar.

title: Section 3C.07 Option 7 - Ladder Crosswalks
text:
Section 3C.07 Option 7 - Ladder Crosswalks
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3C. Crosswalk Markings
Page: 592

Where it might be necessary to alleviate a distortion due to perspective (foreshortening) caused by approaching roadway geometry that curves or to accommodate low approach angles of the approaching motorists, the interior longitudinal bars may be rotated up to 45 degrees to the transverse lines to remain parallel to approaching traffic. Rev. 1

title: Section 3C.08 Support 1 - Bar Pair Crosswalks
text:
Section 3C.08 Support 1 - Bar Pair Crosswalks
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3C. Crosswalk Markings
Page: 592

Bar pair crosswalks (see Figure 3C-1) can provide the same benefits as other high-visibility crosswalk designs with the opportunity for less maintenance.

title: Section 3C.08 Support 2 - Bar Pair Crosswalks
text:
Section 3C.08 Support 2 - Bar Pair Crosswalks
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3C. Crosswalk Markings
Page: 593

Bar pair crosswalks can be useful in locations that are susceptible to slip and fall incidents exacerbated by extreme or inclement weather, or in locations where high motorcycle or bicycle use is expected, in order to maximize wheel traction with the road surface. December 2025 MUTCD 11th Edition - Revision 1

title: Section 3C.08 Standard 3 - Bar Pair Crosswalks
text:
Section 3C.08 Standard 3 - Bar Pair Crosswalks
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3C. Crosswalk Markings
Page: 593

The width of an individual longitudinal bar that establishes one-half of the bar pair shall not be less than 8 inches or greater than 12 inches. The lateral spacing between successive individual longitudinal bars within the same bar pair shall be equal to the width of one longitudinal bar.

title: Section 3C.08 Standard 4 - Bar Pair Crosswalks
text:
Section 3C.08 Standard 4 - Bar Pair Crosswalks
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3C. Crosswalk Markings
Page: 593

The lateral spacing between subsequent longitudinal bar pairs shall not be less than 24 inches or greater than 60 inches, or 2.5 times the width of the total width of a bar pair.

title: Section 3C.08 Standard 5 - Bar Pair Crosswalks
text:
Section 3C.08 Standard 5 - Bar Pair Crosswalks
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3C. Crosswalk Markings
Page: 593

Longitudinal bar pair crosswalks shall not be installed with accompanying transverse lines.

title: Section 3C.09 Standard 1 - Crosswalk Markings at Circular Intersections
text:
Section 3C.09 Standard 1 - Crosswalk Markings at Circular Intersections
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3C. Crosswalk Markings
Page: 593

Crosswalk markings shall not be provided to or from the central island of a roundabout.

title: Section 3C.09 Guidance 2 - Crosswalk Markings at Circular Intersections
text:
Section 3C.09 Guidance 2 - Crosswalk Markings at Circular Intersections
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3C. Crosswalk Markings
Page: 593

If pedestrian facilities are provided, crosswalks should be marked across roundabout entrances and exits to indicate where pedestrians are intended to cross.

title: Section 3C.09 Guidance 3 - Crosswalk Markings at Circular Intersections
text:
Section 3C.09 Guidance 3 - Crosswalk Markings at Circular Intersections
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3C. Crosswalk Markings
Page: 593

On an approach to a circular intersection controlled by a YIELD sign and at uncontrolled exits, crosswalks should be a minimum of 20 feet from the edge of the circulatory roadway.

title: Section 3C.09 Support 4 - Crosswalk Markings at Circular Intersections
text:
Section 3C.09 Support 4 - Crosswalk Markings at Circular Intersections
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3C. Crosswalk Markings
Page: 593

Chapter 3D provides figures that illustrate examples of crosswalk markings for roundabouts.

title: Section 3C.10 Option 1 - Crosswalks for Exclusive Pedestrian Phases that Permit Diagonal Crossings
text:
Section 3C.10 Option 1 - Crosswalks for Exclusive Pedestrian Phases that Permit Diagonal Crossings
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3C. Crosswalk Markings
Page: 593

When an exclusive pedestrian phase that permits diagonal crossing of an intersection is provided at a traffic control signal, a marking as shown in Figure 3C-2 may be used for the crosswalk.

metadata.section_title: Crosswalks for Exclusive Pedestrian Phases that Permit Diagonal Crossings

title: Section 3C.10 Guidance 2 - Crosswalks for Exclusive Pedestrian Phases that Permit Diagonal Crossings
text:
Section 3C.10 Guidance 2 - Crosswalks for Exclusive Pedestrian Phases that Permit Diagonal Crossings
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3C. Crosswalk Markings
Page: 593

The segments of the crosswalk marking that facilitate the diagonal crossing should not use high-visibility crosswalk markings.

metadata.section_title: Crosswalks for Exclusive Pedestrian Phases that Permit Diagonal Crossings

title: Section 3C.11 Support 1 - Crosswalks at Diamond Interchanges with a Transposed Alignment Crossroad
text:
Section 3C.11 Support 1 - Crosswalks at Diamond Interchanges with a Transposed Alignment Crossroad
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3C. Crosswalk Markings
Page: 593

Diamond interchanges with a transposed alignment crossroad, also known as double- crossover diamond interchanges or diverging diamond interchanges, include directional crossovers on either side of the interchange that transpose the crossroad which results in vehicles traveling on the left-hand side of the street or highway between the crossover intersections. The potential for altered travel paths for pedestrians and the associated, unique, operational aspects such as traffic approaching from unexpected directions and unfamiliar signal phasing schemes are important considerations.

metadata.section_title: Crosswalks at Diamond Interchanges with a Transposed Alignment Crossroad

title: Section 3C.11 Guidance 2 - Crosswalks at Diamond Interchanges with a Transposed Alignment Crossroad
text:
Section 3C.11 Guidance 2 - Crosswalks at Diamond Interchanges with a Transposed Alignment Crossroad
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3C. Crosswalk Markings
Page: 593

If pedestrian facilities are provided, pedestrian crossing movements of the crossroads at a diamond interchange with a transposed alignment crossroad should be marked at the crossover intersections where motor vehicle traffic becomes transposed.

metadata.section_title: Crosswalks at Diamond Interchanges with a Transposed Alignment Crossroad

title: Section 3C.11 Guidance 3 - Crosswalks at Diamond Interchanges with a Transposed Alignment Crossroad
text:
Section 3C.11 Guidance 3 - Crosswalks at Diamond Interchanges with a Transposed Alignment Crossroad
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3C. Crosswalk Markings
Page: 593

If pedestrian facilities are provided, crosswalks should be marked across ramp terminals at diamond interchanges with a transposed alignment crossroad to indicate where pedestrians are intended to cross.

metadata.section_title: Crosswalks at Diamond Interchanges with a Transposed Alignment Crossroad

title: Section 3C.11 Guidance 4 - Crosswalks at Diamond Interchanges with a Transposed Alignment Crossroad
text:
Section 3C.11 Guidance 4 - Crosswalks at Diamond Interchanges with a Transposed Alignment Crossroad
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3C. Crosswalk Markings
Page: 594

Crosswalks across ramps at diamond interchanges with a transposed alignment crossroad with yield controlled vehicle movements should be located a minimum of 20 feet from the edge of an intersecting ramp. December 2025 MUTCD 11th Edition - Revision 1

metadata.section_title: Crosswalks at Diamond Interchanges with a Transposed Alignment Crossroad

title: Section 3C.12 Support 1 - Pedestrian Islands and Medians
text:
Section 3C.12 Support 1 - Pedestrian Islands and Medians
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3C. Crosswalk Markings
Page: 595

Raised islands or raised medians of sufficient width that are placed in the center area of a street or highway can serve as a place of refuge for pedestrians who are attempting to cross at a midblock or intersection location. Center islands or medians allow pedestrians to find an adequate gap in one direction of traffic at a time, as the pedestrians are able to stop, if necessary, in the center island or median area and wait for an adequate gap in the other direction of traffic before crossing the second half of the street or highway. The U.S. Department of Justice 2010 ADA Standards for Accessible Design, September 15, 2010, 28 CFR 35 and 36, Americans with Disabilities Act of 1990 contains specifications for the design of detectable warning surfaces and provides technical requirements that can be used to determine the minimum width for accessible refuge islands. December 2025

title: Section 3D.01 Guidance 1 - General
text:
Section 3D.01 Guidance 1 - General
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3D. Circular Intersection Markings
Page: 595

Pavement markings and signing for a circular intersection should be integrally designed to correspond to the geometric design and intended lane use of a circular intersection.

title: Section 3D.01 Guidance 2 - General
text:
Section 3D.01 Guidance 2 - General
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3D. Circular Intersection Markings
Page: 595

Markings on the approaches to a circular intersection and on the circulatory roadway should be compatible with each other to provide a consistent message to road users. The markings should supplement the signing, both conveying the optional and mandatory movements such that road users will know to choose the proper lane in the approach to the circular intersection and remain in that lane throughout departure from the circulatory roadway.

title: Section 3D.01 Support 3 - General
text:
Section 3D.01 Support 3 - General
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3D. Circular Intersection Markings
Page: 595

Common circular intersection types include roundabouts, rotaries, and traffic circles (see definitions in Section 1C.02). Traffic circles and rotaries are often much larger than roundabouts. Modern roundabouts feature channelized, curved approaches that reduce vehicle speed. Traffic calming circles are smaller and are typically used on urban or suburban neighborhood streets.

title: Section 3D.01 Support 4 - General
text:
Section 3D.01 Support 4 - General
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3D. Circular Intersection Markings
Page: 595

Figure 3D-1 provides an example of the pavement markings for approach and circulatory roadways at a roundabout. Figures 3D-2 through 3D-8 illustrate examples of markings for roundabouts of various geometric and lane-use configurations.

title: Section 3D.01 Support 5 - General
text:
Section 3D.01 Support 5 - General
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3D. Circular Intersection Markings
Page: 595

Actuated LED pedestrian warning signs (see Section 2A.12), traffic control signals, pedestrian hybrid beacons, and rectangular rapid flashing beacons (see Part 4) are sometimes used at roundabouts to facilitate the crossing of pedestrians or to meter traffic.

title: Section 3D.02 Standard 1 - White Lane Line Pavement Markings for Roundabouts
text:
Section 3D.02 Standard 1 - White Lane Line Pavement Markings for Roundabouts
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3D. Circular Intersection Markings
Page: 595

Multi-lane approaches to roundabouts shall have lane lines.

metadata.section_title: White Lane Line Pavement Markings for Roundabouts

title: Section 3D.02 Standard 2 - White Lane Line Pavement Markings for Roundabouts
text:
Section 3D.02 Standard 2 - White Lane Line Pavement Markings for Roundabouts
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3D. Circular Intersection Markings
Page: 595

A through lane on a roadway that becomes a dropped lane (mandatory left-turn or right-turn lane) at a roundabout shall be marked with a dotted white lane line in accordance with Section 3B.07.

metadata.section_title: White Lane Line Pavement Markings for Roundabouts

title: Section 3D.02 Guidance 3 - White Lane Line Pavement Markings for Roundabouts
text:
Section 3D.02 Guidance 3 - White Lane Line Pavement Markings for Roundabouts
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3D. Circular Intersection Markings
Page: 595

Multi-lane roundabouts should have lane line markings within the circulatory roadway to continuously channelize traffic in the circulatory roadway and through the departure movement.

metadata.section_title: White Lane Line Pavement Markings for Roundabouts

title: Section 3D.02 Standard 4 - White Lane Line Pavement Markings for Roundabouts
text:
Section 3D.02 Standard 4 - White Lane Line Pavement Markings for Roundabouts
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3D. Circular Intersection Markings
Page: 595

Continuous concentric lane lines shall not be used within the circulatory roadway of a roundabout.

metadata.section_title: White Lane Line Pavement Markings for Roundabouts

title: Section 3D.02 Option 5 - White Lane Line Pavement Markings for Roundabouts
text:
Section 3D.02 Option 5 - White Lane Line Pavement Markings for Roundabouts
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3D. Circular Intersection Markings
Page: 595

Channelizing lines (see Section 3B.08) and chevron and diagonal markings (see Section 3B.25) may be used on the approaches to and within the circulatory roadway of multi-lane roundabouts to separate traffic lanes, discourage lane changing, and/or compensate for off-tracking of larger trucks and vehicles.

metadata.section_title: White Lane Line Pavement Markings for Roundabouts

title: Section 3D.02 Support 6 - White Lane Line Pavement Markings for Roundabouts
text:
Section 3D.02 Support 6 - White Lane Line Pavement Markings for Roundabouts
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3D. Circular Intersection Markings
Page: 595

Reducing the spacing between lines of a broken lane line allows better delineation of the lower-radius curves typically found in circular intersections.

metadata.section_title: White Lane Line Pavement Markings for Roundabouts

title: Section 3D.03 Guidance 1 - Edge Line Pavement Markings for Roundabout Circulatory Roadways
text:
Section 3D.03 Guidance 1 - Edge Line Pavement Markings for Roundabout Circulatory Roadways
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3D. Circular Intersection Markings
Page: 595

A white edge line should be used on the outer (right-hand) edge of the circulatory roadway.

metadata.section_title: Edge Line Pavement Markings for Roundabout Circulatory Roadways

title: Section 3D.03 Guidance 2 - Edge Line Pavement Markings for Roundabout Circulatory Roadways
text:
Section 3D.03 Guidance 2 - Edge Line Pavement Markings for Roundabout Circulatory Roadways
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3D. Circular Intersection Markings
Page: 595

Where a white edge line is used for the circulatory roadway, it should be as follows (see Figure 3D-1): A. A solid line adjacent to the splitter island, and B. A wide dotted line across the lane(s) entering the roundabout.

metadata.section_title: Edge Line Pavement Markings for Roundabout Circulatory Roadways

title: Section 3D.03 Standard 3 - Edge Line Pavement Markings for Roundabout Circulatory Roadways
text:
Section 3D.03 Standard 3 - Edge Line Pavement Markings for Roundabout Circulatory Roadways
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3D. Circular Intersection Markings
Page: 595

Edge lines and edge line extensions shall not be placed across the exits from the circulatory roadway at roundabouts.

metadata.section_title: Edge Line Pavement Markings for Roundabout Circulatory Roadways

title: Section 3D.03 Option 4 - Edge Line Pavement Markings for Roundabout Circulatory Roadways
text:
Section 3D.03 Option 4 - Edge Line Pavement Markings for Roundabout Circulatory Roadways
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3D. Circular Intersection Markings
Page: 605

A yellow edge line may be placed around the inner (left-hand) edge of the circulatory roadway (see Figure 3D-1) and may be used to channelize traffic (see Drawing B in Figure 3D-3). Figure 3D-1. Example of Markings for Approach and Circulatory Roadways at a Roundabout Figure 3D-2. Example of Markings for a One-Lane Roundabout Figure 3D-3. Example of Markings for a Two-Lane Roundabout with One-Lane and Two-Lane Approaches (Sheet 1 of 2) A - Unextended central island Figure 3D-3. Example of Markings for a Two-Lane Roundabout with One-Lane and Two-Lane Approaches (Sheet 2 of 2) B - Central island extended by pavement markings C - Central island extended by a truck apron Figure 3D-4. Example of Markings for a Two-Lane Roundabout with One-Lane Exits Figure 3D-5. Example of Markings for a Two-Lane Roundabout with Two-Lane Exits Figure 3D-6. Example of Markings for a Two-Lane Roundabout with a Double Left Turn Figure 3D-7. Example of Markings for a Two-Lane Roundabout with a Double Right Turn Figure 3D-8. Example of Markings for a Diamond Interchange with Two Circular-Shaped Roundabout Ramp Terminals

metadata.section_title: Edge Line Pavement Markings for Roundabout Circulatory Roadways

title: Section 3D.05 Option 1 - Word and Symbol Pavement Markings for Roundabouts
text:
Section 3D.05 Option 1 - Word and Symbol Pavement Markings for Roundabouts
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3D. Circular Intersection Markings
Page: 605

YIELD (word) (see Figure 3D-1) and YIELD AHEAD (symbol or word) pavement markings may be used on approaches to roundabouts.

metadata.section_title: Word and Symbol Pavement Markings for Roundabouts

title: Section 3D.05 Option 2 - Word and Symbol Pavement Markings for Roundabouts
text:
Section 3D.05 Option 2 - Word and Symbol Pavement Markings for Roundabouts
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3D. Circular Intersection Markings
Page: 605

Word and/or route shield pavement markings may be used on an approach to or within the circulatory roadway of a roundabout to provide route and/or destination guidance information to road users (see Figure 3D-8).

metadata.section_title: Word and Symbol Pavement Markings for Roundabouts

title: Section 3D.06 Guidance 1 - Arrow Pavement Markings for Roundabouts
text:
Section 3D.06 Guidance 1 - Arrow Pavement Markings for Roundabouts
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3D. Circular Intersection Markings
Page: 605

Lane-use arrow pavement markings should not be used on single-lane approaches to circular intersections.

title: Section 3D.06 Guidance 2 - Arrow Pavement Markings for Roundabouts
text:
Section 3D.06 Guidance 2 - Arrow Pavement Markings for Roundabouts
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3D. Circular Intersection Markings
Page: 605

Lane-use arrows should be used on approaches to circular intersections with double left or double right turns.

title: Section 3D.06 Standard 3 - Arrow Pavement Markings for Roundabouts
text:
Section 3D.06 Standard 3 - Arrow Pavement Markings for Roundabouts
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3D. Circular Intersection Markings
Page: 605

Lane-use arrow pavement markings shall not be provided between a crosswalk and a wide dotted line across the lane(s) entering the circular roadway.

title: Section 3D.06 Option 4 - Arrow Pavement Markings for Roundabouts
text:
Section 3D.06 Option 4 - Arrow Pavement Markings for Roundabouts
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3D. Circular Intersection Markings
Page: 605

Where lane-use arrows are used on the approaches to a roundabout, they may be either normal or curved-stem (see Drawing F in Figure 3B-21).

title: Section 3D.06 Option 5 - Arrow Pavement Markings for Roundabouts
text:
Section 3D.06 Option 5 - Arrow Pavement Markings for Roundabouts
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3D. Circular Intersection Markings
Page: 605

An oval or circle may be used with the lane-use arrows to symbolize the central island (see Drawing F in Figure 3B-21).

title: Section 3D.06 Guidance 6 - Arrow Pavement Markings for Roundabouts
text:
Section 3D.06 Guidance 6 - Arrow Pavement Markings for Roundabouts
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3D. Circular Intersection Markings
Page: 605

If lane-use arrows are used on the approaches to a roundabout, the style used should match the style of the lane-use arrows (normal or curved-stem) used on the regulatory lane-use signs on the approach.

title: Section 3D.06 Guidance 7 - Arrow Pavement Markings for Roundabouts
text:
Section 3D.06 Guidance 7 - Arrow Pavement Markings for Roundabouts
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3D. Circular Intersection Markings
Page: 605

If lane-use arrow pavement markings are used within the circulatory roadway of multi-lane roundabouts, normal lane-use arrows (see Section 3B.23 and Figure 3B-21) should be used.

title: Section 3D.06 Support 8 - Arrow Pavement Markings for Roundabouts
text:
Section 3D.06 Support 8 - Arrow Pavement Markings for Roundabouts
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3D. Circular Intersection Markings
Page: 605

Details and sizes of the standard and curved-stem arrows that can be used for circular intersections are contained in the “Standard Highway Signs” publication (see Section 1A.05).

title: Section 3D.07 Option 1 - Markings for Other Circular Intersections
text:
Section 3D.07 Option 1 - Markings for Other Circular Intersections
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3D. Circular Intersection Markings
Page: 606

The markings shown in this Chapter may be used at other circular intersections if engineering judgment indicates that their presence will benefit drivers, pedestrians, or other road users. Figure 2B-21 provides an example of markings at a mini-roundabout.

title: Section 3E.01 Support 1 - General
text:
Section 3E.01 Support 1 - General
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3E. Preferential Lane Markings For Motor Vehicles
Page: 606

Preferential lanes are established for one or more of a wide variety of special uses, including, but not limited to, high-occupancy vehicle (HOV) lanes, electronic toll collection (ETC) lanes, price-managed lanes, bus only lanes, taxi only lanes, and light rail transit only lanes.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 3E. Preferential Lane Markings For Motor Vehicles

title: Section 3E.01 Support 2 - General
text:
Section 3E.01 Support 2 - General
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3E. Preferential Lane Markings For Motor Vehicles
Page: 606

This Chapter contains the pavement marking provisions for preferential lanes used by motor vehicles and light rail transit. Part 9 contains information for pavement markings for bicycle lanes.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 3E. Preferential Lane Markings For Motor Vehicles

title: Section 3E.01 Support 3 - General
text:
Section 3E.01 Support 3 - General
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3E. Preferential Lane Markings For Motor Vehicles
Page: 606

Chapter 3H contains information for the use and application of colored pavement that can be used in preferential lanes to supplement the pavement markings described in this Chapter.

title: Section 3E.02 Support 1 - Longitudinal Markings
text:
Section 3E.02 Support 1 - Longitudinal Markings
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3E. Preferential Lane Markings For Motor Vehicles
Page: 606

Preferential lanes can take many forms depending on the level of usage and the design of the facility. They might be barrier-separated or buffer-separated from the adjacent general-purpose lanes, or they might be contiguous with the adjacent general-purpose lanes. Barrier-separated preferential lanes might be operated in a constant direction or be operated as reversible lanes. Some reversible preferential lanes on a divided highway might be operated counter-flow to the direction of traffic on the immediately adjacent general-purpose lanes. Section 1C.02 contains definitions of these terms.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 3E. Preferential Lane Markings For Motor Vehicles

title: Section 3E.02 Support 2 - Longitudinal Markings
text:
Section 3E.02 Support 2 - Longitudinal Markings
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3E. Preferential Lane Markings For Motor Vehicles
Page: 606

Preferential lanes might be operated full-time (24 hours per day on all days), for extended periods of the day, part-time (restricted usage during specific hours on specified days), or on a variable basis (such as a strategy for a managed lane).

metadata.chapter: Chapter 3E. Preferential Lane Markings For Motor Vehicles

If there are two or more preferential lanes for traffic moving in the same direction, the lane lines between the preferential lanes shall be normal width broken white lines.

Page: 606

Where preferential lanes and other travel lanes are separated by a buffer space wider than 4 feet and crossing the buffer space is prohibited, chevron markings (see Section 3B.25) should be placed in the buffer area (see Drawing A in Figure 3E-2).

Section 3E.02 Guidance 9 - Longitudinal Markings

The buffer space for a conventional road should be designed so that it is not misinterpreted as on-street parking, a bicycle lane, or any other type of lane.

Section 3E.02 Option 10 - Longitudinal Markings

If a full-time or part-time contiguous preferential lane is separated from the other travel lanes by a wide broken single white line (see Drawing C in Figure 3E-3), the spacing or skip pattern of the line may be reduced and the width of the line may be increased.

Section 3E.02 Standard 11 - Longitudinal Markings

Page: 606

At direct exits from a preferential lane, dotted white line markings shall be used to separate the tapered or parallel deceleration lane for the direct exit (including the taper) from the adjacent continuing preferential through lane, to reduce the chance of unintended exit maneuvers.

text:
Section 3E.03 Standard 2 - Preferential Lane Word and Symbol Markings
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3E. Preferential Lane Markings For Motor Vehicles
Page: 611

When a preferential lane is established, the preferential lane shall be marked with one or more of the following word or symbol markings for the preferential lane use specified: A. HOV lane-white lines formed in a diamond-shaped symbol or the word message HOV. The diamond shall be at least 2.5 feet wide and 12 feet in length. The lines shall be at least 6 inches in width. B. ETC Account-Only lane-except as provided in Paragraph 8 of this Section, a word marking or pictograph using the name of the ETC payment system required for use of the lane, such as E-Z PASS ONLY. C. Price-managed lane-the word marking EXPRESS or EXPRESS LANE(S) (see Section 2G.17). D. Bus only lane or bus stop-the word marking BUS ONLY or BUS STOP. E. Taxi only lane or taxi stand -the word marking TAXI ONLY or TAXI STAND. F. Light rail transit lane-the word marking LRT ONLY. G. Other type of preferential lane-a word marking appropriate to the restriction. Figure 3E-2. Markings for Buffer-Separated Preferential Lanes (Sheet 2 of 2) C - Preferential lane(s) where enter/exit movements are PERMITTED D - Right-hand side preferential lane(s) Buf If no barrier or median is present and the left-hand side of the lane is the center line of a two-way roadway, use a double yellow center line Example of preferential lane word pavement markings Table 3E-2.
