text:
Section 3E.03 Guidance 3 - Preferential Lane Word and Symbol Markings
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3E. Preferential Lane Markings For Motor Vehicles
Page: 611

If multiple preferential lane uses are allowed in a single lane, the word or symbol marking for each preferential lane should be used.

metadata.section_title: Preferential Lane Word and Symbol Markings
metadata.chapter: Chapter 3E. Preferential Lane Markings For Motor Vehicles

title: Section 3E.03 Standard 4 - Preferential Lane Word and Symbol Markings
text:
Section 3E.03 Standard 4 - Preferential Lane Word and Symbol Markings
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3E. Preferential Lane Markings For Motor Vehicles
Page: 611

Pavement word or symbol markings for motorcycles and Inherently Low Emission Vehicles (ILEV) shall not be used to mark the preferential lane if motorcycles and ILEVs are allowed to use the preferential lane.

metadata.section_title: Preferential Lane Word and Symbol Markings
metadata.chapter: Chapter 3E. Preferential Lane Markings For Motor Vehicles

title: Section 3E.03 Support 5 - Preferential Lane Word and Symbol Markings
text:
Section 3E.03 Support 5 - Preferential Lane Word and Symbol Markings
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3E. Preferential Lane Markings For Motor Vehicles
Page: 611

Motorcycles and Inherently Low Emission Vehicles (ILEV) that are allowed to use a preferential lane are granted an exception such as through an established High-Occupancy Vehicle (HOV) regulation. Communicating that motorcycles and ILEVs are allowed to use the preferential lane is accomplished through regulatory signing (see Sections 2G.03 and 2G.04) that complements HOV signing.

metadata.section_title: Preferential Lane Word and Symbol Markings
metadata.chapter: Chapter 3E. Preferential Lane Markings For Motor Vehicles

text:
Section 3E.03 Standard 6 - Preferential Lane Word and Symbol Markings
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3E. Preferential Lane Markings For Motor Vehicles
Page: 612

Static or changeable message regulatory signs (see Sections 2G.03 through 2G.07) shall be used with preferential lane word or symbol markings. December 2025

metadata.section_title: Preferential Lane Word and Symbol Markings
metadata.chapter: Chapter 3E. Preferential Lane Markings For Motor Vehicles

text:
Section 3E.03 Standard 7 - Preferential Lane Word and Symbol Markings
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3E. Preferential Lane Markings For Motor Vehicles
Page: 612

All preferential lane word and symbol markings shall be white and shall be positioned laterally in the approximate center of the preferential lane.

metadata.section_title: Preferential Lane Word and Symbol Markings
metadata.chapter: Chapter 3E. Preferential Lane Markings For Motor Vehicles

text:
Section 3E.03 Option 8 - Preferential Lane Word and Symbol Markings
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3E. Preferential Lane Markings For Motor Vehicles
Page: 612

Preferential lane-use symbol or word markings may be omitted at toll plazas where physical conditions preclude the use of the markings.

metadata.section_title: Preferential Lane Word and Symbol Markings
metadata.chapter: Chapter 3E. Preferential Lane Markings For Motor Vehicles

text:
Section 3E.03 Option 9 - Preferential Lane Word and Symbol Markings
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3E. Preferential Lane Markings For Motor Vehicles
Page: 612

Lane-use arrow markings may be placed on the curb lanes on approaches to intersections to signify non- preferential road users can use the lane for turning movements.

metadata.section_title: Preferential Lane Word and Symbol Markings
metadata.chapter: Chapter 3E. Preferential Lane Markings For Motor Vehicles

title: Section 3E.03 Guidance 10 - Preferential Lane Word and Symbol Markings
text:
Section 3E.03 Guidance 10 - Preferential Lane Word and Symbol Markings
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3E. Preferential Lane Markings For Motor Vehicles
Page: 612

All longitudinal pavement markings, as well as word and symbol pavement markings, associated with a preferential lane should end at approximately where the Preferential Lane Ends (R3-12a or R3-12c) sign (see Section 2G.07) designating the downstream end of the preferential only lane restriction is installed.

metadata.section_title: Preferential Lane Word and Symbol Markings
metadata.chapter: Chapter 3E. Preferential Lane Markings For Motor Vehicles

title: Section 3E.03 Guidance 11 - Preferential Lane Word and Symbol Markings
text:
Section 3E.03 Guidance 11 - Preferential Lane Word and Symbol Markings
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3E. Preferential Lane Markings For Motor Vehicles
Page: 612

The spacing of the markings should be based on engineering judgment that considers the operating speed, block lengths, distance from intersections, and other factors that affect clear communication to the road user.

metadata.section_title: Preferential Lane Word and Symbol Markings
metadata.chapter: Chapter 3E. Preferential Lane Markings For Motor Vehicles

title: Section 3E.03 Guidance 12 - Preferential Lane Word and Symbol Markings
text:
Section 3E.03 Guidance 12 - Preferential Lane Word and Symbol Markings
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3E. Preferential Lane Markings For Motor Vehicles
Page: 612

In addition to a regular spacing interval, the preferential lane marking should be placed at strategic locations such as major decision points, direct exit ramp departures from the preferential lane, and along access openings to and from adjacent general-purpose lanes. At decision points, the preferential lane marking should be placed on all applicable lanes and should be visible to approaching traffic for all available departures. At direct exits from preferential lanes where extra emphasis is needed, the use of word markings (such as “EXIT” or “EXIT ONLY”) in the deceleration lane for the direct exit and/or on the direct exit ramp itself just beyond the exit gore should be considered.

metadata.section_title: Preferential Lane Word and Symbol Markings
metadata.chapter: Chapter 3E. Preferential Lane Markings For Motor Vehicles

text:
Section 3E.03 Option 13 - Preferential Lane Word and Symbol Markings
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3E. Preferential Lane Markings For Motor Vehicles
Page: 612

A numeral indicating the vehicle occupancy requirements established for a high-occupancy vehicle lane may be included in sequence after the diamond symbol or HOV word message.

metadata.section_title: Preferential Lane Word and Symbol Markings
metadata.chapter: Chapter 3E. Preferential Lane Markings For Motor Vehicles

title: Section 3E.04 Support 1 - Markings for Part-Time Travel on a Shoulder
text:
Section 3E.04 Support 1 - Markings for Part-Time Travel on a Shoulder
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3E. Preferential Lane Markings For Motor Vehicles
Page: 612

Shoulders are sometimes used to add capacity to a roadway in peak hour conditions to provide for transit or HOV priority or to provide higher throughput when open to all traffic.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 3E. Preferential Lane Markings For Motor Vehicles

text:
Section 3E.04 Support 2 - Markings for Part-Time Travel on a Shoulder
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3E. Preferential Lane Markings For Motor Vehicles
Page: 612

A shoulder that has been opened to travel on a permanent, rather than a part-time basis is considered to be a travel lane and is signed and marked in accordance with other provisions of this Manual.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 3E. Preferential Lane Markings For Motor Vehicles

text:
Section 3E.04 Standard 3 - Markings for Part-Time Travel on a Shoulder
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3E. Preferential Lane Markings For Motor Vehicles
Page: 612

When part-time travel on a shoulder is open to all traffic, pavement word and symbol markings shall not be used in the shoulder.

metadata.section_title: Markings for Part-Time Travel on a Shoulder
metadata.chapter: Chapter 3E. Preferential Lane Markings For Motor Vehicles

title: Section 3E.04 Standard 4 - Markings for Part-Time Travel on a Shoulder
text:
Section 3E.04 Standard 4 - Markings for Part-Time Travel on a Shoulder
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3E. Preferential Lane Markings For Motor Vehicles
Page: 612

When a shoulder is assigned part-time to a particular class or classes of vehicles, the shoulder shall be marked with one or more pavement word markings that identify the special use of the shoulder such as BUS ONLY, TRANSIT ONLY, HOV, or instead of the HOV pavement word marking, white lines formed in a diamond-shaped symbol (see Section 3E.03). A pavement word or symbol marking shall be provided in the shoulder immediately after exit and entry ramps (see Figure 3E-5) or immediately departing an intersection at the full-width shoulder (see Figure 3E-6). Appropriate regulatory signing (see Section 2G.03) shall be installed with the pavement word or symbol markings.

metadata.section_title: Markings for Part-Time Travel on a Shoulder
metadata.chapter: Chapter 3E. Preferential Lane Markings For Motor Vehicles

title: Section 3E.04 Standard 5 - Markings for Part-Time Travel on a Shoulder
text:
Section 3E.04 Standard 5 - Markings for Part-Time Travel on a Shoulder
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3E. Preferential Lane Markings For Motor Vehicles
Page: 612

The channelizing line emanating from the entrance ramp shall be a wide dotted line through the intersecting alignment of the shoulder to the theoretical gore (see Drawings A and B in Figure 3E-5). At exit ramps, the channelizing line proceeding from the theoretical gore across the intersecting alignment of the shoulder shall be a wide dotted line (see Figure 3E-5).

metadata.section_title: Markings for Part-Time Travel on a Shoulder
metadata.chapter: Chapter 3E. Preferential Lane Markings For Motor Vehicles

text:
Section 3E.04 Standard 6 - Markings for Part-Time Travel on a Shoulder
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3E. Preferential Lane Markings For Motor Vehicles
Page: 612

If used, the extension of the channelizing line at entrance ramps proceeding from the theoretical gore across the opening of the on-ramp alignment shall be a wide dotted line (see Drawing C in Figure 3E-5) where it is demonstrated that traffic entering from an on-ramp stops or yields to traffic on the shoulder of the highway mainline.

metadata.section_title: Markings for Part-Time Travel on a Shoulder
metadata.chapter: Chapter 3E. Preferential Lane Markings For Motor Vehicles

text:
Section 3E.04 Standard 7 - Markings for Part-Time Travel on a Shoulder
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3E. Preferential Lane Markings For Motor Vehicles
Page: 612

An additional outside solid edge line shall be provided on the shoulder in accordance with Sections 3B.09 and 3B.10.

metadata.section_title: Markings for Part-Time Travel on a Shoulder
metadata.chapter: Chapter 3E. Preferential Lane Markings For Motor Vehicles

text:
Section 3E.04 Guidance 8 - Markings for Part-Time Travel on a Shoulder

Changes in edge line pattern or direction should occur at appropriate regulatory signs.

Page: 612

At locations where traffic is allowed to enter, exit, or merge with the shoulder, a dotted edge line may be used either in a continuous manner or angled to the pavement edge (see Figure 3E-6).

metadata.chapter: Chapter 3E. Preferential Lane Markings For Motor Vehicles

Page: 612

Red-colored pavement (see Section 3H.07) may be used on shoulders that allow only transit vehicles.

Section 3F.01 Support 1 - General
Part: Part 3 Markings

At toll plazas, pavement markings help road users identify the proper lane(s) to use for the type of toll payment they plan to use, to channelize movements into the various lanes, and to delineate obstructions in the roadway.

text:
Section 3F.02 Guidance 1 - Longitudinal Markings
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3F. Markings For Toll Plazas
Page: 617

Solid white lane line markings should be used to separate toll lanes, payment methods, or to channelize movements at toll plazas.

title: Section 3F.02 Guidance 2 - Longitudinal Markings
text:
Section 3F.02 Guidance 2 - Longitudinal Markings
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3F. Markings For Toll Plazas
Page: 617

Solid white lane line markings should begin at the upstream end of the full-width toll lane and be continued to the toll plaza.

title: Section 3F.02 Option 3 - Longitudinal Markings
text:
Section 3F.02 Option 3 - Longitudinal Markings
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3F. Markings For Toll Plazas
Page: 617

For a toll plaza approach lane that is restricted to use only by vehicles with registered ETC accounts, the solid white lane line or edge line on the right-hand side of the ETC Account-Only lane and the solid white lane line or solid yellow edge line on the left-hand side of the ETC Account-Only lane may be supplemented with purple solid longitudinal markings placed contiguous to the inside edges of the lines defining the lane.

title: Section 3F.02 Standard 4 - Longitudinal Markings
text:
Section 3F.02 Standard 4 - Longitudinal Markings
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3F. Markings For Toll Plazas
Page: 617

If the purple solid longitudinal markings described in Paragraph 3 of this Section are used, the purple markings shall be at least 3 inches wide.

title: Section 3F.02 Guidance 5 - Longitudinal Markings
text:
Section 3F.02 Guidance 5 - Longitudinal Markings
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3F. Markings For Toll Plazas
Page: 617

If the purple solid longitudinal markings described in Paragraph 3 of this Section are used, the purple markings should not be wider than the line they supplement.

title: Section 3F.02 Standard 6 - Longitudinal Markings
text:
Section 3F.02 Standard 6 - Longitudinal Markings
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3F. Markings For Toll Plazas
Page: 617

Toll booths and the islands on which they are located are considered to be obstructions in the roadway and they shall be provided with markings that comply with the provisions of Section 3B.13 and Chapter 3J.

title: Section 3F.02 Option 7 - Longitudinal Markings
text:
Section 3F.02 Option 7 - Longitudinal Markings
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3F. Markings For Toll Plazas
Page: 617

Longitudinal pavement markings may be omitted alongside toll booth islands between the approach markings and any departure markings.

title: Section 3G.01 Support 1 - General
text:
Section 3G.01 Support 1 - General
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3G. Delineators
Page: 618

Delineators are particularly beneficial at locations where the alignment might be confusing or unexpected, such as at lane-reduction transitions and curves. Delineators are effective guidance devices at night and during adverse weather. An important advantage of delineators in certain locations is that they remain visible when the roadway is wet or covered by snow.

title: Section 3G.01 Support 2 - General
text:
Section 3G.01 Support 2 - General
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3G. Delineators
Page: 618

Delineators are considered guidance devices to help road users navigate the roadway alignment, rather than warning devices.

title: Section 3G.01 Option 3 - General
text:
Section 3G.01 Option 3 - General
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3G. Delineators
Page: 618

Delineators may be used on long continuous sections of highway or through short stretches where there are changes in horizontal alignment.

title: Section 3G.02 Standard 1 - Design
text:
Section 3G.02 Standard 1 - Design
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3G. Delineators
Page: 618

Delineators shall consist of retroreflective devices that are capable of clearly retroreflecting light under normal atmospheric conditions from a distance of 1,000 feet when illuminated by the high beams of standard automobile lights. They shall be mounted on crashworthy (see definition in Section 1C.02) supports.

title: Section 3G.02 Standard 2 - Design
text:
Section 3G.02 Standard 2 - Design
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3G. Delineators
Page: 618

Retroreflective elements for delineators shall have a minimum vertical and horizontal dimension of 3 inches, or a minimum diameter dimension of 3 inches when circular.

title: Section 3G.02 Support 3 - Design
text:
Section 3G.02 Support 3 - Design
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3G. Delineators
Page: 618

Within a series of delineators along a roadway, delineators for a given direction of travel at a specific location are referred to as single delineators if they have one retroreflective element for that direction, double delineators if they have two identical retroreflective elements for that direction mounted together, or vertically-elongated delineators if they have a single retroreflective element with an elongated vertical dimension to approximate the vertical dimension of two separate single delineators.

title: Section 3G.02 Option 4 - Design
text:
Section 3G.02 Option 4 - Design
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3G. Delineators
Page: 618

A vertically-elongated delineator of appropriate size may be used in place of a double delineator.

title: Section 3G.03 Standard 1 - Application
text:
Section 3G.03 Standard 1 - Application
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3G. Delineators
Page: 618

The color of delineators shall comply with the color of edge lines stipulated in Sections 3A.03 and 3B.09.

title: Section 3G.03 Standard 2 - Application
text:
Section 3G.03 Standard 2 - Application
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3G. Delineators
Page: 618

A series of single delineators shall be provided on the right-hand side of freeways and expressways and on at least one side of interchange ramps, except when either Condition A or Condition B is met, as follows: A. On tangent sections of freeways and expressways when both of the following conditions are met: 1. Raised pavement markers are used continuously on lane lines throughout all curves and on all tangents to supplement pavement markings, and 2. Roadside delineators are used to lead into all curves, or B. On sections of roadways where continuous lighting is in operation between interchanges.

title: Section 3G.03 Option 3 - Application
text:
Section 3G.03 Option 3 - Application
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3G. Delineators
Page: 618

Delineators may be provided on other classes of roads.

title: Section 3G.03 Option 4 - Application
text:
Section 3G.03 Option 4 - Application
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3G. Delineators
Page: 618

A series of single delineators may be provided on the left-hand side of roadways.

title: Section 3G.03 Option 5 - Application
text:
Section 3G.03 Option 5 - Application
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3G. Delineators
Page: 618

Chevron Alignment (W1-8) signs may be used instead of or in addition to standard delineators, as provided in Section 2C.08.

title: Section 3G.03 Standard 6 - Application
text:
Section 3G.03 Standard 6 - Application
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3G. Delineators
Page: 618

Delineators on the left-hand side of a two-way roadway shall be white (see Figure 3G-1).

title: Section 3G.03 Guidance 7 - Application
text:
Section 3G.03 Guidance 7 - Application
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3G. Delineators
Page: 618

A series of single delineators should be provided on the outside of curves on interchange ramps.

title: Section 3G.03 Guidance 8 - Application
text:
Section 3G.03 Guidance 8 - Application
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3G. Delineators
Page: 620

Where median crossovers are provided for official or emergency use on divided highways and where these crossovers are to be marked with pavement markings, a double yellow delineator should be placed on the left- hand side of the through roadway on the far side of the crossover for each roadway. Figure 3G-1. Examples of Delineator Placement Notes: 1. Delineators should be placed at a constant distance from the roadway edge, except that when an obstruction exists near the pavement edge, the line of delineators should make a smooth transition to the inside of the obstruction. 2. All delineators shown on this figure are white, including the delineators on the outside of the curve facing northbound drivers. 3. Chevron Alignment signs (W1-8) may be used instead of or in addition to standard delineators (see Section 2C.08).

title: Section 3G.03 Guidance 9 - Application
text:
Section 3G.03 Guidance 9 - Application
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3G. Delineators
Page: 620

Double or vertically-elongated delineators should be installed at approximately 100-foot intervals along acceleration and deceleration lanes.

title: Section 3G.03 Guidance 10 - Application
text:
Section 3G.03 Guidance 10 - Application
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3G. Delineators
Page: 620

A series of delineators should be used wherever guardrail or other longitudinal barriers are present along a roadway or ramp.

title: Section 3G.03 Option 11 - Application
text:
Section 3G.03 Option 11 - Application
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3G. Delineators
Page: 620

Red delineators may be used on the reverse side of any delineator where it would be viewed by a road user traveling in the wrong direction on that particular ramp or roadway.

title: Section 3G.03 Guidance 12 - Application
text:
Section 3G.03 Guidance 12 - Application
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3G. Delineators
Page: 620

Except as provided in Paragraph 13 of Section 3B.12, delineators of the appropriate color should be used to indicate a lane-reduction transition where either an outside or inside lane merges into an adjacent lane.

title: Section 3G.03 Guidance 13 - Application
text:
Section 3G.03 Guidance 13 - Application
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3G. Delineators
Page: 620

When used for lane-reduction transitions, the delineators should be installed adjacent to the lane or lanes reduced for the full length of the transition and should be so placed and spaced to show the reduction (see Section 3B.12 and Figure 3B-14).

title: Section 3G.03 Guidance 14 - Application
text:
Section 3G.03 Guidance 14 - Application
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3G. Delineators
Page: 620

On a highway with continuous delineation on either or both sides, delineators should be carried through transitions.

title: Section 3G.03 Standard 15 - Application
text:
Section 3G.03 Standard 15 - Application
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3G. Delineators
Page: 620

When used on a truck escape ramp, delineators shall be red.

title: Section 3G.03 Guidance 16 - Application
text:
Section 3G.03 Guidance 16 - Application
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3G. Delineators
Page: 620

Red delineators should be placed on both sides of truck escape ramps.

title: Section 3G.04 Guidance 1 - Placement and Spacing
text:
Section 3G.04 Guidance 1 - Placement and Spacing
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3G. Delineators
Page: 620

Except as provided in Paragraph 2 of this Section, delineators should be mounted at a height, measured vertically from the bottom of the lowest retroreflective device to the elevation of the near edge of the roadway, of approximately 4 feet.

title: Section 3G.04 Option 2 - Placement and Spacing
text:
Section 3G.04 Option 2 - Placement and Spacing
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3G. Delineators
Page: 620

When mounted on the face of or on top of guardrails or other longitudinal barriers, delineators may be mounted at a lower elevation than the normal delineator height recommended in Paragraph 1 of this Section.

title: Section 3G.04 Guidance 3 - Placement and Spacing
text:
Section 3G.04 Guidance 3 - Placement and Spacing
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3G. Delineators
Page: 620

Delineators should be placed 2 to 8 feet outside the outer edge of the shoulder, or if appropriate, in line with the roadside barrier that is 8 feet or less outside the outer edge of the shoulder.

title: Section 3G.04 Guidance 4 - Placement and Spacing
text:
Section 3G.04 Guidance 4 - Placement and Spacing
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3G. Delineators
Page: 620

Delineators should be placed at a constant distance from the edge of the roadway, except that where an obstruction intrudes into the space between the pavement edge and the extension of the line of the delineators, the delineators should be transitioned to be in line with or inside the innermost edge of the obstruction. If the obstruction is a guardrail or other longitudinal barrier, the delineators should be transitioned to be just behind, directly above (in line with), or on the innermost edge of the guardrail or longitudinal barrier.

title: Section 3G.04 Guidance 5 - Placement and Spacing
text:
Section 3G.04 Guidance 5 - Placement and Spacing
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3G. Delineators
Page: 620

Delineators should not present a vertical or horizontal clearance obstacle for pedestrians.

title: Section 3G.04 Guidance 6 - Placement and Spacing
text:
Section 3G.04 Guidance 6 - Placement and Spacing
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3G. Delineators
Page: 620

Delineators should be spaced 200 to 530 feet apart on mainline tangent sections. Delineators should be spaced 100 feet apart on ramp tangent sections.

title: Section 3G.04 Option 7 - Placement and Spacing
text:
Section 3G.04 Option 7 - Placement and Spacing
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3G. Delineators
Page: 620

On a highway with continuous delineation on either or both sides, the spacing between a series of delineators may be closer.

title: Section 3G.04 Option 8 - Placement and Spacing
text:
Section 3G.04 Option 8 - Placement and Spacing
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3G. Delineators
Page: 620

When uniform spacing is interrupted by such features as driveways and intersections, delineators which would ordinarily be located within the features may be relocated in either direction for a distance not exceeding ¼ of the uniform spacing. Delineators still falling within such features may be eliminated.

title: Section 3G.04 Option 9 - Placement and Spacing
text:
Section 3G.04 Option 9 - Placement and Spacing
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3G. Delineators
Page: 620

Delineators may be transitioned in advance of a lane transition or obstruction as a guide for oncoming traffic.

title: Section 3G.04 Guidance 10 - Placement and Spacing
text:
Section 3G.04 Guidance 10 - Placement and Spacing
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3G. Delineators
Page: 620

The spacing of delineators should be adjusted on approaches to and throughout horizontal curves so that several delineators are always simultaneously visible to the road user. The approximate spacing shown in Table 3G-1 should be used.

title: Section 3G.04 Guidance 11 - Placement and Spacing
text:
Section 3G.04 Guidance 11 - Placement and Spacing
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3G. Delineators
Page: 621

The spacing between red delineators that are placed on both sides of a truck escape ramp should not exceed 50 feet for a distance that is sufficient to identify the ramp entrance. The spacing between red delineators that are placed beyond the ramp entrance should be such that adequate guidance is provided based on the length and design of the escape ramp.

title: Section 3G.04 Option 12 - Placement and Spacing
text:
Section 3G.04 Option 12 - Placement and Spacing
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3G. Delineators
Page: 621

When needed for special conditions, delineators of the appropriate color may be mounted in a closely-spaced manner on the face of or on top of guardrails or other longitudinal barriers to form a continuous or nearly- continuous “ribbon” of delineation.

title: Section 3G.04 Support 13 - Placement and Spacing
text:
Section 3G.04 Support 13 - Placement and Spacing
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3G. Delineators
Page: 622

Examples of delineator installations are shown in Figure 3G-1. Table 3G-1. Approximate Spacing for Delineators on Horizontal Curves Radius (R) of Curve Approximate Spacing (S) on Curve 50 feet 20 feet 115 feet 25 feet 180 feet 35 feet 250 feet 40 feet 300 feet 50 feet 400 feet 55 feet 500 feet 65 feet 600 feet 70 feet 700 feet 75 feet 800 feet 80 feet 900 feet 85 feet 1,000 feet 90 feet Notes: 1. Spacing for specific radii may be interpolated from table. 2. The minimum spacing should be 20 feet. 3. The spacing on curves should not exceed 300 feet. 4. In advance of or beyond a curve, and proceeding away from the end of the curve, the spacing of the first delineator is 2S, the second 3S, and the third 6S, but not to exceed 300 feet. 5. S refers to the delineator spacing for specific radii computed from the formula S=3√R-50. 6. The distances for S shown in the table above were rounded to the nearest 5 feet.

title: Section 3H.01 Support 1 - Standardization of Application
text:
Section 3H.01 Support 1 - Standardization of Application
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3H. Colored Pavement
Page: 622

Colored pavements consist of differently-colored road paving materials, such as colored asphalt or concrete. Other surface treatments can be applied to the surface of a road, island, or area outside the traveled way to simulate a colored pavement.

title: Section 3H.01 Support 2 - Standardization of Application
text:
Section 3H.01 Support 2 - Standardization of Application
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3H. Colored Pavement
Page: 622

If non-retroreflective colored pavement is used as a purely aesthetic surface treatment (see Section 3H.03) within the provisions of this Chapter and are not intended to communicate regulations, warnings, guidance, or other information to road users, the colored pavement is not considered to be a traffic control device, even if it is located between the lines of a crosswalk.

title: Section 3H.01 Standard 3 - Standardization of Application
text:
Section 3H.01 Standard 3 - Standardization of Application
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3H. Colored Pavement
Page: 622

If colored pavement is used within the traveled way, on flush or raised islands, or on shoulders to communicate regulations, warnings, guidance, or other information to road users, or if retroreflectivity is used, the colored pavement shall be considered a traffic control device and shall be limited to the colors and applications specified in this Chapter.

title: Section 3H.01 Standard 4 - Standardization of Application
text:
Section 3H.01 Standard 4 - Standardization of Application
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3H. Colored Pavement
Page: 622

Except as provided in Paragraph 5 of Section 3H.07, colored pavement shall only be used if the corresponding regulations, warnings, or guidance are applicable at all times.

title: Section 3H.01 Guidance 5 - Standardization of Application
text:
Section 3H.01 Guidance 5 - Standardization of Application
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3H. Colored Pavement
Page: 622

Colored pavements used as traffic control devices should only be used where the color pavement contrasts significantly with adjoining paved areas.

title: Section 3H.01 Support 6 - Standardization of Application
text:
Section 3H.01 Support 6 - Standardization of Application
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3H. Colored Pavement
Page: 622

The chromaticity coordinates that define the ranges of acceptable colors for traffic control devices are found in the Appendix to Subpart F of 23 CFR 655.

title: Section 3H.01 Standard 7 - Standardization of Application
text:
Section 3H.01 Standard 7 - Standardization of Application
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3H. Colored Pavement
Page: 622

If used, colored pavement shall only be used to supplement other markings as provided in this Manual.

title: Section 3H.01 Support 8 - Standardization of Application
text:
Section 3H.01 Support 8 - Standardization of Application
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3H. Colored Pavement
Page: 622

Longitudinal pavement markings, crosswalks, pavement marking symbols, and elongated route markers are not considered colored pavements.

title: Section 3H.02 Option 1 - Materials
text:
Section 3H.02 Option 1 - Materials
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3H. Colored Pavement
Page: 622

Colored pavements may be either retroreflective or non-retroreflective, in accordance with the provisions of this Chapter for specific applications.

title: Section 3H.02 Guidance 2 - Materials
text:
Section 3H.02 Guidance 2 - Materials
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3H. Colored Pavement
Page: 622

If surface treatments are applied to the surface of a road, island, or other area outside the traveled way to simulate a colored pavement, pavement marking materials should be selected that will minimize loss of traction for road users (see Paragraph 2 of Section 3A.02).

title: Section 3H.02 Support 3 - Materials
text:
Section 3H.02 Support 3 - Materials
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3H. Colored Pavement
Page: 622

Providing for retroreflectivity, such as incorporating glass beads, can affect the skid resistance of pavement markings.

title: Section 3H.02 Support 4 - Materials
text:
Section 3H.02 Support 4 - Materials
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3H. Colored Pavement
Page: 622

Installation of colored pavement to one lane or an area or portion of a multi-lane traveled way can create differentials in skid resistance values between the areas of colored pavement and non-colored pavement that might be unexpected by the road user.

title: Section 3H.03 Support 1 - Aesthetic Surface Treatments
text:
Section 3H.03 Support 1 - Aesthetic Surface Treatments
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3H. Colored Pavement
Page: 622

Aesthetic surface treatments are sometimes used between the transverse lines within a crosswalk, in islands, in medians, in shoulders, within sidewalk extensions designated by pavement markings, or in other areas outside of the traveled way.

title: Section 3H.03 Support 2 - Aesthetic Surface Treatments
text:
Section 3H.03 Support 2 - Aesthetic Surface Treatments
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3H. Colored Pavement
Page: 622

Common examples of materials used as aesthetic surface treatments include brick, paving bricks, paving stones, or other materials designed to simulate such paving. Some examples of geometries for aesthetic surface treatments include honeycomb, lattice, mesh, grid, and regular polygon patterns.

title: Section 3H.03 Support 3 - Aesthetic Surface Treatments
text:
Section 3H.03 Support 3 - Aesthetic Surface Treatments
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3H. Colored Pavement
Page: 623

Surfaces with individual units laid out of plane and those that are heavily-textured, rough, or chamfered, could increase rolling resistance and subject pedestrians who use wheelchairs to the effects of vibration; it is desirable to minimize surface discontinuities. MUTCD 11th Edition - Revision 1

title: Section 3H.03 Support 4 - Aesthetic Surface Treatments
text:
Section 3H.03 Support 4 - Aesthetic Surface Treatments
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3H. Colored Pavement
Page: 623

Common examples of colors for aesthetic surface treatments incorporated into the material or geometry are brick red, rust, brown, burgundy, clay, tan, or similar earth-tone equivalents (see Figure 3H-1).

title: Section 3H.03 Standard 5 - Aesthetic Surface Treatments
text:
Section 3H.03 Standard 5 - Aesthetic Surface Treatments
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3H. Colored Pavement
Page: 623

Aesthetic surface treatments shall not interfere with traffic control devices.

title: Section 3H.03 Standard 6 - Aesthetic Surface Treatments
text:
Section 3H.03 Standard 6 - Aesthetic Surface Treatments
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3H. Colored Pavement
Page: 623

Aesthetic surface treatments shall not be of a surface that can confuse pedestrians with vision disabilities that rely on tactile treatments or cues for navigation.

title: Section 3H.03 Standard 7 - Aesthetic Surface Treatments
text:
Section 3H.03 Standard 7 - Aesthetic Surface Treatments
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3H. Colored Pavement
Page: 623

Colors used for aesthetic surface treatments shall be outside the chromaticity coordinates that define the ranges of acceptable colors for traffic control devices.

title: Section 3H.03 Standard 8 - Aesthetic Surface Treatments
text:
Section 3H.03 Standard 8 - Aesthetic Surface Treatments
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3H. Colored Pavement
Page: 623

Patterns that constitute a purely aesthetic surface treatment shall be devoid of advertising and shall not contain elements of retroreflectivity.

title: Section 3H.03 Standard 9 - Aesthetic Surface Treatments
text:
Section 3H.03 Standard 9 - Aesthetic Surface Treatments
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3H. Colored Pavement
Page: 623

Patterns that constitute a purely aesthetic surface treatment for the interior area of a crosswalk shall not be designed to encourage road users to remain in the crosswalk, engage or interact with the pattern, or otherwise inhibit users from crossing the street in a safe and efficient manner.

title: Section 3H.03 Guidance 10 - Aesthetic Surface Treatments
text:
Section 3H.03 Guidance 10 - Aesthetic Surface Treatments
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3H. Colored Pavement
Page: 623

Aesthetic surface treatments should not use colors or patterns that degrade the contrast of markings used to delineate an area, or that might be mistaken by road users as a traffic control application.

title: Section 3H.03 Guidance 11 - Aesthetic Surface Treatments
text:
Section 3H.03 Guidance 11 - Aesthetic Surface Treatments
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3H. Colored Pavement
Page: 623

To provide contrast, a gap of at least one-half the width of the white transverse line used to establish the crosswalk, but not less than 6 inches, should be used between the white crosswalk lines and the aesthetic surface treatment, such as unmarked pavement or a black contrast line (see Section 3A.03).

title: Section 3H.03 Guidance 12 - Aesthetic Surface Treatments
text:
Section 3H.03 Guidance 12 - Aesthetic Surface Treatments
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3H. Colored Pavement
Page: 623

To provide contrast, a gap of at least the width of the longitudinal line used to establish the area should be used between the longitudinal line and the aesthetic surface treatment, such as unmarked pavement or a black contrast line (see Section 3A.03). If the longitudinal line is a double line, the gap should be at least the width of one of the lines that makes up the double line.

title: Section 3H.03 Guidance 13 - Aesthetic Surface Treatments
text:
Section 3H.03 Guidance 13 - Aesthetic Surface Treatments
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3H. Colored Pavement
Page: 623

Aesthetic surface treatments should not contain pictographs, illusions, or symbols. Rev. 1

title: Section 3H.04 Support 1 - Yellow-Colored Pavement
text:
Section 3H.04 Support 1 - Yellow-Colored Pavement
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3H. Colored Pavement
Page: 623

Yellow-colored pavement is used to enhance the conspicuity of areas separating traffic traveling in opposite directions of travel and the left-hand edge of the roadway.

title: Section 3H.04 Standard 2 - Yellow-Colored Pavement
text:
Section 3H.04 Standard 2 - Yellow-Colored Pavement
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3H. Colored Pavement
Page: 623

If used, yellow-colored pavement shall be limited to: A. Flush or raised median islands separating traffic flows in opposite directions, B. Left-hand shoulders of divided highways, and C. Left-hand shoulders of one-way streets or ramps.

title: Section 3H.04 Standard 3 - Yellow-Colored Pavement
text:
Section 3H.04 Standard 3 - Yellow-Colored Pavement
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3H. Colored Pavement
Page: 623

Yellow-colored pavement shall not be incorporated into elements of the roadway that function as reversible lanes or two-way left-turn lanes.

title: Section 3H.04 Standard 4 - Yellow-Colored Pavement
text:
Section 3H.04 Standard 4 - Yellow-Colored Pavement
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3H. Colored Pavement
Page: 624

Yellow-colored pavement shall not be used on channelizing islands where traffic travels in the same general direction on both sides. Figure 3H-1. Aesthetic Treatments for Transverse Crosswalks December 2025

title: Section 3H.04 Option 5 - Yellow-Colored Pavement
text:
Section 3H.04 Option 5 - Yellow-Colored Pavement
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3H. Colored Pavement
Page: 624

Yellow-colored pavement may be installed for the entire length of the roadway, island, or shoulder, or for only a portion or portions of the roadway, island, or shoulder.

title: Section 3H.04 Support 6 - Yellow-Colored Pavement
text:
Section 3H.04 Support 6 - Yellow-Colored Pavement
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3H. Colored Pavement
Page: 624

An example of an application of yellow-colored pavement is shown in Figure 3H-2.

title: Section 3H.05 Support 1 - White-Colored Pavement
text:
Section 3H.05 Support 1 - White-Colored Pavement
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3H. Colored Pavement
Page: 624

White-colored pavement is used to enhance the conspicuity of areas separating traffic traveling in the same direction of travel and the right-hand edge of the roadway.

title: Section 3H.05 Standard 2 - White-Colored Pavement
text:
Section 3H.05 Standard 2 - White-Colored Pavement
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3H. Colored Pavement
Page: 624

If used, white-colored pavement shall be limited to: A. Flush or raised channelizing islands where traffic passes on both sides in the same general direction, B. Right-hand shoulders, C. Exit gore areas, and D. Entrance gore areas.

title: Section 3H.05 Guidance 3 - White-Colored Pavement
text:
Section 3H.05 Guidance 3 - White-Colored Pavement
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3H. Colored Pavement
Page: 624

When used on right-hand shoulders, white-colored pavement should be limited to areas not intended for use by motor vehicle traffic except those shoulders designated for emergency use.

title: Section 3H.05 Option 4 - White-Colored Pavement
text:
Section 3H.05 Option 4 - White-Colored Pavement
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3H. Colored Pavement
Page: 624

White-colored pavement may be installed for the entire length of the roadway, island, or shoulder, or for only a portion or portions of the roadway, island, or shoulder.

title: Section 3H.05 Option 5 - White-Colored Pavement
text:
Section 3H.05 Option 5 - White-Colored Pavement
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3H. Colored Pavement
Page: 624

White-colored pavement may be used instead of chevron markings (see Sections 3B.13 and 3B.25) in neutral areas.

title: Section 3H.05 Support 6 - White-Colored Pavement
text:
Section 3H.05 Support 6 - White-Colored Pavement
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3H. Colored Pavement
Page: 625

An example of an application of white-colored pavement is shown in Figure 3H-3. Figure 3H-2. Examples of Yellow-Colored Pavement Applications Note: The use of colored pavement is optional. Figure 3H-3. Examples of White-Colored Pavement Applications

title: Section 3H.06 Support 1 - Green-Colored Pavement for Bicycle Facilities
text:
Section 3H.06 Support 1 - Green-Colored Pavement for Bicycle Facilities
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3H. Colored Pavement
Page: 625

Green-colored pavement is used to enhance the conspicuity of locations where bicyclists are expected to operate, and areas where bicyclists and other traffic might have potentially conflicting, weaving, or crossing movements. Green-colored pavement is also used to enhance the conspicuity of word, symbol, and/or arrow pavement markings when these markings are used in certain bicycle facilities.

title: Section 3H.06 Standard 2 - Green-Colored Pavement for Bicycle Facilities
text:
Section 3H.06 Standard 2 - Green-Colored Pavement for Bicycle Facilities
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3H. Colored Pavement
Page: 626

If used, green-colored pavement shall be limited to: A. Bicycle lanes (see Sections 9E.01, 9E.06, 9E.07, and 9E.08), B. Extensions of bicycle lanes through intersections (see Section 9E.03), C. Extensions of bicycle lanes through areas where motor vehicles enter a mandatory turn lane in which motor vehicles must weave across bicyclists in bicycle lanes (see Section 9E.02), D. Two-stage bicycle turn boxes (see Section 9E.11), E. Bicycle Boxes (see Section 9E.12), and F. As a background for bicycle detector symbols (see Section 9E.15). MUTCD 11th Edition - Revision 1

title: Section 3H.06 Standard 3 - Green-Colored Pavement for Bicycle Facilities
text:
Section 3H.06 Standard 3 - Green-Colored Pavement for Bicycle Facilities
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3H. Colored Pavement
Page: 626

Green-colored pavement shall not be: A. Incorporated into electric-vehicle parking stations or parking stalls, B. Incorporated into crosswalks (see Chapter 3C), C. Used as a background for shared-lane markings (see Section 9E.09), or D. Used instead of the required markings for bicycle facilities (see Chapter 9E).

title: Section 3H.06 Standard 4 - Green-Colored Pavement for Bicycle Facilities
text:
Section 3H.06 Standard 4 - Green-Colored Pavement for Bicycle Facilities
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3H. Colored Pavement
Page: 626

If used, the pattern of the green-colored pavement supplementing dotted extension lines shall match the pattern of the dotted lines, thus filling in only the areas that are directly between a pair of dotted line segments. If used, the pattern of the green-colored pavement supplementing a dotted longitudinal line, which defines a bicycle lane (see Paragraph 11 of Section 9E.02), shall match the pattern of the dotted line, thus filling in only the areas that are directly between a line segment and the curb, or, in the absence of a curb, the edge of the roadway.

title: Section 3H.06 Guidance 5 - Green-Colored Pavement for Bicycle Facilities
text:
Section 3H.06 Guidance 5 - Green-Colored Pavement for Bicycle Facilities
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3H. Colored Pavement
Page: 626

If green-colored pavement is used within separated bicycle lanes on an independent alignment, it should be used only at the entrances to those facilities from roadways open to public travel or at conflict, weaving, or crossing locations.

title: Section 3H.06 Guidance 6 - Green-Colored Pavement for Bicycle Facilities
text:
Section 3H.06 Guidance 6 - Green-Colored Pavement for Bicycle Facilities
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3H. Colored Pavement
Page: 626

If green-colored pavement is used within shared-use paths, it should be used only where pedestrian and bicyclist movements are separated and for only a portion (or portions) of the path designated for bicyclist use.

title: Section 3H.06 Option 7 - Green-Colored Pavement for Bicycle Facilities
text:
Section 3H.06 Option 7 - Green-Colored Pavement for Bicycle Facilities
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3H. Colored Pavement
Page: 626

Green-colored pavement may be installed for the entire length of a bicycle lane or bicycle lane extension or for only a portion (or portions) of the bicycle lane or bicycle lane extension.

title: Section 3H.06 Option 8 - Green-Colored Pavement for Bicycle Facilities
text:
Section 3H.06 Option 8 - Green-Colored Pavement for Bicycle Facilities
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3H. Colored Pavement
Page: 626

Green-colored pavement may be installed for the entire length of a physically-separated bikeway within the roadway or for only a portion (or portions) of the physically-separated bikeway within the roadway.

title: Section 3H.06 Guidance 9 - Green-Colored Pavement for Bicycle Facilities
text:
Section 3H.06 Guidance 9 - Green-Colored Pavement for Bicycle Facilities
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3H. Colored Pavement
Page: 626

Appropriate regulatory (see Chapter 9B) or guide signing (see Chapter 9D) should be installed to provide related information to the presence of the colored pavement.

title: Section 3H.06 Support 10 - Green-Colored Pavement for Bicycle Facilities
text:
Section 3H.06 Support 10 - Green-Colored Pavement for Bicycle Facilities
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3H. Colored Pavement
Page: 626

Examples of applications of green-colored pavement are shown in Figure 3H-4.

title: Section 3H.07 Support 1 - Red-Colored Pavement for Public Transit Systems
text:
Section 3H.07 Support 1 - Red-Colored Pavement for Public Transit Systems
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3H. Colored Pavement
Page: 626

Red-colored pavement is used to enhance the conspicuity of locations, station stops, or travel lanes in the roadway exclusively reserved for vehicles of public transit systems or multi-modal facilities where public transit is the primary mode. These public transit vehicles include buses, streetcars, trolleys, light-rail trains, and rapid transit fleets.

metadata.section_title: Red-Colored Pavement for Public Transit Systems

title: Section 3H.07 Option 2 - Red-Colored Pavement for Public Transit Systems
text:
Section 3H.07 Option 2 - Red-Colored Pavement for Public Transit Systems
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3H. Colored Pavement
Page: 626

Red-colored pavement may be used where engineering judgment determines that one or more of the following conditions are expected to result from its application: A. Increased travel speeds will be expected by the public transport vehicle after an exclusive lane or facility is provided, B. Reduced overall service time through the corridor will be expected by the public transport vehicle, C. Decreased rates of illegal parking or occupation of the transit or multi-mode lane or facility will be expected.

metadata.section_title: Red-Colored Pavement for Public Transit Systems

title: Section 3H.07 Standard 3 - Red-Colored Pavement for Public Transit Systems
text:
Section 3H.07 Standard 3 - Red-Colored Pavement for Public Transit Systems
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3H. Colored Pavement
Page: 626

If used, red-colored pavement shall be applied only in lanes, areas, or locations where general-purpose traffic is not allowed to use, queue, wait, idle, or otherwise occupy the lane, area, or location where red- colored pavement is used.

metadata.section_title: Red-Colored Pavement for Public Transit Systems

title: Section 3H.07 Standard 4 - Red-Colored Pavement for Public Transit Systems
text:
Section 3H.07 Standard 4 - Red-Colored Pavement for Public Transit Systems
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3H. Colored Pavement
Page: 626

Red-colored pavement shall be installed for the full width of the lane.

metadata.section_title: Red-Colored Pavement for Public Transit Systems

title: Section 3H.07 Option 5 - Red-Colored Pavement for Public Transit Systems
text:
Section 3H.07 Option 5 - Red-Colored Pavement for Public Transit Systems
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3H. Colored Pavement
Page: 626

Red-colored pavement may be used for full-time or part-time operations.

metadata.section_title: Red-Colored Pavement for Public Transit Systems

title: Section 3H.07 Option 6 - Red-Colored Pavement for Public Transit Systems
text:
Section 3H.07 Option 6 - Red-Colored Pavement for Public Transit Systems
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3H. Colored Pavement
Page: 626

Red-colored pavement may be installed for the entire length of a restricted lane or for only a portion (or portions) of the restricted lane.

metadata.section_title: Red-Colored Pavement for Public Transit Systems

title: Section 3H.07 Option 7 - Red-Colored Pavement for Public Transit Systems
text:
Section 3H.07 Option 7 - Red-Colored Pavement for Public Transit Systems
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3H. Colored Pavement
Page: 628

Red-colored pavement may be installed in a broken or dotted pattern where entrance into the transit lane is permitted by general traffic, for example where general traffic is allowed in a transit lane in advance of a turn. Rev. 1 December 2025 Figure 3H-4. Examples of Green-Colored Pavement Applications Notes: 1. The use of colored pavement is optional. 2. See Chapter 9E for bicycle facility markings.

metadata.section_title: Red-Colored Pavement for Public Transit Systems

title: Section 3H.07 Standard 8 - Red-Colored Pavement for Public Transit Systems
text:
Section 3H.07 Standard 8 - Red-Colored Pavement for Public Transit Systems
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3H. Colored Pavement
Page: 628

Regulatory signs (see Sections 2B.02 and 2G.03) shall be used to establish the allowable use of the lane, area, or location. Regulatory signs shall also be used when it is determined that other vehicles will be allowed to enter the lane to turn or bypass queues.

metadata.section_title: Red-Colored Pavement for Public Transit Systems

title: Section 3H.07 Guidance 9 - Red-Colored Pavement for Public Transit Systems
text:
Section 3H.07 Guidance 9 - Red-Colored Pavement for Public Transit Systems
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3H. Colored Pavement
Page: 628

If red-colored pavement is used on public transit facilities separated from the roadway or on facilities on an independent alignment, it should be used only at the entrances to those facilities from roadways open to public travel.

metadata.section_title: Red-Colored Pavement for Public Transit Systems

title: Section 3H.07 Support 10 - Red-Colored Pavement for Public Transit Systems
text:
Section 3H.07 Support 10 - Red-Colored Pavement for Public Transit Systems
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3H. Colored Pavement
Page: 628

Examples of applications of red-colored pavement are shown in Figure 3H-5.

metadata.section_title: Red-Colored Pavement for Public Transit Systems

title: Section 3H.08 Standard 1 - Purple-Colored Pavement for Electronic Toll Collection (ETC) Account-Only Preferential Lanes
text:
Section 3H.08 Standard 1 - Purple-Colored Pavement for Electronic Toll Collection (ETC) Account-Only Preferential Lanes
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3H. Colored Pavement
Page: 628

Purple-colored pavement shall be limited to: A. Lanes on the approach to a toll plaza where the lane is restricted to use only with a registered ETC account; and B. Lanes or approaches to an open-road tolling (ORT) collection facility that bypasses the physical toll plaza, where the ORT facility is restricted for use only by vehicles with registered ETC accounts.

metadata.section_title: Purple-Colored Pavement for Electronic Toll Collection (ETC) Account-Only Preferential Lanes

title: Section 3H.08 Standard 2 - Purple-Colored Pavement for Electronic Toll Collection (ETC) Account-Only Preferential Lanes
text:
Section 3H.08 Standard 2 - Purple-Colored Pavement for Electronic Toll Collection (ETC) Account-Only Preferential Lanes
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3H. Colored Pavement
Page: 628

Purple-colored pavement shall not be used in an approach lane that also facilitates additional payment methods downstream.

metadata.section_title: Purple-Colored Pavement for Electronic Toll Collection (ETC) Account-Only Preferential Lanes

title: Section 3H.08 Standard 3 - Purple-Colored Pavement for Electronic Toll Collection (ETC) Account-Only Preferential Lanes
text:
Section 3H.08 Standard 3 - Purple-Colored Pavement for Electronic Toll Collection (ETC) Account-Only Preferential Lanes
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3H. Colored Pavement
Page: 628

If used approaching a physical toll plaza, purple-colored pavement shall be flanked by white solid longitudinal lines that establish the toll lane.

metadata.section_title: Purple-Colored Pavement for Electronic Toll Collection (ETC) Account-Only Preferential Lanes

title: Section 3H.08 Standard 4 - Purple-Colored Pavement for Electronic Toll Collection (ETC) Account-Only Preferential Lanes
text:
Section 3H.08 Standard 4 - Purple-Colored Pavement for Electronic Toll Collection (ETC) Account-Only Preferential Lanes
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3H. Colored Pavement
Page: 628

If used on an ORT collection facility that bypasses the physical toll plaza, purple-colored pavement shall be flanked by appropriate edge lines, and if applicable in multi-lane bypasses, appropriate longitudinal solid or broken white lane lines.

metadata.section_title: Purple-Colored Pavement for Electronic Toll Collection (ETC) Account-Only Preferential Lanes

title: Section 3H.08 Option 5 - Purple-Colored Pavement for Electronic Toll Collection (ETC) Account-Only Preferential Lanes
text:
Section 3H.08 Option 5 - Purple-Colored Pavement for Electronic Toll Collection (ETC) Account-Only Preferential Lanes
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3H. Colored Pavement
Page: 628

Purple-colored pavement may be installed for the entire length of a toll lane or ORT collection facility or for only a portion (or portions) of the toll lane or ORT collection facility.

metadata.section_title: Purple-Colored Pavement for Electronic Toll Collection (ETC) Account-Only Preferential Lanes

title: Section 3H.08 Support 6 - Purple-Colored Pavement for Electronic Toll Collection (ETC) Account-Only Preferential Lanes
text:
Section 3H.08 Support 6 - Purple-Colored Pavement for Electronic Toll Collection (ETC) Account-Only Preferential Lanes
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3H. Colored Pavement
Page: 632

Figure 3H-6 illustrates examples of purple-colored pavement for use at toll plazas. MUTCD 11th Edition - Revision 1 Figure 3H-5. Examples of Red-Colored Pavement Applications A - Bus only lane B - Bus only lane at terminals or station stops C - Buffer-separated bus only lane Rev. 1 Notes: 1. See Chapter 2G for preferential lane signs. 2. See Chapter 3E for preferential lane markings. 3. The use of colored pavement is optional. December 2025 Figure 3H-6. Examples of Purple-Colored Pavement Applications (Sheet 1 of 2) Notes: 1. The ETC Account-Only word markings and ETC pictographs that are shown are only examples. The word markings and pictograph for the toll facility’s adopted ETC system shall be used (see Section 3E.03). 2. See Chapter 2F for toll road signs. 3. See Chapter 3F for markings at toll plazas. 4. The use of colored pavement is optional. Figure 3H-6. Examples of Purple-Colored Pavement Applications (Sheet 2 of 2) Notes: 1. The ETC Account-Only word markings and ETC pictographs that are shown are only examples. The word markings and pictograph for the toll facility’s adopted ETC system shall be used (see Section 3E.03). 2. See Chapter 2F for toll road signs. 3. See Chapter 3F for markings at toll plazas. 4. The use of colored pavement is optional.

metadata.section_title: Purple-Colored Pavement for Electronic Toll Collection (ETC) Account-Only Preferential Lanes

title: Section 3I.01 Option 1 - Channelizing Devices
text:
Section 3I.01 Option 1 - Channelizing Devices
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3I. Channelizing Devices Used For Emphasis Of Pavement Marking Patterns
Page: 632

Channelizing devices (see Sections 6K.01 through 6K.07 and Figure 6K-1) such as cones, tubular markers, vertical panels, lane separators, drums, and barricades may be used for general traffic control purposes such as adding emphasis to reversible lane delineation, channelizing lines, islands, pedestrian facilities, or bicycle facilities. Channelizing devices may also be used along a center line to preclude turns or along lane lines to preclude lane changing, as determined by engineering judgment.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 3I. Channelizing Devices Used For Emphasis Of Pavement Marking Patterns

title: Section 3I.01 Support 2 - Channelizing Devices
text:
Section 3I.01 Support 2 - Channelizing Devices
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3I. Channelizing Devices Used For Emphasis Of Pavement Marking Patterns
Page: 632

Although they are not considered to be traffic control devices, raised islands (see Chapter 3J) are also sometimes used to channelize traffic.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 3I. Channelizing Devices Used For Emphasis Of Pavement Marking Patterns

title: Section 3I.01 Standard 3 - Channelizing Devices
text:
Section 3I.01 Standard 3 - Channelizing Devices
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3I. Channelizing Devices Used For Emphasis Of Pavement Marking Patterns
Page: 632

Except for color, the design of channelizing devices, including, but not limited to, retroreflectivity, minimum dimensions, and mounting height, shall comply with the provisions of Chapter 6K.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 3I. Channelizing Devices Used For Emphasis Of Pavement Marking Patterns

title: Section 3I.01 Standard 4 - Channelizing Devices
text:
Section 3I.01 Standard 4 - Channelizing Devices
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3I. Channelizing Devices Used For Emphasis Of Pavement Marking Patterns
Page: 632

Except as provided in Paragraph 5 of this Section, the color of channelizing devices used outside of temporary traffic control zones shall be the same color as the pavement marking that they supplement, or for which they are substituted, in accordance with Section 3A.03.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 3I. Channelizing Devices Used For Emphasis Of Pavement Marking Patterns

title: Section 3I.01 Option 5 - Channelizing Devices
text:
Section 3I.01 Option 5 - Channelizing Devices
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3I. Channelizing Devices Used For Emphasis Of Pavement Marking Patterns
Page: 632

The color of channelizing devices used to emphasize pavement marking patterns outside of temporary traffic control zones may be orange provided that the application of the orange-colored channelizing device is not permanent.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 3I. Channelizing Devices Used For Emphasis Of Pavement Marking Patterns

title: Section 3I.01 Support 6 - Channelizing Devices
text:
Section 3I.01 Support 6 - Channelizing Devices
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3I. Channelizing Devices Used For Emphasis Of Pavement Marking Patterns
Page: 632

Emergency incidents and planned special events are the most common temporary traffic control zones that would justify orange channelizing devices to emphasize standard pavement marking colors. These events do not necessitate police officers or other authorized personnel to obtain and deploy channelizing devices that match the color of the existing pavement marking.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 3I. Channelizing Devices Used For Emphasis Of Pavement Marking Patterns

title: Section 3I.01 Standard 7 - Channelizing Devices
text:
Section 3I.01 Standard 7 - Channelizing Devices
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3I. Channelizing Devices Used For Emphasis Of Pavement Marking Patterns
Page: 632

For nighttime use, channelizing devices shall be retroreflective (as described in Part 6) or internally illuminated. On channelizing devices used outside of temporary traffic control zones, retroreflective sheeting or bands shall be white if the devices separate traffic flows in the same direction and shall be yellow if the devices separate traffic flows in the opposite direction or are placed along the left-hand edge line of a one-way roadway or ramp.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 3I. Channelizing Devices Used For Emphasis Of Pavement Marking Patterns

title: Section 3I.02 Standard 1 - Tubular Markers
text:
Section 3I.02 Standard 1 - Tubular Markers
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3I. Channelizing Devices Used For Emphasis Of Pavement Marking Patterns
Page: 632

Tubular markers for permanent installations shall be a minimum of 28 inches in height and shall be a minimum of 2 inches wide facing road users.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 3I. Channelizing Devices Used For Emphasis Of Pavement Marking Patterns

title: Section 3I.02 Guidance 2 - Tubular Markers
text:
Section 3I.02 Guidance 2 - Tubular Markers
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3I. Channelizing Devices Used For Emphasis Of Pavement Marking Patterns
Page: 632

Tubular markers should be affixed to the pavement or other surface either directly or by means of an attachment system that is affixed to the pavement or other surface. Tubular markers should normally be spaced no greater than N as cited in Section 3B.14.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 3I. Channelizing Devices Used For Emphasis Of Pavement Marking Patterns

title: Section 3I.02 Option 3 - Tubular Markers
text:
Section 3I.02 Option 3 - Tubular Markers
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3I. Channelizing Devices Used For Emphasis Of Pavement Marking Patterns
Page: 632

Other spacing may be used based on engineering judgment.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 3I. Channelizing Devices Used For Emphasis Of Pavement Marking Patterns

title: Section 3I.02 Support 4 - Tubular Markers
text:
Section 3I.02 Support 4 - Tubular Markers
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3I. Channelizing Devices Used For Emphasis Of Pavement Marking Patterns
Page: 632

Tubular markers are sometimes used to provide additional emphasis or improve lane discipline in advance of an unsignalized crosswalk (see Figure 3I-1).

metadata.chapter: Chapter 3I. Channelizing Devices Used For Emphasis Of Pavement Marking Patterns

title: Section 3I.02 Guidance 5 - Tubular Markers
text:
Section 3I.02 Guidance 5 - Tubular Markers
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3I. Channelizing Devices Used For Emphasis Of Pavement Marking Patterns
Page: 632

When tubular markers are used to supplement a R1-6 series sign (see Section 2B.20) that is either on the center line, lane line, or median island, they should not be used on the same pavement marking line where the R1-6 series sign is installed.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 3I. Channelizing Devices Used For Emphasis Of Pavement Marking Patterns

title: Section 3J.01 Support 1 - General
text:
Section 3J.01 Support 1 - General
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3J. Marking And Delineation Of Islands And Sidewalk Extensions
Page: 635

This Chapter addresses the marking and delineation of islands (see definition in Section 1C.02) and sidewalk extensions designated by pavement markings. Definitions, types, sizes, and other criteria for the design of islands are set forth in “A Policy on Geometric Design of Highways and Streets,” 2018 Edition, AASHTO.”

metadata.chapter: Chapter 3J. Marking And Delineation Of Islands And Sidewalk Extensions

title: Section 3J.02 Support 1 - Approach-End Treatment
text:
Section 3J.02 Support 1 - Approach-End Treatment
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3J. Marking And Delineation Of Islands And Sidewalk Extensions
Page: 635

An approach-end treatment to an island consists of longitudinal pavement markings and/or channelizing devices upstream of the island followed by a divergence of those pavement markings and/or channelizing devices concluding with a transition to other pavement markings that demarcate or outline the island (see Figure 3J-1).

metadata.chapter: Chapter 3J. Marking And Delineation Of Islands And Sidewalk Extensions

title: Section 3J.03 Standard 1 - Islands Designated by Pavement Markings
text:
Section 3J.03 Standard 1 - Islands Designated by Pavement Markings
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3J. Marking And Delineation Of Islands And Sidewalk Extensions
Page: 635

Except as provided in Paragraph 2 of this Section, islands formed by pavement markings only shall be established using channelizing lines, and shall be white when separating traffic flows in the same general direction or yellow when separating opposing directions of traffic.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 3J. Marking And Delineation Of Islands And Sidewalk Extensions

title: Section 3J.03 Standard 2 - Islands Designated by Pavement Markings
text:
Section 3J.03 Standard 2 - Islands Designated by Pavement Markings
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3J. Marking And Delineation Of Islands And Sidewalk Extensions
Page: 635

If a continuous flush median island separating travel in opposite directions is used, two sets of double solid yellow lines shall be used to form the island (see Figure 3B-5). Other markings in the median island area, such as diagonal lines (see Section 3B.25), shall also be yellow, except crosswalk markings which shall be white (see Chapter 3C).

metadata.chapter: Chapter 3J. Marking And Delineation Of Islands And Sidewalk Extensions

title: Section 3J.03 Standard 3 - Islands Designated by Pavement Markings
text:
Section 3J.03 Standard 3 - Islands Designated by Pavement Markings
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3J. Marking And Delineation Of Islands And Sidewalk Extensions
Page: 636

If used, chevron or diagonal markings (see Section 3B.25) within the island shall be the same color as the channelizing line. Figure 3J-1. Example of Markings for an Approach-End Treatment to an Island

metadata.chapter: Chapter 3J. Marking And Delineation Of Islands And Sidewalk Extensions

title: Section 3J.03 Option 4 - Islands Designated by Pavement Markings
text:
Section 3J.03 Option 4 - Islands Designated by Pavement Markings
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3J. Marking And Delineation Of Islands And Sidewalk Extensions
Page: 636

Both chevron and diagonal markings of the same color may be used within the same island based on engineering judgment.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 3J. Marking And Delineation Of Islands And Sidewalk Extensions

title: Section 3J.03 Option 5 - Islands Designated by Pavement Markings
text:
Section 3J.03 Option 5 - Islands Designated by Pavement Markings
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3J. Marking And Delineation Of Islands And Sidewalk Extensions
Page: 636

The area within the flush island delineated by pavement markings may use colored pavement in accordance with the provisions of Chapter 3H.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 3J. Marking And Delineation Of Islands And Sidewalk Extensions

title: Section 3J.03 Support 6 - Islands Designated by Pavement Markings
text:
Section 3J.03 Support 6 - Islands Designated by Pavement Markings
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3J. Marking And Delineation Of Islands And Sidewalk Extensions
Page: 636

Figure 3J-2 illustrates examples of islands designated by pavement markings.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 3J. Marking And Delineation Of Islands And Sidewalk Extensions

title: Section 3J.04 Standard 1 - Curb Markings for Raised Islands
text:
Section 3J.04 Standard 1 - Curb Markings for Raised Islands
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3J. Marking And Delineation Of Islands And Sidewalk Extensions
Page: 636

Where curbs are marked for delineation or visibility purposes, the colors shall comply with the general principles of markings (see Section 3A.03).

metadata.chapter: Chapter 3J. Marking And Delineation Of Islands And Sidewalk Extensions

title: Section 3J.04 Guidance 2 - Curb Markings for Raised Islands
text:
Section 3J.04 Guidance 2 - Curb Markings for Raised Islands
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3J. Marking And Delineation Of Islands And Sidewalk Extensions
Page: 636

Retroreflective solid yellow curb markings should be placed on the approach ends of raised medians and curbs of islands that are located in the line of traffic flow where the curb serves to channel traffic to the right of the obstruction (see Figure 3J-3).

metadata.chapter: Chapter 3J. Marking And Delineation Of Islands And Sidewalk Extensions

title: Section 3J.04 Guidance 3 - Curb Markings for Raised Islands
text:
Section 3J.04 Guidance 3 - Curb Markings for Raised Islands
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3J. Marking And Delineation Of Islands And Sidewalk Extensions
Page: 636

Retroreflective solid white curb markings should be used when traffic is permitted to pass on either side of the island (see Figure 3J-3).

metadata.chapter: Chapter 3J. Marking And Delineation Of Islands And Sidewalk Extensions

title: Section 3J.04 Guidance 4 - Curb Markings for Raised Islands
text:
Section 3J.04 Guidance 4 - Curb Markings for Raised Islands
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3J. Marking And Delineation Of Islands And Sidewalk Extensions
Page: 636

The retroreflective area should be of sufficient length to denote the general alignment of the edge of the island along which vehicles travel, including the approach end, when viewed from the approach to the island.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 3J. Marking And Delineation Of Islands And Sidewalk Extensions

title: Section 3J.04 Option 5 - Curb Markings for Raised Islands
text:
Section 3J.04 Option 5 - Curb Markings for Raised Islands
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3J. Marking And Delineation Of Islands And Sidewalk Extensions
Page: 636

Where the curbs of the islands become parallel to the direction of traffic flow or where the island is illuminated or marked with delineators, curb markings may be discontinued based on engineering judgment or study.

text:
Section 3J.07 Support 1 - Sidewalk Extensions Designated by Pavement Markings
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3J. Marking And Delineation Of Islands And Sidewalk Extensions
Page: 639

Sidewalk extensions reclaim a portion of the roadway, sometimes including a portion of parking lanes, shoulders, and/or the traveled way, and repurpose that area for non-vehicular uses. They extend the sidewalk or other pedestrian space, shorten pedestrian crossing distances, alter the roadway geometry for speed management or channelizing, or serve other purposes.

metadata.section_title: Sidewalk Extensions Designated by Pavement Markings
metadata.chapter: Chapter 3J. Marking And Delineation Of Islands And Sidewalk Extensions

text:
Section 3J.07 Support 2 - Sidewalk Extensions Designated by Pavement Markings
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3J. Marking And Delineation Of Islands And Sidewalk Extensions
Page: 639

Sidewalk extensions, sometimes referred to as curb extensions, neckdowns, or bulb-outs, typically are created by physical infrastructure including concrete or asphalt to form a physical narrowing of the roadway with the finished surface at the same level as the adjoining sidewalk.

metadata.section_title: Sidewalk Extensions Designated by Pavement Markings

text:

Page: 639

Where an adjoining curb and raised sidewalk are present, this type of application results in a multi-level sidewalk due to the difference in elevation between the adjoining pedestrian surfaces.

Page: 639

Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3J. Marking And Delineation Of Islands And Sidewalk Extensions
Page: 640

The paved area between the double solid line forming the sidewalk extension designated by pavement markings and the sidewalk or other roadside area is not part of the roadway. Sidewalk extensions designated by pavement markings formed by double solid lines are distinct from areas such as shoulders or gore areas where travel is discouraged by the presence of a single line, or flush medians where travel is prohibited by a double solid line. Sidewalk extensions designated by pavement markings with double solid lines designate areas outside the roadway where vehicle traversal is prohibited.

Page: 640

These areas are not considered a sidewalk extension, and provisions to delineate areas where vehicle traversal is discouraged include channelizing lines (see Section 3B.08), edge lines (see Section 3B.09), and diagonal markings (see Section 3B.25).

title: Section 3K.01 Support 1 - Longitudinal Rumble Strip Markings
text:
Section 3K.01 Support 1 - Longitudinal Rumble Strip Markings
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3K. Rumble Strip Markings
Page: 642

Longitudinal rumble strips consist of a series of rough-textured or slightly raised or depressed road surfaces intended to alert inattentive drivers through vibration and sound that their vehicle has left the travel lane. Shoulder rumble strips are typically installed along the shoulder near the travel lane. On divided highways, rumble strips are sometimes installed on the median side (left-hand side) shoulder as well as on the outside (right-hand side) shoulder. On two-way roadways, rumble strips are sometimes installed along the center line.

title: Section 3K.01 Support 2 - Longitudinal Rumble Strip Markings
text:
Section 3K.01 Support 2 - Longitudinal Rumble Strip Markings
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3K. Rumble Strip Markings
Page: 642

This Manual contains no provisions regarding the design and placement of longitudinal rumble strips. The provisions in this Manual address the use of markings in combination with a longitudinal rumble strip. Figure 3K-1 illustrates markings used with or near longitudinal rumble strips.

title: Section 3K.02 Support 1 - Transverse Rumble Strip Markings
text:
Section 3K.02 Support 1 - Transverse Rumble Strip Markings
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3K. Rumble Strip Markings
Page: 642

Transverse rumble strips consist of intermittent narrow, transverse areas of rough-textured or slightly raised or depressed road surface that extend across the travel lanes to alert drivers to unusual vehicular traffic conditions. Through noise and vibration, they attract the attention of road users to features such as unexpected changes in alignment and conditions requiring a reduction in speed or a stop.

title: Section 3K.02 Support 2 - Transverse Rumble Strip Markings
text:
Section 3K.02 Support 2 - Transverse Rumble Strip Markings
Part: Part 3 Markings
Chapter: Chapter 3K. Rumble Strip Markings
Page: 642

This Manual contains no provisions regarding the design and placement of transverse rumble strips that approximate the color of the pavement. The provisions in this Manual address the use of markings in combination with a transverse rumble strip.

title: Section 4A.01 Support 1 - Types
text:
Section 4A.01 Support 1 - Types
Part: Part 4 Highway Traffic Signals
Chapter: Chapter 4A. General
Page: 643

The following types and uses of highway traffic signals are discussed in Part 4: traffic control signals; bicycle signal faces; pedestrian signal heads; hybrid beacons; rectangular rapid flashing beacons; emergency-vehicle traffic control signals; traffic control signals for one-lane, two-way facilities; traffic control signals for freeway entrance ramps; movable bridge traffic signals; toll plaza traffic signals; flashing beacons; lane-use control signals; and in- roadway warning lights.

title: Section 4A.02 Support 1 - Meanings of Signal Indications
text:
Section 4A.02 Support 1 - Meanings of Signal Indications
Part: Part 4 Highway Traffic Signals
Chapter: Chapter 4A. General
Page: 643

The “Uniform Vehicle Code” (see Section 1A.06) is the primary source for the standards for the meanings of vehicular signal indications to both vehicle operators and pedestrians as provided in Sections 4A.03 and 4A.04, the standards for the meanings of separate bicycle signal face indications as provided in Section 4A.05, and the standards for the meanings of separate pedestrian signal head indications as provided in Section 4A.06.

title: Section 4A.02 Support 2 - Meanings of Signal Indications
text:
Section 4A.02 Support 2 - Meanings of Signal Indications
Part: Part 4 Highway Traffic Signals
