title: Section 6L.08 Option 1 - High-Level Warning Devices (Flag Trees)
text:
Section 6L.08 Option 1 - High-Level Warning Devices (Flag Trees)
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6L. Other Ttc Zone Traffic Control Devices
Page: 836

A high-level warning device (flag tree) may supplement other TTC devices in TTC zones.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 6L. Other Ttc Zone Traffic Control Devices

title: Section 6L.08 Support 2 - High-Level Warning Devices (Flag Trees)
text:
Section 6L.08 Support 2 - High-Level Warning Devices (Flag Trees)
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6L. Other Ttc Zone Traffic Control Devices
Page: 836

A high-level warning device is designed to be seen over the top of typical passenger cars. A typical high-level warning device is shown in Figure 6F-1.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 6L. Other Ttc Zone Traffic Control Devices

title: Section 6L.08 Standard 3 - High-Level Warning Devices (Flag Trees)
text:
Section 6L.08 Standard 3 - High-Level Warning Devices (Flag Trees)
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6L. Other Ttc Zone Traffic Control Devices
Page: 836

A high-level warning device shall consist of a minimum of two flags with or without a Type B high- intensity flashing warning light. The distance from the roadway to the bottom of the lens of the light and to the lowest point of the flag material shall be not less than 8 feet. The flag shall be 16 inches square or larger and shall be orange or fluorescent red-orange in color.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 6L. Other Ttc Zone Traffic Control Devices

title: Section 6L.08 Option 4 - High-Level Warning Devices (Flag Trees)
text:
Section 6L.08 Option 4 - High-Level Warning Devices (Flag Trees)
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6L. Other Ttc Zone Traffic Control Devices
Page: 836

An appropriate warning sign may be mounted below the flags.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 6L. Other Ttc Zone Traffic Control Devices

title: Section 6L.08 Support 5 - High-Level Warning Devices (Flag Trees)
text:
Section 6L.08 Support 5 - High-Level Warning Devices (Flag Trees)
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6L. Other Ttc Zone Traffic Control Devices
Page: 837

High-level warning devices are most commonly used in high-density road user situations to warn road users of short-term operations.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 6L. Other Ttc Zone Traffic Control Devices

title: Section 6M.01 Support 1 - General
text:
Section 6M.01 Support 1 - General
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6M. Other Ttc Zone Design Features And Safety Devices
Page: 837

Although certain devices and design features, such as lighting, barriers, dividers, crash cushions, and screens, are sometimes used in TTC zones to supplement traffic control devices or enhance traffic operations or safety for road users, they are not considered to be traffic control devices. The following Sections describe the most commonly used devices and design features. Section 1D.04 contains additional information about these devices and design features.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 6M. Other Ttc Zone Design Features And Safety Devices

title: Section 6M.02 Support 1 - Positive Protection and Temporary Traffic Barriers
text:
Section 6M.02 Support 1 - Positive Protection and Temporary Traffic Barriers
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6M. Other Ttc Zone Design Features And Safety Devices
Page: 837

Temporary traffic barriers, including portable or movable barriers, are devices designed to help prevent penetration by vehicles while minimizing injuries to vehicle occupants, and to protect workers, bicyclists, and pedestrians.

metadata.section_title: Positive Protection and Temporary Traffic Barriers
metadata.chapter: Chapter 6M. Other Ttc Zone Design Features And Safety Devices

title: Section 6M.02 Guidance 2 - Positive Protection and Temporary Traffic Barriers
text:
Section 6M.02 Guidance 2 - Positive Protection and Temporary Traffic Barriers
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6M. Other Ttc Zone Design Features And Safety Devices
Page: 837

Except as otherwise required, at a minimum, longitudinal traffic barriers and/or other positive protection devices should be considered in work zone situations that place workers at increased risk from motorized traffic, and where positive protection devices offer the highest potential for improved safety for workers and road users.

metadata.section_title: Positive Protection and Temporary Traffic Barriers
metadata.chapter: Chapter 6M. Other Ttc Zone Design Features And Safety Devices

title: Section 6M.02 Support 3 - Positive Protection and Temporary Traffic Barriers
text:
Section 6M.02 Support 3 - Positive Protection and Temporary Traffic Barriers
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6M. Other Ttc Zone Design Features And Safety Devices
Page: 837

Considerations for positive protection include, but are not limited to, the following circumstances: A. Work zones that provide workers no means of escape from motorized traffic such as tunnels or bridges; B. Long-term stationary work zones of two weeks or more resulting in substantial worker exposure to motorized traffic; C. Projects with anticipated operating speeds of 45 mph or greater, especially when combined with high traffic volumes; D. Work operations that place workers, pedestrians, or bicyclists close to travel lanes open to traffic; and E. Roadside hazards, such as drop-offs or unfinished bridge decks, that will remain in place overnight or longer.

metadata.section_title: Positive Protection and Temporary Traffic Barriers
metadata.chapter: Chapter 6M. Other Ttc Zone Design Features And Safety Devices

title: Section 6M.02 Support 4 - Positive Protection and Temporary Traffic Barriers
text:
Section 6M.02 Support 4 - Positive Protection and Temporary Traffic Barriers
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6M. Other Ttc Zone Design Features And Safety Devices
Page: 837

Work zone setups vary depending on the nature of the positive protection used.

metadata.section_title: Positive Protection and Temporary Traffic Barriers
metadata.chapter: Chapter 6M. Other Ttc Zone Design Features And Safety Devices

title: Section 6M.02 Support 5 - Positive Protection and Temporary Traffic Barriers
text:
Section 6M.02 Support 5 - Positive Protection and Temporary Traffic Barriers
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6M. Other Ttc Zone Design Features And Safety Devices
Page: 837

23 CFR Part 630.1108(a) contains additional requirements for certain projects.

metadata.section_title: Positive Protection and Temporary Traffic Barriers
metadata.chapter: Chapter 6M. Other Ttc Zone Design Features And Safety Devices

title: Section 6M.02 Option 6 - Positive Protection and Temporary Traffic Barriers
text:
Section 6M.02 Option 6 - Positive Protection and Temporary Traffic Barriers
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6M. Other Ttc Zone Design Features And Safety Devices
Page: 837

Temporary traffic barriers may be used to separate two-way vehicular traffic.

metadata.section_title: Positive Protection and Temporary Traffic Barriers
metadata.chapter: Chapter 6M. Other Ttc Zone Design Features And Safety Devices

title: Section 6M.02 Standard 7 - Positive Protection and Temporary Traffic Barriers
text:
Section 6M.02 Standard 7 - Positive Protection and Temporary Traffic Barriers
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6M. Other Ttc Zone Design Features And Safety Devices
Page: 837

Temporary traffic barriers shall be supplemented with standard delineation, pavement markings, or channelizing devices for improved daytime and nighttime visibility if they are used to channelize vehicular traffic. The delineation color shall match the applicable pavement marking color.

metadata.section_title: Positive Protection and Temporary Traffic Barriers
metadata.chapter: Chapter 6M. Other Ttc Zone Design Features And Safety Devices

title: Section 6M.02 Standard 8 - Positive Protection and Temporary Traffic Barriers
text:
Section 6M.02 Standard 8 - Positive Protection and Temporary Traffic Barriers
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6M. Other Ttc Zone Design Features And Safety Devices
Page: 837

Temporary traffic barriers, including their end treatments, shall be crashworthy (see definition in Section 1C.02).

metadata.section_title: Positive Protection and Temporary Traffic Barriers
metadata.chapter: Chapter 6M. Other Ttc Zone Design Features And Safety Devices

title: Section 6M.02 Standard 9 - Positive Protection and Temporary Traffic Barriers
text:
Section 6M.02 Standard 9 - Positive Protection and Temporary Traffic Barriers
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6M. Other Ttc Zone Design Features And Safety Devices
Page: 837

Short intermittent segments of temporary traffic barrier shall not be used because they nullify the containment and redirective capabilities of the temporary traffic barrier, increase the potential for serious injury both to vehicle occupants and pedestrians, and encourage the presence of blunt leading ends. Adjacent temporary traffic barrier segments shall be properly connected in order to provide the overall strength required for the temporary traffic barrier to perform properly.

metadata.section_title: Positive Protection and Temporary Traffic Barriers
metadata.chapter: Chapter 6M. Other Ttc Zone Design Features And Safety Devices

title: Section 6M.02 Option 10 - Positive Protection and Temporary Traffic Barriers
text:
Section 6M.02 Option 10 - Positive Protection and Temporary Traffic Barriers
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6M. Other Ttc Zone Design Features And Safety Devices
Page: 837

Steady-burn warning lights (see Section 6L.07) may be mounted on temporary traffic barrier installations.

metadata.section_title: Positive Protection and Temporary Traffic Barriers
metadata.chapter: Chapter 6M. Other Ttc Zone Design Features And Safety Devices

title: Section 6M.02 Support 11 - Positive Protection and Temporary Traffic Barriers
text:
Section 6M.02 Support 11 - Positive Protection and Temporary Traffic Barriers
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6M. Other Ttc Zone Design Features And Safety Devices
Page: 838

Temporary traffic barrier includes portable concrete, portable steel, or movable barrier which can all be moved laterally and/or longitudinally when needed and/or from site to site. More specific information on the use of temporary traffic barriers is contained in Chapters 8 and 9 of “Roadside Design Guide,” 4th Edition, 2011, AASHTO.

metadata.section_title: Positive Protection and Temporary Traffic Barriers
metadata.chapter: Chapter 6M. Other Ttc Zone Design Features And Safety Devices

title: Section 6M.03 Standard 1 - Temporary Raised Islands
text:
Section 6M.03 Standard 1 - Temporary Raised Islands
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6M. Other Ttc Zone Design Features And Safety Devices
Page: 838

Temporary raised islands shall be used only in combination with pavement striping and other suitable channelizing devices.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 6M. Other Ttc Zone Design Features And Safety Devices

title: Section 6M.03 Option 2 - Temporary Raised Islands
text:
Section 6M.03 Option 2 - Temporary Raised Islands
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6M. Other Ttc Zone Design Features And Safety Devices
Page: 838

A temporary raised island may be used to separate vehicular traffic flows in two-lane, two-way operations on roadways having a vehicular traffic volume range of 4,000 to 15,000 average daily traffic (ADT) and on freeways having a vehicular traffic volume range of 22,000 ADT to 60,000 ADT.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 6M. Other Ttc Zone Design Features And Safety Devices

title: Section 6M.03 Option 3 - Temporary Raised Islands
text:
Section 6M.03 Option 3 - Temporary Raised Islands
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6M. Other Ttc Zone Design Features And Safety Devices
Page: 838

Temporary raised islands also may be used in other than two-lane, two-way operations where physical separation of vehicular traffic from the TTC zone is not required.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 6M. Other Ttc Zone Design Features And Safety Devices

title: Section 6M.03 Guidance 4 - Temporary Raised Islands
text:
Section 6M.03 Guidance 4 - Temporary Raised Islands
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6M. Other Ttc Zone Design Features And Safety Devices
Page: 838

Temporary raised islands should have the basic dimensions of 4 inches high by at least 12 inches wide and have rounded or chamfered corners.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 6M. Other Ttc Zone Design Features And Safety Devices

title: Section 6M.03 Guidance 5 - Temporary Raised Islands
text:
Section 6M.03 Guidance 5 - Temporary Raised Islands
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6M. Other Ttc Zone Design Features And Safety Devices
Page: 838

The temporary raised islands should not be designed in such a manner that they would cause a motorist to lose control of the vehicle if the vehicle inadvertently strikes the temporary raised island. If struck, pieces of the island should not be dislodged to the extent that they could penetrate the occupant compartment or involve other vehicles.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 6M. Other Ttc Zone Design Features And Safety Devices

title: Section 6M.03 Standard 6 - Temporary Raised Islands
text:
Section 6M.03 Standard 6 - Temporary Raised Islands
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6M. Other Ttc Zone Design Features And Safety Devices
Page: 838

At pedestrian crossing locations, temporary raised islands shall have an opening or be shortened to provide at least a 60-inch wide passageway for the crossing pedestrian.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 6M. Other Ttc Zone Design Features And Safety Devices

title: Section 6M.04 Support 1 - Detectable Edging for Pedestrians
text:
Section 6M.04 Support 1 - Detectable Edging for Pedestrians
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6M. Other Ttc Zone Design Features And Safety Devices
Page: 838

Individual channelizing devices, tape or rope used to connect individual devices, other discontinuous barriers and devices, and pavement markings are not detectable by persons with vision disabilities and are incapable of providing detectable path guidance on temporary or realigned sidewalks or other pedestrian facilities.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 6M. Other Ttc Zone Design Features And Safety Devices

title: Section 6M.04 Guidance 2 - Detectable Edging for Pedestrians
text:
Section 6M.04 Guidance 2 - Detectable Edging for Pedestrians
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6M. Other Ttc Zone Design Features And Safety Devices
Page: 838

A continuously-detectable edging should be provided throughout the length of a temporary pedestrian facility such that it can be followed by pedestrians using long canes for guidance. This edging should extend at least 8 inches above the surface of the sidewalk or pathway, with the bottom of the edging a maximum of 2 inches above the surface. This edging should be continuous throughout the length of the facility except for gaps at locations where pedestrians or vehicles will be turning or crossing. This edging should consist of a prefabricated or formed-in-place curbing or other continuous device that is placed along the edge of the sidewalk or walkway. This edging should be firmly attached to the ground or to other devices. Adjacent sections of this edging should be interconnected such that the edging is not displaced by pedestrian or vehicular traffic or work operations, and such that it does not constitute a hazard to pedestrians, workers, or other road users.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 6M. Other Ttc Zone Design Features And Safety Devices

title: Section 6M.04 Support 3 - Detectable Edging for Pedestrians
text:
Section 6M.04 Support 3 - Detectable Edging for Pedestrians
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6M. Other Ttc Zone Design Features And Safety Devices
Page: 838

Examples of detectable edging for pedestrians include: A. Prefabricated lightweight sections of plastic, metal, or other suitable materials that are interconnected and fixed in place to form a continuous edge. B. Prefabricated lightweight sections of plastic, metal, or other suitable materials that are interconnected, fixed in place, and placed at ground level to provide a continuous connection between channelizing devices located at intervals along the edge of the sidewalk or walkway. C. Sections of lumber interconnected and fixed in place to form a continuous edge. D. Formed-in-place asphalt or concrete curb. E. Prefabricated concrete curb sections that are interconnected and fixed in place to form a continuous edge. F. Continuous temporary traffic barrier or longitudinal channelizing barricades placed along the edge of the sidewalk or walkway that provides a pedestrian edging at ground level. G. Chain link or other fencing equipped with a continuous bottom rail.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 6M. Other Ttc Zone Design Features And Safety Devices

title: Section 6M.04 Guidance 4 - Detectable Edging for Pedestrians
text:
Section 6M.04 Guidance 4 - Detectable Edging for Pedestrians
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6M. Other Ttc Zone Design Features And Safety Devices
Page: 839

Detectable pedestrian edging should be orange, white, or yellow and should match the color of the adjacent channelizing devices or traffic control devices, if any are present.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 6M. Other Ttc Zone Design Features And Safety Devices

title: Section 6M.05 Support 1 - Crash Cushions
text:
Section 6M.05 Support 1 - Crash Cushions
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6M. Other Ttc Zone Design Features And Safety Devices
Page: 839

Crash cushions are systems that mitigate the effects of errant vehicles that strike obstacles, either by smoothly decelerating the vehicle to a stop when hit head-on, or by redirecting the errant vehicle. The two types of crash cushions that are used in TTC zones are stationary crash cushions and truck-mounted attenuators. Crash cushions in TTC zones help protect the drivers from the exposed ends of barriers, fixed objects, shadow vehicles, and other obstacles. Specific information on the use of crash cushions can be found in “Roadside Design Guide,” 4th Edition, 2011, AASHTO.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 6M. Other Ttc Zone Design Features And Safety Devices

title: Section 6M.05 Standard 2 - Crash Cushions
text:
Section 6M.05 Standard 2 - Crash Cushions
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6M. Other Ttc Zone Design Features And Safety Devices
Page: 839

Crash cushions shall be crashworthy (see definition in Section 1C.02). They shall also be designed for each application to stop or redirect errant vehicles under prescribed conditions. Crash cushions shall be periodically inspected to verify that they have not been hit or damaged. Damaged crash cushions shall be promptly repaired or replaced to maintain their crashworthiness.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 6M. Other Ttc Zone Design Features And Safety Devices

title: Section 6M.05 Support 3 - Crash Cushions
text:
Section 6M.05 Support 3 - Crash Cushions
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6M. Other Ttc Zone Design Features And Safety Devices
Page: 839

Stationary crash cushions are used in the same manner as permanent highway installations to protect drivers from the exposed ends of barriers, fixed objects, and other obstacles.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 6M. Other Ttc Zone Design Features And Safety Devices

title: Section 6M.05 Standard 4 - Crash Cushions
text:
Section 6M.05 Standard 4 - Crash Cushions
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6M. Other Ttc Zone Design Features And Safety Devices
Page: 839

Stationary crash cushions shall be designed for the specific application intended.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 6M. Other Ttc Zone Design Features And Safety Devices

title: Section 6M.05 Standard 5 - Crash Cushions
text:
Section 6M.05 Standard 5 - Crash Cushions
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6M. Other Ttc Zone Design Features And Safety Devices
Page: 839

Truck-mounted attenuators shall be energy-absorbing devices attached to the rear of shadow trailers or trucks and shall be used in accordance with the manufacturer’s specifications. If used, the shadow vehicle with the attenuator shall be located in advance of the work area, workers, or equipment to reduce the severity of rear-end crashes from errant vehicles.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 6M. Other Ttc Zone Design Features And Safety Devices

title: Section 6M.05 Support 6 - Crash Cushions
text:
Section 6M.05 Support 6 - Crash Cushions
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6M. Other Ttc Zone Design Features And Safety Devices
Page: 839

Trucks or trailers are often used as shadow vehicles to protect workers or work equipment from errant vehicles. These shadow vehicles are normally equipped with flashing arrows, changeable message signs, and/or high-intensity rotating, flashing, oscillating, or strobe lights and are located properly in advance of the workers and/or equipment that they are protecting. However, these shadow vehicles might themselves cause injuries to occupants of the errant vehicles if they are not equipped with truck-mounted attenuators.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 6M. Other Ttc Zone Design Features And Safety Devices

title: Section 6M.05 Guidance 7 - Crash Cushions
text:
Section 6M.05 Guidance 7 - Crash Cushions
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6M. Other Ttc Zone Design Features And Safety Devices
Page: 839

The shadow truck should be positioned a sufficient distance in advance of the workers or equipment being protected so that there will be sufficient distance, but not so much so that errant vehicles will travel around the shadow truck and strike the protected workers and/or equipment.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 6M. Other Ttc Zone Design Features And Safety Devices

title: Section 6M.05 Support 8 - Crash Cushions
text:
Section 6M.05 Support 8 - Crash Cushions
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6M. Other Ttc Zone Design Features And Safety Devices
Page: 839

Chapter 9 of “Roadside Design Guide,” 4th Edition, 2011, AASHTO contains additional information regarding the use of shadow vehicles.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 6M. Other Ttc Zone Design Features And Safety Devices

title: Section 6M.06 Support 1 - Rumble Strips
text:
Section 6M.06 Support 1 - Rumble Strips
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6M. Other Ttc Zone Design Features And Safety Devices
Page: 839

Transverse rumble strips consist of intermittent, narrow, transverse areas of rough-textured or slightly-raised or depressed road surface that extend across the travel lanes to alert drivers to unusual vehicular traffic conditions. Through noise and vibration they attract the driver’s attention to such features as unexpected changes in alignment and to conditions requiring a stop.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 6M. Other Ttc Zone Design Features And Safety Devices

title: Section 6M.06 Support 2 - Rumble Strips
text:
Section 6M.06 Support 2 - Rumble Strips
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6M. Other Ttc Zone Design Features And Safety Devices
Page: 839

Longitudinal rumble strips consist of a series of rough-textured or slightly-raised or depressed road surfaces located along the shoulder to alert road users that they are leaving the travel lanes.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 6M. Other Ttc Zone Design Features And Safety Devices

title: Section 6M.06 Standard 3 - Rumble Strips
text:
Section 6M.06 Standard 3 - Rumble Strips
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6M. Other Ttc Zone Design Features And Safety Devices
Page: 839

If it is desirable to use a color other than the color of the pavement for a longitudinal rumble strip, the color of the rumble strip shall be the same color as the longitudinal line the rumble strip supplements.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 6M. Other Ttc Zone Design Features And Safety Devices

title: Section 6M.06 Standard 4 - Rumble Strips
text:
Section 6M.06 Standard 4 - Rumble Strips
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6M. Other Ttc Zone Design Features And Safety Devices
Page: 839

If the color of a transverse rumble strip used within a travel lane is not the color of the pavement, the color of the rumble strip shall be white, black, or orange.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 6M. Other Ttc Zone Design Features And Safety Devices

title: Section 6M.06 Option 5 - Rumble Strips
text:
Section 6M.06 Option 5 - Rumble Strips
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6M. Other Ttc Zone Design Features And Safety Devices
Page: 840

Intervals between transverse rumble strips may be reduced as the distance to the approached conditions is diminished in order to convey an impression that a closure speed is too fast and/or that an action is imminent. A sign warning drivers of the onset of rumble strips may be placed in advance of any transverse rumble strip installation. MUTCD 11th Edition - Revision 1

metadata.chapter: Chapter 6M. Other Ttc Zone Design Features And Safety Devices

title: Section 6M.06 Guidance 6 - Rumble Strips
text:
Section 6M.06 Guidance 6 - Rumble Strips
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6M. Other Ttc Zone Design Features And Safety Devices
Page: 840

Transverse rumble strips should be placed transverse to vehicular traffic movement. They should not adversely affect overall pavement skid resistance under wet or dry conditions.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 6M. Other Ttc Zone Design Features And Safety Devices

title: Section 6M.06 Guidance 7 - Rumble Strips
text:
Section 6M.06 Guidance 7 - Rumble Strips
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6M. Other Ttc Zone Design Features And Safety Devices
Page: 840

In urban areas, even though a closer spacing might be warranted, transverse rumble strips should be designed in a manner that does not promote unnecessary braking or erratic steering maneuvers by road users.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 6M. Other Ttc Zone Design Features And Safety Devices

title: Section 6M.06 Guidance 8 - Rumble Strips
text:
Section 6M.06 Guidance 8 - Rumble Strips
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6M. Other Ttc Zone Design Features And Safety Devices
Page: 840

Transverse rumble strips should not be placed on sharp horizontal or vertical curves.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 6M. Other Ttc Zone Design Features And Safety Devices

title: Section 6M.06 Guidance 9 - Rumble Strips
text:
Section 6M.06 Guidance 9 - Rumble Strips
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6M. Other Ttc Zone Design Features And Safety Devices
Page: 840

Rumble strips should not be placed through pedestrian crossings or on bicycle routes.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 6M. Other Ttc Zone Design Features And Safety Devices

title: Section 6M.06 Guidance 10 - Rumble Strips
text:
Section 6M.06 Guidance 10 - Rumble Strips
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6M. Other Ttc Zone Design Features And Safety Devices
Page: 840

Transverse rumble strips should not be placed on roadways used by bicyclists unless a minimum clear path of 4 feet is provided at each edge of the roadway or on each paved shoulder.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 6M. Other Ttc Zone Design Features And Safety Devices

title: Section 6M.06 Guidance 11 - Rumble Strips
text:
Section 6M.06 Guidance 11 - Rumble Strips
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6M. Other Ttc Zone Design Features And Safety Devices
Page: 840

Longitudinal rumble strips should not be placed on the shoulder of a roadway that is used by bicyclists unless a minimum clear path of 4 feet is also provided on the shoulder.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 6M. Other Ttc Zone Design Features And Safety Devices

title: Section 6M.07 Support 1 - Screens
text:
Section 6M.07 Support 1 - Screens
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6M. Other Ttc Zone Design Features And Safety Devices
Page: 840

Screens are used to block the road users’ view of activities that can be distracting. Screens might improve safety and motor vehicle traffic flow where volumes approach the roadway capacity because they discourage gawking and reduce headlight glare from oncoming motor vehicle traffic.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 6M. Other Ttc Zone Design Features And Safety Devices

title: Section 6M.07 Guidance 2 - Screens
text:
Section 6M.07 Guidance 2 - Screens
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6M. Other Ttc Zone Design Features And Safety Devices
Page: 840

Screens should not be mounted where they could adversely restrict road user visibility and sight distance and adversely affect the operation of vehicles.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 6M. Other Ttc Zone Design Features And Safety Devices

title: Section 6M.07 Option 3 - Screens
text:
Section 6M.07 Option 3 - Screens
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6M. Other Ttc Zone Design Features And Safety Devices
Page: 840

Screens may be mounted on the top of temporary traffic barriers that separate two-way motor vehicle traffic.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 6M. Other Ttc Zone Design Features And Safety Devices

title: Section 6M.07 Guidance 4 - Screens
text:
Section 6M.07 Guidance 4 - Screens
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6M. Other Ttc Zone Design Features And Safety Devices
Page: 840

Design of screens should be in accordance with Chapter 9 of “Roadside Design Guide,” 4th Edition, 2011, AASHTO.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 6M. Other Ttc Zone Design Features And Safety Devices

title: Section 6M.08 Support 1 - Lighting for Night Work
text:
Section 6M.08 Support 1 - Lighting for Night Work
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6M. Other Ttc Zone Design Features And Safety Devices
Page: 840

Utility, maintenance, or construction activities on highways are frequently conducted during nighttime periods when vehicular traffic volumes are lower. Large construction projects are sometimes operated on a double-shift basis requiring night work (see Section 6N.18).

metadata.chapter: Chapter 6M. Other Ttc Zone Design Features And Safety Devices

title: Section 6M.08 Guidance 2 - Lighting for Night Work
text:
Section 6M.08 Guidance 2 - Lighting for Night Work
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6M. Other Ttc Zone Design Features And Safety Devices
Page: 840

When nighttime work is being performed, floodlights should be used to illuminate the work area, equipment crossings, and other areas.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 6M. Other Ttc Zone Design Features And Safety Devices

title: Section 6M.08 Guidance 3 - Lighting for Night Work
text:
Section 6M.08 Guidance 3 - Lighting for Night Work
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6M. Other Ttc Zone Design Features And Safety Devices
Page: 840

When used, floodlighting should be installed in a manner that minimizes glare to approaching road users, flaggers, or workers.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 6M. Other Ttc Zone Design Features And Safety Devices

title: Section 6M.08 Guidance 4 - Lighting for Night Work
text:
Section 6M.08 Guidance 4 - Lighting for Night Work
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6M. Other Ttc Zone Design Features And Safety Devices
Page: 840

The adequacy of the floodlight placement and elimination of potential glare should be determined by driving through and observing the floodlighted area from each direction on all approaching roadways after the initial floodlight setup, at night, and periodically. Lighting should be sufficient so as to give road users the capability to identify a worker as a person. Care should be taken to minimize the potential for shadows to conceal workers within the work area.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 6M. Other Ttc Zone Design Features And Safety Devices

title: Section 6M.08 Support 5 - Lighting for Night Work
text:
Section 6M.08 Support 5 - Lighting for Night Work
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6M. Other Ttc Zone Design Features And Safety Devices
Page: 840

Desired illumination levels vary depending upon the nature of the task involved. An average horizontal luminance of 5 foot-candles can be adequate for general activities. Tasks requiring high levels of precision and extreme care can require an average horizontal luminance of 20 foot-candles.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 6M. Other Ttc Zone Design Features And Safety Devices

title: Section 6M.08 Standard 6 - Lighting for Night Work
text:
Section 6M.08 Standard 6 - Lighting for Night Work
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6M. Other Ttc Zone Design Features And Safety Devices
Page: 841

Except in emergency situations, flagger stations shall be illuminated at night. December 2025

metadata.chapter: Chapter 6M. Other Ttc Zone Design Features And Safety Devices

title: Section 6N.01 Support 1 - Work Duration
text:
Section 6N.01 Support 1 - Work Duration
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities
Page: 841

Work duration is a major factor in determining the number and types of devices used in TTC zones. The duration of a TTC zone is defined relative to the length of time a work operation occupies a spot location.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities

title: Section 6N.01 Standard 2 - Work Duration
text:
Section 6N.01 Standard 2 - Work Duration
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities
Page: 841

The five categories of work duration and their time at a location shall be defined as follows: A. Long-term stationary is work that occupies a location more than 3 days. B. Intermediate-term stationary is work that occupies a location more than one daylight period up to 3 days, or nighttime work lasting more than 1 hour. C. Short-term stationary is daytime work that occupies a location for more than 1 hour within a single daylight period. D. Short duration is work that occupies a location up to 1 hour. E. Mobile is work that moves intermittently or continuously.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities

title: Section 6N.01 Support 3 - Work Duration
text:
Section 6N.01 Support 3 - Work Duration
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities
Page: 841

At long-term stationary TTC zones, there is ample time to install and realize benefits from the full range of TTC procedures and devices that are available for use. Larger channelizing devices, temporary roadways, and temporary traffic barriers are frequently used.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities

title: Section 6N.01 Standard 4 - Work Duration
text:
Section 6N.01 Standard 4 - Work Duration
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities
Page: 841

Since long-term operations extend into nighttime, retroreflective and/or illuminated devices shall be used in long-term stationary TTC zones.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities

title: Section 6N.01 Support 5 - Work Duration
text:
Section 6N.01 Support 5 - Work Duration
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities
Page: 841

In intermediate-term stationary TTC zones, it might not be feasible or practical to use procedures or devices that would be desirable for long-term stationary TTC zones, such as altered pavement markings, temporary traffic barriers, and temporary roadways. The increased time to place and remove these devices in some cases could significantly lengthen the project, thus increasing exposure time.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities

title: Section 6N.01 Standard 6 - Work Duration
text:
Section 6N.01 Standard 6 - Work Duration
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities
Page: 841

Since intermediate-term operations extend into nighttime, retroreflective and/or illuminated devices shall be used in intermediate-term stationary TTC zones.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities

title: Section 6N.01 Support 7 - Work Duration
text:
Section 6N.01 Support 7 - Work Duration
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities
Page: 841

Most maintenance and utility operations are short-term stationary work.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities

title: Section 6N.01 Support 8 - Work Duration
text:
Section 6N.01 Support 8 - Work Duration
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities
Page: 841

As compared to stationary operations, mobile and short-duration operations are activities that might involve different treatments. Devices having greater mobility might be necessary such as signs mounted on trucks. Devices that are larger, more imposing, or more visible can be used effectively and economically. The mobility of the TTC zone is important.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities

title: Section 6N.01 Guidance 9 - Work Duration
text:
Section 6N.01 Guidance 9 - Work Duration
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities
Page: 841

Safety in short-duration or mobile operations should not be compromised by using fewer devices simply because the operation will frequently change its location.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities

title: Section 6N.01 Support 10 - Work Duration
text:
Section 6N.01 Support 10 - Work Duration
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities
Page: 841

During short-duration work, it often takes longer to set up and remove the TTC zone than to perform the work. Workers face hazards in setting up and taking down the TTC zone. Also, since the work time is short, delays affecting road users are significantly increased when additional devices are installed and removed.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities

title: Section 6N.01 Option 11 - Work Duration
text:
Section 6N.01 Option 11 - Work Duration
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities
Page: 841

Considering these factors, simplified control procedures may be warranted for short-duration work. A reduction in the number of devices may be offset by the use of other more dominant devices such as high-intensity rotating, flashing, oscillating, or strobe lights on work vehicles.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities

title: Section 6N.01 Support 12 - Work Duration
text:
Section 6N.01 Support 12 - Work Duration
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities
Page: 841

Mobile operations often involve frequent short stops for activities such as litter cleanup, pothole patching, or utility operations, and are similar to short-duration operations.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities

title: Section 6N.01 Option 13 - Work Duration
text:
Section 6N.01 Option 13 - Work Duration
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities
Page: 842

Flags and/or channelizing devices may additionally be used and moved periodically to keep them near the mobile work area.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities

title: Section 6N.01 Option 14 - Work Duration
text:
Section 6N.01 Option 14 - Work Duration
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities
Page: 842

Flaggers may be used for mobile operations that often involve frequent short stops.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities

title: Section 6N.01 Support 15 - Work Duration
text:
Section 6N.01 Support 15 - Work Duration
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities
Page: 842

Mobile operations also include work activities where workers and equipment move along the road without stopping, usually at slow speeds. The advance warning area moves with the work area.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities

title: Section 6N.01 Guidance 16 - Work Duration
text:
Section 6N.01 Guidance 16 - Work Duration
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities
Page: 842

When mobile operations are being performed, a shadow vehicle equipped with an arrow board or a sign should follow the work vehicle, especially when vehicular traffic speeds or volumes are high. Where feasible, warning signs should be placed along the roadway and moved periodically as work progresses.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities

title: Section 6N.01 Guidance 17 - Work Duration
text:
Section 6N.01 Guidance 17 - Work Duration
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities
Page: 842

To avoid high-volume conditions, consideration should be given to scheduling mobile operations work during off-peak hours.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities

title: Section 6N.01 Guidance 18 - Work Duration
text:
Section 6N.01 Guidance 18 - Work Duration
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities
Page: 842

If there are mobile operations on a high-speed travel lane of a multi-lane divided highway, arrow boards should be used.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities

title: Section 6N.01 Standard 19 - Work Duration
text:
Section 6N.01 Standard 19 - Work Duration
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities
Page: 842

Mobile operations shall have appropriate devices on the equipment (that is, high-intensity rotating, flashing, oscillating, or strobe lights, signs, or special lighting), or shall use a separate vehicle with appropriate warning devices. Although vehicle hazard warning lights are permitted to be used to supplement high-intensity rotating, flashing, oscillating, or strobe lights, they shall not be used instead of these devices.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities

title: Section 6N.01 Option 20 - Work Duration
text:
Section 6N.01 Option 20 - Work Duration
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities
Page: 842

For mobile operations that move at speeds of less than 3 mph, mobile signs or stationary signing that is periodically retrieved and repositioned in the advance warning area may be used.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities

title: Section 6N.01 Support 21 - Work Duration
text:
Section 6N.01 Support 21 - Work Duration
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities
Page: 842

A rolling roadblock is a method of TTC used to slow or stop traffic as a means of temporarily removing traffic from a roadway segment downstream of the road block. The rolling roadblock closes all lanes of traffic by using pacing vehicles to create a gap so that construction activities can be performed. Rolling roadblocks are used where long-term road closures using TTC devices are not needed. A rolling roadblock consists of one blocking/pacing vehicle per lane of traffic, a clearing vehicle, and an advance warning vehicle. The rolling roadblock is normally performed by law enforcement officers during off-peak hours.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities

title: Section 6N.02 Support 1 - Location of Work
text:
Section 6N.02 Support 1 - Location of Work
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities
Page: 842

Chapter 6C and Sections 6M.04 and 6N.04 contain additional information regarding the steps to follow when pedestrian or bicycle facilities are affected by the worksite.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities

title: Section 6N.02 Support 2 - Location of Work
text:
Section 6N.02 Support 2 - Location of Work
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities
Page: 842

The choice of TTC needed for a TTC zone depends upon where the work is located. As a general rule, the closer the work is to road users (including bicyclists and pedestrians), the greater the number of TTC devices that are needed. Procedures are described later in this Chapter for establishing TTC zones in the following locations: A. Outside the shoulder, B. On the shoulder with no encroachment, C. On the shoulder with minor encroachment, D. Within the median, and E. Within the traveled way.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities

title: Section 6N.02 Standard 3 - Location of Work
text:
Section 6N.02 Standard 3 - Location of Work
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities
Page: 842

When the work space is within the traveled way, except for short-duration and mobile operations, advance warning shall provide a general message that work is taking place and shall supply information about highway conditions. TTC devices shall clearly delineate the path roadway users are to follow through the TTC zone.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities

title: Section 6N.03 Support 1 - Modifications to Fulfill Special Needs
text:
Section 6N.03 Support 1 - Modifications to Fulfill Special Needs
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities
Page: 842

The typical applications in Chapter 6P illustrate commonly encountered situations in which TTC devices are employed.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities

title: Section 6N.03 Option 2 - Modifications to Fulfill Special Needs
text:
Section 6N.03 Option 2 - Modifications to Fulfill Special Needs
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities
Page: 843

Other devices may be added to supplement the devices provided in the typical applications, and device spacing may be adjusted to provide additional reaction time. When conditions are less complex than those depicted in the typical applications, fewer devices may be needed. MUTCD 11th Edition - Revision 1

metadata.chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities

title: Section 6N.03 Guidance 3 - Modifications to Fulfill Special Needs
text:
Section 6N.03 Guidance 3 - Modifications to Fulfill Special Needs
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities
Page: 843

When conditions are more complex, typical applications should be modified by giving particular attention to the provisions set forth in Chapter 6A and by incorporating appropriate devices and practices from the following list: A. Additional devices: 1. Signs 2. Arrow boards 3. More channelizing devices at closer spacing (see Section 6M.04 for information regarding detectable edging for pedestrians) 4. Temporary raised pavement markers 5. High-level warning devices 6. Portable changeable message signs 7. Temporary traffic control signals (including accessible pedestrian signals where not otherwise required) 8. Temporary traffic barriers 9. Crash cushions 10. Screens 11. Rumble strips 12. More delineation B. Upgrading of devices: 1. A full complement of standard pavement markings 2. Brighter and/or wider pavement markings 3. Larger and/or brighter signs 4. Channelizing devices with greater conspicuity 5. Temporary traffic barriers in place of channelizing devices C. Improved geometrics at detours or crossovers D. Increased distances: 1. Longer advance warning area 2. Longer tapers E. Lighting: 1. Temporary roadway lighting 2. Steady-burn lights used with channelizing devices 3. Flashing lights for isolated hazards 4. Illuminated signs 5. Floodlights F. Pedestrian routes and temporary facilities G. Bicycle diversions and temporary facilities

metadata.chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities

title: Section 6N.04 Support 1 - Work Affecting Pedestrian and Bicycle Facilities
text:
Section 6N.04 Support 1 - Work Affecting Pedestrian and Bicycle Facilities
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities
Page: 843

It is not uncommon, particularly in urban areas, that road work and the associated TTC will affect existing pedestrian or bicycle facilities. It is essential that the needs of all road users, including pedestrians with disabilities, are considered in TTC zones.

metadata.section_title: Work Affecting Pedestrian and Bicycle Facilities
metadata.chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities

title: Section 6N.04 Support 2 - Work Affecting Pedestrian and Bicycle Facilities
text:
Section 6N.04 Support 2 - Work Affecting Pedestrian and Bicycle Facilities
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities
Page: 843

In addition to specific provisions identified in Sections 6N.05 through 6N.13, there are a number of provisions that might be applicable for all of the types of activities identified in this Chapter.

metadata.section_title: Work Affecting Pedestrian and Bicycle Facilities
metadata.chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities

title: Section 6N.04 Guidance 3 - Work Affecting Pedestrian and Bicycle Facilities
text:
Section 6N.04 Guidance 3 - Work Affecting Pedestrian and Bicycle Facilities
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities
Page: 843

Where pedestrian or bicyclist usage is high, the typical applications should be modified by giving particular attention to the provisions set forth in Chapter 6C, this Chapter, Sections 6K.02 and 6M.04, and in other Sections of Part 6 related to accessibility and detectability provisions in TTC zones.

metadata.section_title: Work Affecting Pedestrian and Bicycle Facilities
metadata.chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities

title: Section 6N.04 Guidance 4 - Work Affecting Pedestrian and Bicycle Facilities
text:
Section 6N.04 Guidance 4 - Work Affecting Pedestrian and Bicycle Facilities
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities
Page: 843

Pedestrians should be separated from the worksite by appropriate devices that maintain the accessibility and detectability for pedestrians with disabilities.

metadata.section_title: Work Affecting Pedestrian and Bicycle Facilities
metadata.chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities

title: Section 6N.04 Guidance 5 - Work Affecting Pedestrian and Bicycle Facilities
text:
Section 6N.04 Guidance 5 - Work Affecting Pedestrian and Bicycle Facilities
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities
Page: 843

Bicyclists and pedestrians should not be exposed to unprotected excavations, open utility access, overhanging equipment, or other such conditions.

metadata.section_title: Work Affecting Pedestrian and Bicycle Facilities
metadata.chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities

title: Section 6N.04 Guidance 6 - Work Affecting Pedestrian and Bicycle Facilities
text:
Section 6N.04 Guidance 6 - Work Affecting Pedestrian and Bicycle Facilities
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities
Page: 844

Except for short-term and mobile operations, when a highway shoulder is occupied, a SHOULDER WORK (W21-5) sign should be placed in advance of the activity area. When work is performed on a paved shoulder 8 feet or more in width, channelizing devices should be placed on a taper having a length that conforms to the requirements of a shoulder taper. Signs should be placed such that they do not narrow any existing pedestrian passages to less than 48 inches. Rev. 1 December 2025

metadata.section_title: Work Affecting Pedestrian and Bicycle Facilities
metadata.chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities

title: Section 6N.04 Guidance 7 - Work Affecting Pedestrian and Bicycle Facilities
text:
Section 6N.04 Guidance 7 - Work Affecting Pedestrian and Bicycle Facilities
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities
Page: 844

Pedestrian detours should be avoided since pedestrians rarely observe them and the cost of providing accessibility and detectability might outweigh the cost of maintaining a continuous route. Whenever possible, work should be done in a manner that does not create a need to detour pedestrians from existing routes or crossings.

metadata.section_title: Work Affecting Pedestrian and Bicycle Facilities
metadata.chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities

title: Section 6N.04 Standard 8 - Work Affecting Pedestrian and Bicycle Facilities
text:
Section 6N.04 Standard 8 - Work Affecting Pedestrian and Bicycle Facilities
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities
Page: 844

Where pedestrian routes are closed, alternate pedestrian routes shall be provided.

metadata.section_title: Work Affecting Pedestrian and Bicycle Facilities
metadata.chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities

title: Section 6N.04 Standard 9 - Work Affecting Pedestrian and Bicycle Facilities
text:
Section 6N.04 Standard 9 - Work Affecting Pedestrian and Bicycle Facilities
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities
Page: 844

When existing pedestrian facilities are disrupted, closed, or relocated in a TTC zone, the temporary facilities shall be detectable and shall include accessibility features consistent with the features present in the existing pedestrian facility.

metadata.section_title: Work Affecting Pedestrian and Bicycle Facilities
metadata.chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities

title: Section 6N.04 Guidance 10 - Work Affecting Pedestrian and Bicycle Facilities
text:
Section 6N.04 Guidance 10 - Work Affecting Pedestrian and Bicycle Facilities
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities
Page: 844

The continuity of a bikeway should be maintained through the TTC zone if practical.

metadata.section_title: Work Affecting Pedestrian and Bicycle Facilities
metadata.chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities

title: Section 6N.04 Support 11 - Work Affecting Pedestrian and Bicycle Facilities
text:
Section 6N.04 Support 11 - Work Affecting Pedestrian and Bicycle Facilities
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities
Page: 844

The continuity of a bikeway through the TTC zone is particularly important where bicyclists have been traveling on a shoulder, bicycle lane, or shared-use path adjacent to a general-purpose lane (having a speed limit greater than or equal to 35 miles per hour) and there would be a significant safety concern if bicyclists were to share that general-purpose lane through the TTC zone.

metadata.section_title: Work Affecting Pedestrian and Bicycle Facilities
metadata.chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities

title: Section 6N.04 Support 12 - Work Affecting Pedestrian and Bicycle Facilities
text:
Section 6N.04 Support 12 - Work Affecting Pedestrian and Bicycle Facilities
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities
Page: 844

On roadways which are not bikeways but where bicyclists (when present) typically share lanes with motor vehicle traffic, the TTC plan and Typical Applications for general traffic will usually be adequate for bicyclists as well.

metadata.section_title: Work Affecting Pedestrian and Bicycle Facilities
metadata.chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities

title: Section 6N.04 Support 13 - Work Affecting Pedestrian and Bicycle Facilities
text:
Section 6N.04 Support 13 - Work Affecting Pedestrian and Bicycle Facilities
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities
Page: 844

In order to maintain room for bicycle lanes through the TTC zone on a multi-lane roadway, one or more travel lanes could be closed.

metadata.section_title: Work Affecting Pedestrian and Bicycle Facilities
metadata.chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities

title: Section 6N.04 Guidance 14 - Work Affecting Pedestrian and Bicycle Facilities
text:
Section 6N.04 Guidance 14 - Work Affecting Pedestrian and Bicycle Facilities
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities
Page: 844

If a bikeway detour is unavoidable, it should be as short and direct as practical.

metadata.section_title: Work Affecting Pedestrian and Bicycle Facilities
metadata.chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities

title: Section 6N.04 Guidance 15 - Work Affecting Pedestrian and Bicycle Facilities
text:
Section 6N.04 Guidance 15 - Work Affecting Pedestrian and Bicycle Facilities
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities
Page: 844

On-road bicyclists should not be directed onto a path or sidewalk intended for pedestrian use except where such a path or sidewalk is a shared-use path, or where no practical alternative is available (such as might be the case on a bridge in the course of a rehabilitation project).

metadata.section_title: Work Affecting Pedestrian and Bicycle Facilities
metadata.chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities

title: Section 6N.04 Guidance 16 - Work Affecting Pedestrian and Bicycle Facilities
text:
Section 6N.04 Guidance 16 - Work Affecting Pedestrian and Bicycle Facilities
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities
Page: 844

If a portion of a bikeway is to be closed due to construction activities and the detoured bikeway follows a complex path not in the original bikeway corridor, then a full detour plan should be developed and implemented. The TTC for the detour of the bikeway should include all necessary advance warning (W21 series) signs, detour (W4-9 series) signs, and any other TTC devices necessary to guide bicyclists along the detour route.

metadata.section_title: Work Affecting Pedestrian and Bicycle Facilities
metadata.chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities

title: Section 6N.04 Support 17 - Work Affecting Pedestrian and Bicycle Facilities
text:
Section 6N.04 Support 17 - Work Affecting Pedestrian and Bicycle Facilities
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities
Page: 844

Figures 6P-47 through 6P-51 provide examples and contain additional information for accommodating bicycles through or around typical TTC zones.

metadata.section_title: Work Affecting Pedestrian and Bicycle Facilities
metadata.chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities

title: Section 6N.04 Option 18 - Work Affecting Pedestrian and Bicycle Facilities
text:
Section 6N.04 Option 18 - Work Affecting Pedestrian and Bicycle Facilities
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities
Page: 844

If an on-street bikeway had a wide travel lane or lanes in which bicyclists traveled side by side with motor vehicles prior to construction, and construction activities reduce the lane width(s) to less than 14 feet through the TTC zone, then the BICYCLISTS ALLOWED USE OF FULL LANE (R9-20) sign may be used.

metadata.section_title: Work Affecting Pedestrian and Bicycle Facilities
metadata.chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities

title: Section 6N.04 Standard 19 - Work Affecting Pedestrian and Bicycle Facilities
text:
Section 6N.04 Standard 19 - Work Affecting Pedestrian and Bicycle Facilities
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities
Page: 844

The minimum TTC sign and plaque sizes for shared-use paths shall conform to those shown in Table 9A-1. The minimum TTC sign and plaque sizes for on-street bikeways shall conform to Chapters 6G, 6H, and 6I.

metadata.section_title: Work Affecting Pedestrian and Bicycle Facilities
metadata.chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities

title: Section 6N.05 Support 1 - Work Outside of the Shoulder
text:
Section 6N.05 Support 1 - Work Outside of the Shoulder
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities
Page: 845

When work is being performed beyond the shoulders, but within the right-of-way, little or no TTC might be needed. TTC generally is not needed where work is confined to an area 15 feet or more from the edge of the traveled way. However, TTC is appropriate where distracting situations exist, such as vehicles parked on the shoulder, vehicles accessing the worksite via the highway, and equipment traveling on or crossing the roadway to perform the work operations (for example, mowing). A typical application for work beyond the shoulder is shown in Figure 6P-1.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities

title: Section 6N.05 Guidance 2 - Work Outside of the Shoulder
text:
Section 6N.05 Guidance 2 - Work Outside of the Shoulder
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities
Page: 845

Where the situations described in Paragraph 1 of this Section exist, a single warning sign, such as ROAD WORK AHEAD (W20-1), should be used. If the equipment travels on the roadway, the equipment should be equipped with appropriate flags, high-intensity rotating, flashing, oscillating, or strobe lights, and/or a SLOW MOVING VEHICLE (W21-4) sign.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities

title: Section 6N.05 Guidance 3 - Work Outside of the Shoulder
text:
Section 6N.05 Guidance 3 - Work Outside of the Shoulder
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities
Page: 845

If work vehicles are on the shoulder, a SHOULDER WORK (W21-5) sign should be used.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities

title: Section 6N.05 Guidance 4 - Work Outside of the Shoulder
text:
Section 6N.05 Guidance 4 - Work Outside of the Shoulder
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities
Page: 845

A general warning sign like ROAD MACHINERY AHEAD (W21-3) should be used if workers and equipment must occasionally move onto the shoulder.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities

title: Section 6N.05 Option 5 - Work Outside of the Shoulder
text:
Section 6N.05 Option 5 - Work Outside of the Shoulder
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities
Page: 845

For mowing operations, the sign MOWING AHEAD (W21-8) may be used.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities

title: Section 6N.05 Option 6 - Work Outside of the Shoulder
text:
Section 6N.05 Option 6 - Work Outside of the Shoulder
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities
Page: 845

Where the activity is spread out over a distance of more than 2 miles, the SHOULDER WORK (W21-5) sign may be repeated every 1 mile.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities

title: Section 6N.05 Option 7 - Work Outside of the Shoulder
text:
Section 6N.05 Option 7 - Work Outside of the Shoulder
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities
Page: 845

A supplementary plaque with the message NEXT XX MILES (W7-3aP) may be used.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities

title: Section 6N.06 Support 1 - Work on the Shoulder with No Encroachment
text:
Section 6N.06 Support 1 - Work on the Shoulder with No Encroachment
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities
Page: 845

The provisions of this Section apply to short-term through long-term stationary operations.

metadata.section_title: Work on the Shoulder with No Encroachment
metadata.chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities

title: Section 6N.06 Standard 2 - Work on the Shoulder with No Encroachment
text:
Section 6N.06 Standard 2 - Work on the Shoulder with No Encroachment
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities
Page: 845

When paved shoulders having a width of 8 feet or more are closed, at least one advance warning sign shall be used. In addition, channelizing devices shall be used to close the shoulder in advance to delineate the beginning of the work space and direct motor vehicle traffic to remain within the traveled way.

metadata.section_title: Work on the Shoulder with No Encroachment
metadata.chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities

title: Section 6N.06 Guidance 3 - Work on the Shoulder with No Encroachment
text:
Section 6N.06 Guidance 3 - Work on the Shoulder with No Encroachment
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities
Page: 845

When paved shoulders having a width of 8 feet or more are closed on freeways and expressways, road users should be warned about potential disabled vehicles that cannot get off the traveled way. An initial general warning sign, such as ROAD WORK AHEAD (W20-1), should be used, followed by a RIGHT or LEFT SHOULDER CLOSED (W21-5a) sign. Where the downstream end of the shoulder closure extends beyond the distance that can be perceived by road users, a supplementary plaque bearing the message NEXT XX FEET (W16-4P) or MILES (W7-3aP) should be placed below the SHOULDER CLOSED (W21-5a) sign. On multi-lane, divided highways, signs advising of shoulder work or the condition of the shoulder should be placed only on the side of the affected shoulder.

metadata.section_title: Work on the Shoulder with No Encroachment
metadata.chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities

title: Section 6N.06 Guidance 4 - Work on the Shoulder with No Encroachment
text:
Section 6N.06 Guidance 4 - Work on the Shoulder with No Encroachment
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities
Page: 845

When an improved shoulder is closed on a high-speed roadway, it should be treated as a closure of a portion of the road system because road users expect to be able to use it in emergencies. Road users should be given ample advance warning that shoulders are closed for use as refuge areas throughout a specified length of the approaching TTC zone. The sign(s) should read SHOULDER CLOSED (W21-5a) with distances indicated. The work space on the shoulder should be closed off by a taper or channelizing devices with a length of ¹⁄3 L using the formulas in Tables 6B-3 and 6B-4.

When work takes up part of a lane, vehicular traffic volumes, vehicle mix (buses, trucks, cars, and bicycles), speed, and capacity should be analyzed to determine whether the affected lane should be closed. Unless the lane encroachment permits a remaining lane width of 10 feet, the lane should be closed.

Section 6N.09 Support 2 - Work within the Traveled Way of a Two-Lane Highway
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities
Page: 846

Detour signs are used to direct road users onto another roadway. At diversions, road users are directed onto a temporary roadway or alignment placed within or adjacent to the right-of-way. Typical applications for detouring or diverting road users on two-lane highways are shown in Figures 6P-7, 6P-8, and 6P-9. Figure 6P-7 illustrates the controls around an area where a section of roadway has been closed and a diversion has been constructed. Channelizing devices and pavement markings are used to indicate the transition to the temporary roadway.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities

Section 6N.09 Guidance 3 - Work within the Traveled Way of a Two-Lane Highway
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities
Page: 846

When a detour is long, Detour (M4-8, M4-9) signs should be installed to remind and reassure road users periodically that they are still successfully following the detour.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities

text:
Section 6N.09 Guidance 4 - Work within the Traveled Way of a Two-Lane Highway
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities
Page: 846

When an entire roadway is closed, as illustrated in Figure 6P-8, a detour should be provided and road users should be warned in advance of the closure, which in this example is a closure 10 miles from the intersection. If local road users are allowed to use the roadway up to the closure, the ROAD CLOSED AHEAD, LOCAL TRAFFIC ONLY (R11-3a) sign should be used. The portion of the road open to local road users should have adequate signing, marking, and delineation.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities

Detours should be signed so that road users will be able to traverse the entire detour route and back to the original roadway as shown in Figure 6P-9.

Pedestrian traffic needs separate attention. Chapter 6C contains information regarding pedestrian movements near TTC zones.

Where transit stops are affected or relocated because of work activity, both pedestrian and vehicular access to the affected or relocated transit stops shall be provided.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities

Section 6N.10 Guidance 6 - Work within the Traveled Way of an Urban Street

Chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities
Page: 847

If a designated bicycle route is closed because of the work being done, a signed alternate route should be provided. Bicyclists should not be directed onto the path used by pedestrians.

metadata.section_title: Work within the Traveled Way of an Urban Street
metadata.chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities

Page: 847

Worksites within the intersection should be protected against inadvertent pedestrian incursion by providing detectable channelizing devices.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities

text:
Section 6N.10 Support 8 - Work within the Traveled Way of an Urban Street
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities
Page: 847

Utility work takes place both within and outside the roadway to construct and maintain services such as power, gas, light, water, or telecommunications. Operations often involve intersections, since that is where many of the network junctions occur. The work force is usually small, only a few vehicles are involved, and the number and types of TTC devices placed in the TTC zone is usually minimal.

metadata.section_title: Work within the Traveled Way of an Urban Street
metadata.chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities

title: Section 6N.10 Guidance 9 - Work within the Traveled Way of an Urban Street
text:
Section 6N.10 Guidance 9 - Work within the Traveled Way of an Urban Street
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities
Page: 847

As discussed under short-duration projects, however, the reduced number of devices in utility TTC zones should be offset by the use of high-visibility devices, such as high-intensity rotating, flashing, oscillating, or strobe lights on work vehicles or high-level warning devices.

Figures 6P-6, 6P-10, 6P-15, 6P-18, 6P-21, 6P-22, 6P-23, 6P-26, and 6P-33 are examples of typical applications for utility operations. Other typical applications might apply as well.
