text:
Section 6N.11 Support 2 - Work within the Traveled Way of a Multi-Lane, Non-Access Controlled Highway
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities
Page: 847

Work on multi-lane (two or more lanes of moving motor vehicle traffic in one direction) highways is divided into right-lane closures, left-lane closures, interior-lane closures, multiple-lane closures, and closures on five-lane roadways.

metadata.section_title: Work within the Traveled Way of a Multi-Lane, Non-Access Controlled Highway
metadata.chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities

title: Section 6N.11 Standard 3 - Work within the Traveled Way of a Multi-Lane, Non-Access Controlled Highway
text:
Section 6N.11 Standard 3 - Work within the Traveled Way of a Multi-Lane, Non-Access Controlled Highway
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities
Page: 847

When a lane is closed on a multi-lane road for other than a mobile operation, a transition area containing a merging taper shall be used.

metadata.section_title: Work within the Traveled Way of a Multi-Lane, Non-Access Controlled Highway
metadata.chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities

title: Section 6N.11 Guidance 4 - Work within the Traveled Way of a Multi-Lane, Non-Access Controlled Highway
text:
Section 6N.11 Guidance 4 - Work within the Traveled Way of a Multi-Lane, Non-Access Controlled Highway
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities
Page: 847

When justified by an engineering study, temporary traffic barriers (see Section 6K.09) should be used to prevent incursions of errant vehicles into hazardous areas or work space.

metadata.section_title: Work within the Traveled Way of a Multi-Lane, Non-Access Controlled Highway
metadata.chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities

title: Section 6N.11 Support 5 - Work within the Traveled Way of a Multi-Lane, Non-Access Controlled Highway
text:
Section 6N.11 Support 5 - Work within the Traveled Way of a Multi-Lane, Non-Access Controlled Highway
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities
Page: 847

Figure 6P-34 illustrates a lane closure in which temporary traffic barriers are used.

metadata.section_title: Work within the Traveled Way of a Multi-Lane, Non-Access Controlled Highway
metadata.chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities

title: Section 6N.11 Option 6 - Work within the Traveled Way of a Multi-Lane, Non-Access Controlled Highway
text:
Section 6N.11 Option 6 - Work within the Traveled Way of a Multi-Lane, Non-Access Controlled Highway
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities
Page: 848

When the right-hand lane is closed, TTC similar to that shown in Figure 6P-33 may be used for undivided or divided four-lane roads.

metadata.section_title: Work within the Traveled Way of a Multi-Lane, Non-Access Controlled Highway
metadata.chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities

title: Section 6N.11 Guidance 7 - Work within the Traveled Way of a Multi-Lane, Non-Access Controlled Highway
text:
Section 6N.11 Guidance 7 - Work within the Traveled Way of a Multi-Lane, Non-Access Controlled Highway
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities
Page: 848

If morning and evening peak hour vehicular traffic volumes in the two directions are uneven and the greater volume is on the side where the work is being done in the right-hand lane, consideration should be given to closing the inside lane for opposing vehicular traffic and making the lane available to the side with heavier vehicular traffic, as shown in Figure 6P-31.

metadata.section_title: Work within the Traveled Way of a Multi-Lane, Non-Access Controlled Highway
metadata.chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities

title: Section 6N.11 Guidance 8 - Work within the Traveled Way of a Multi-Lane, Non-Access Controlled Highway
text:
Section 6N.11 Guidance 8 - Work within the Traveled Way of a Multi-Lane, Non-Access Controlled Highway
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities
Page: 848

If the larger vehicular traffic volume changes to the opposite direction at a different time of the day, the TTC should be changed to allow two lanes for opposing vehicular traffic by moving the devices from the opposing lane to the center line. When it is necessary to create a temporary center line that is not consistent with the pavement markings, channelizing devices should be used and closely spaced.

metadata.section_title: Work within the Traveled Way of a Multi-Lane, Non-Access Controlled Highway
metadata.chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities

title: Section 6N.11 Option 9 - Work within the Traveled Way of a Multi-Lane, Non-Access Controlled Highway
text:
Section 6N.11 Option 9 - Work within the Traveled Way of a Multi-Lane, Non-Access Controlled Highway
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities
Page: 848

When closing a left-hand lane on a multi-lane undivided road, as vehicular traffic flow permits, the two interior lanes may be closed, as shown in Figure 6P-30, to provide drivers and workers additional lateral clearance and to provide access to the work space.

metadata.section_title: Work within the Traveled Way of a Multi-Lane, Non-Access Controlled Highway
metadata.chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities

title: Section 6N.11 Standard 10 - Work within the Traveled Way of a Multi-Lane, Non-Access Controlled Highway
text:
Section 6N.11 Standard 10 - Work within the Traveled Way of a Multi-Lane, Non-Access Controlled Highway
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities
Page: 848

When only the left-hand lane is closed on undivided roads, channelizing devices shall be placed along the center line as well as along the adjacent lane.

metadata.section_title: Work within the Traveled Way of a Multi-Lane, Non-Access Controlled Highway
metadata.chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities

title: Section 6N.11 Guidance 11 - Work within the Traveled Way of a Multi-Lane, Non-Access Controlled Highway
text:
Section 6N.11 Guidance 11 - Work within the Traveled Way of a Multi-Lane, Non-Access Controlled Highway
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities
Page: 848

When an interior lane is closed, an adjacent lane should also be considered for closure to provide additional space for vehicles and materials and to facilitate the movement of equipment within the work space.

metadata.section_title: Work within the Traveled Way of a Multi-Lane, Non-Access Controlled Highway
metadata.chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities

title: Section 6N.11 Guidance 12 - Work within the Traveled Way of a Multi-Lane, Non-Access Controlled Highway
text:
Section 6N.11 Guidance 12 - Work within the Traveled Way of a Multi-Lane, Non-Access Controlled Highway
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities
Page: 848

When multiple lanes in one direction are closed, a capacity analysis should be made to determine the number of lanes needed to accommodate motor vehicle traffic needs. Vehicular traffic should be moved over one lane at a time. As shown in Figure 6P-37, the tapers should be separated by a distance of 2L, with L being determined by the formulas in Tables 6B-3 and 6B-4.

metadata.section_title: Work within the Traveled Way of a Multi-Lane, Non-Access Controlled Highway
metadata.chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities

title: Section 6N.11 Option 13 - Work within the Traveled Way of a Multi-Lane, Non-Access Controlled Highway
text:
Section 6N.11 Option 13 - Work within the Traveled Way of a Multi-Lane, Non-Access Controlled Highway
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities
Page: 848

If operating speeds are 40 mph or less and the space approaching the work area does not permit moving traffic over one lane at a time, a single continuous taper may be used.

metadata.section_title: Work within the Traveled Way of a Multi-Lane, Non-Access Controlled Highway
metadata.chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities

title: Section 6N.11 Standard 14 - Work within the Traveled Way of a Multi-Lane, Non-Access Controlled Highway
text:
Section 6N.11 Standard 14 - Work within the Traveled Way of a Multi-Lane, Non-Access Controlled Highway
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities
Page: 848

When a directional roadway is closed, inapplicable WRONG WAY signs and markings, and other existing traffic control devices at intersections within the temporary two-lane, two-way operations section shall be covered, removed, or obliterated.

metadata.section_title: Work within the Traveled Way of a Multi-Lane, Non-Access Controlled Highway
metadata.chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities

title: Section 6N.11 Option 15 - Work within the Traveled Way of a Multi-Lane, Non-Access Controlled Highway
text:
Section 6N.11 Option 15 - Work within the Traveled Way of a Multi-Lane, Non-Access Controlled Highway
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities
Page: 848

When half the road is closed on an undivided highway, both directions of vehicular traffic may be accommodated as shown in Figure 6P-32. When both interior lanes are closed, temporary traffic controls may be used as provided in Figure 6P-30. Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control

The typical applications for intersections are classified according to the location of the work space with respect to the intersection area (as defined by the extension of the curb or edge lines). The three classifications are near side, far side, and in-the-intersection. Work spaces often extend into more than one portion of the intersection. For example, work in one quadrant often creates a near-side work space on one street and a far-side work space on the cross street. In such instances, an appropriate TTC plan is obtained by combining features shown in two or more of the intersection and pedestrian typical applications.

Such conflicts frequently occur at more complex signalized intersections having such features as traffic signal heads over particular lanes, lanes allocated to specific movements, multiple signal phases, signal detectors for actuated control, and accessible pedestrian signals and detectors.

title: Section 6N.13 Support 1 - Work within the Traveled Way of a Freeway or Expressway
text:
Section 6N.13 Support 1 - Work within the Traveled Way of a Freeway or Expressway
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities
Page: 850

Special conditions encountered where vehicular traffic must be moved through or around TTC zones on high- speed, high-volume roadways can pose challenges to the TTC. Although the general principles outlined in other Sections of this Manual are applicable to all types of highways, high-speed, access-controlled highways need special planning and attention in order to accommodate vehicular traffic while also protecting road users and workers. The traffic volumes, vehicle mix (buses, trucks, cars, and bicycles, if permitted), and speed of vehicles on these facilities require that careful TTC procedures be implemented, for example, to induce critical merging maneuvers well in advance of work spaces and in a manner that creates minimum turbulence and delay in the vehicular traffic stream.

metadata.section_title: Work within the Traveled Way of a Freeway or Expressway
metadata.chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities

title: Section 6N.13 Support 2 - Work within the Traveled Way of a Freeway or Expressway
text:
Section 6N.13 Support 2 - Work within the Traveled Way of a Freeway or Expressway
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities
Page: 850

When the roadway capacity is reduced as a result of lane closures, the demand might exceed the available capacity and result in either a lengthy stopped or slow moving queue of vehicles that might extend past the normal signs used in the typical advance warning area.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities

text:
Section 6N.13 Guidance 3 - Work within the Traveled Way of a Freeway or Expressway
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities
Page: 850

An assessment of the expected queue length should be a part of the TTC plan design process and adjustments to the sign spacing and number of signs as well as the possibility of using more conspicuous devices should be considered to increase the distance and conspicuity of the advance warning area.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities

Page: 850

One strategy often employed to mitigate the extended queue issue is to work during off peak hours or at night. When the work is limited to night hours, increased use of warning lights, illumination of work spaces, and intelligent advance warning systems might be necessary.

Temporary traffic controls for short-duration and mobile operations on freeways are shown in Figure 6P-35. A typical application for shifting vehicular traffic lanes around a work space is shown in Figure 6P-36. TTC for multiple and interior lane closures on a freeway is shown in Figures 6P-37 and 6P-38.

text:
Section 6N.14 Support 1 - Two-Lane, Two-Way Traffic on One Roadway of a Normally-Divided Highway
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities
Page: 850

Two-lane, two-way operation on one roadway of a normally-divided highway is a typical procedure that requires special consideration in the planning, design, and work phases, because unique operational problems (for example, increasing the risk of head-on crashes) can arise with the two-lane, two-way operation.

metadata.section_title: Two-Lane, Two-Way Traffic on One Roadway of a Normally-Divided Highway
metadata.chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities

title: Section 6N.14 Standard 2 - Two-Lane, Two-Way Traffic on One Roadway of a Normally-Divided Highway
text:
Section 6N.14 Standard 2 - Two-Lane, Two-Way Traffic on One Roadway of a Normally-Divided Highway
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities
Page: 850

When two-lane, two-way traffic control must be maintained on one roadway of a normally-divided highway, opposing vehicular traffic shall be separated with either temporary traffic barriers (concrete safety-shape or approved alternate), channelizing devices, Narrow Two-Way Traffic (W6-4) signs on flexible supports (see Section 6H.17), or a temporary raised island throughout the length of the two-way operation. The use of markings and complementary signing, by themselves, shall not be used.

Page: 850

title: Section 6N.15 Guidance 1 - Crossovers
text:
Section 6N.15 Guidance 1 - Crossovers
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities
Page: 851

The following are considered good guiding principles for the design of crossovers: A. Tapers for lane drops should be separated from the crossovers, as shown in Figure 6P-39. B. Crossovers should be designed for speeds no lower than 10 mph below the posted speed, the off-peak 85th-percentile speed prior to the work starting, or the anticipated operating speed of the roadway, unless unusual site conditions require that a lower design speed be used. C. A good array of channelizing devices, delineators, and full-length, properly placed pavement markings should be used to provide drivers with a clearly defined travel path. D. The design of the crossover should accommodate all vehicular traffic, including trucks and buses.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities

title: Section 6N.15 Support 2 - Crossovers
text:
Section 6N.15 Support 2 - Crossovers
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities
Page: 851

Temporary traffic barriers and the excessive use of TTC devices cannot compensate for poor geometric and roadway cross-section design of crossovers.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities

title: Section 6N.16 Guidance 1 - Interchanges
text:
Section 6N.16 Guidance 1 - Interchanges
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities
Page: 851

Access to interchange ramps on limited-access highways should be maintained even if the work space is in the lane adjacent to the ramps. Access to exit ramps should be clearly marked and delineated with channelizing devices. For long-term projects, conflicting pavement markings should be removed and new ones placed. Early coordination with officials having jurisdiction over the affected cross streets and providing emergency services should occur before ramp closings.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities

text:
Section 6N.16 Option 2 - Interchanges
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities
Page: 851

If access is not possible, ramps may be closed by using signs and Type 3 Barricades. As the work space changes, the access area may be changed, as shown in Figure 6P-42. A TTC zone in the exit ramp may be handled as shown in Figure 6P-43.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities

title: Section 6N.16 Option 3 - Interchanges
text:
Section 6N.16 Option 3 - Interchanges
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities
Page: 851

When a work space interferes with an entrance ramp, a lane may need to be closed on the freeway (see Figure 6P-44). A TTC zone in the entrance ramp may require shifting ramp vehicular traffic (see Figure 6P-44).

metadata.chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities

title: Section 6N.17 Standard 1 - Work in the Vicinity of a Grade Crossing
text:
Section 6N.17 Standard 1 - Work in the Vicinity of a Grade Crossing
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities
Page: 851

When grade crossings exist either within or in the vicinity of a TTC zone, lane restrictions, flagging, or other operations shall not create conditions where vehicles can be queued across the tracks. If the queuing of vehicles across the tracks cannot be avoided, a uniformed law enforcement officer or flagger shall be provided at the crossing to prevent vehicles from stopping on the tracks, even if automatic warning devices are in place.

title: Section 6N.19 Support 1 - Late Merge
text:
Section 6N.19 Support 1 - Late Merge
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities
Page: 852

The Late Merge is designed to use all available lanes until the merge point is reached at the lane closure taper rather than merging as soon as possible into the open lane. The Late Merge addresses many of the challenges that are associated with traffic operations in advance of lane closures at TTC zones such as queue length, capacity, and driver satisfaction.

Section 6N.19 Option 2 - Late Merge
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities
Page: 852

metadata.chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities

text:
Section 6N.19 Guidance 3 - Late Merge
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6N. Types Of Temporary Traffic Control Zone Activities
Page: 852

Static Late Merge signing (see Figure 6N-1) should consist of the STAY IN LANE TO MERGE POINT (R4-9a) sign (see Section 6G.07) and the MERGE HERE TAKE TURNS (W9-2a) sign (see Section 6H.08).

Section 6N.19 Option 4 - Late Merge
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control

title: Section 6O.01 Support 1 - General
text:
Section 6O.01 Support 1 - General
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6O. Control Of Traffic Through Traffic Incident Management Areas
Page: 854

The National Incident Management System (NIMS) requires the use of the Incident Command System (ICS) at traffic incident management scenes.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 6O. Control Of Traffic Through Traffic Incident Management Areas

title: Section 6O.01 Support 2 - General
text:
Section 6O.01 Support 2 - General
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6O. Control Of Traffic Through Traffic Incident Management Areas
Page: 854

A traffic incident is an emergency road user occurrence, a natural disaster, or other unplanned event that affects or impedes the normal flow of traffic.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 6O. Control Of Traffic Through Traffic Incident Management Areas

title: Section 6O.01 Support 3 - General
text:
Section 6O.01 Support 3 - General
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6O. Control Of Traffic Through Traffic Incident Management Areas
Page: 854

A traffic incident management area is an area of a highway where temporary traffic controls are installed, as authorized by a public authority or the official having jurisdiction of the roadway, in response to a road user incident, natural disaster, hazardous material spill, or other unplanned incident. It is a type of TTC zone and extends from the first warning device (such as a sign, light, or cone) to the last TTC device or to a point where vehicles return to the original lane alignment and are clear of the incident.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 6O. Control Of Traffic Through Traffic Incident Management Areas

title: Section 6O.01 Support 4 - General
text:
Section 6O.01 Support 4 - General
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6O. Control Of Traffic Through Traffic Incident Management Areas
Page: 854

Traffic incidents can be divided into three general classes of duration, each of which has unique traffic control characteristics and needs. These classes are: A. Major-expected duration of more than 2 hours, B. Intermediate-expected duration of 30 minutes to 2 hours, and C. Minor-expected duration under 30 minutes.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 6O. Control Of Traffic Through Traffic Incident Management Areas

title: Section 6O.01 Support 5 - General
text:
Section 6O.01 Support 5 - General
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6O. Control Of Traffic Through Traffic Incident Management Areas
Page: 854

The primary functions of TTC at a traffic incident management area are to inform road users of the incident and to provide guidance information on the path to follow through the incident area. Alerting road users and establishing a well-defined path to guide road users through the incident area will serve to protect the incident responders and those involved in working at the incident scene and will aid in moving road users expeditiously past or around the traffic incident, will reduce the likelihood of secondary traffic crashes, and will preclude unnecessary use of the surrounding local road system. Examples include a stalled vehicle blocking a lane, a traffic crash blocking the traveled way, a hazardous material spill along a highway, and natural disasters such as floods and severe storm damage.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 6O. Control Of Traffic Through Traffic Incident Management Areas

title: Section 6O.01 Guidance 6 - General
text:
Section 6O.01 Guidance 6 - General
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6O. Control Of Traffic Through Traffic Incident Management Areas
Page: 854

In order to reduce response time for traffic incidents, highway agencies, appropriate public safety agencies (law enforcement, fire and rescue, emergency communications, emergency medical, and other emergency management), and private sector responders (towing and recovery and hazardous materials contractors) should mutually plan for occurrences of traffic incidents along the major and heavily traveled highway and street system.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 6O. Control Of Traffic Through Traffic Incident Management Areas

title: Section 6O.01 Guidance 7 - General
text:
Section 6O.01 Guidance 7 - General
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6O. Control Of Traffic Through Traffic Incident Management Areas
Page: 854

On-scene responder organizations should train their personnel in TTC practices for accomplishing their tasks in and near traffic and in the requirements for traffic incident management contained in this Manual. On-scene responders should take measures to move the incident off the traveled roadway or to provide for appropriate warning. All on-scene responders and news media personnel should constantly be aware of their visibility to oncoming traffic and wear high-visibility apparel. Planning and training should include incorporation of estimated time durations to clear the event as part of their initial incident estimate. When events are deemed as probable Major Traffic Incidents that could generate prolonged lane or road closures, notification of all affected agencies should be initiated as part of the initial incident report that is provided to the emergency communications center who would then be responsible for making notifications to appropriate state, regional, and local agencies and resources for the purpose of ramping up and responding as quickly as possible thus facilitating a more rapid transition from emergency TTC to an MUTCD-compliant TTC zone when warranted.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 6O. Control Of Traffic Through Traffic Incident Management Areas

title: Section 6O.01 Guidance 8 - General
text:
Section 6O.01 Guidance 8 - General
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6O. Control Of Traffic Through Traffic Incident Management Areas
Page: 854

Emergency vehicles arriving at an incident should be positioned in a manner that attempts to protect both the responders performing their duties and road users traveling through the incident scene, while minimizing, to the extent practical, disruption of the adjacent traffic flow. Emergency vehicle positions should optimize traffic flow through the incident scene. All emergency vehicles that subsequently arrive should be positioned in a manner that does not interfere with the established temporary traffic flow.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 6O. Control Of Traffic Through Traffic Incident Management Areas

title: Section 6O.01 Guidance 9 - General
text:
Section 6O.01 Guidance 9 - General
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6O. Control Of Traffic Through Traffic Incident Management Areas
Page: 854

Responders arriving at a traffic incident should estimate the magnitude of the traffic incident, the expected time duration of the traffic incident, and the expected vehicle queue length, and then should set up the appropriate temporary traffic controls for these estimates.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 6O. Control Of Traffic Through Traffic Incident Management Areas

title: Section 6O.01 Option 10 - General
text:
Section 6O.01 Option 10 - General
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6O. Control Of Traffic Through Traffic Incident Management Areas
Page: 854

Warning and guide signs used for TTC traffic incident management situations may have a black legend and border on a fluorescent pink background (see Figure 6O-1).

metadata.chapter: Chapter 6O. Control Of Traffic Through Traffic Incident Management Areas

title: Section 6O.01 Support 11 - General
text:
Section 6O.01 Support 11 - General
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6O. Control Of Traffic Through Traffic Incident Management Areas
Page: 855

While some traffic incidents might be anticipated and planned for, emergencies and disasters might pose more severe and unpredictable problems. The ability to quickly install proper temporary traffic controls might greatly reduce the effects of an incident, such as secondary crashes or excessive traffic delays. An essential part of fire, rescue, spill clean-up, highway agency, and enforcement activities is the proper control of road users through the MUTCD 11th Edition - Revision 1 Figure 6O-1. Examples of Traffic Incident Management Area Signs traffic incident management area in order to protect responders, victims, and other personnel at the site. These operations might need corroborating legislative authority for the implementation and enforcement of appropriate road user regulations, parking controls, and speed zoning. It is desirable for these statutes to provide sufficient flexibility in the authority for, and implementation of, TTC to respond to the needs of changing conditions found in traffic incident management areas.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 6O. Control Of Traffic Through Traffic Incident Management Areas

title: Section 6O.01 Option 12 - General
text:
Section 6O.01 Option 12 - General
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6O. Control Of Traffic Through Traffic Incident Management Areas
Page: 855

For traffic incidents, particularly those of an emergency nature, TTC devices on hand may be used for the initial response as long as they do not themselves create unnecessary additional hazards.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 6O. Control Of Traffic Through Traffic Incident Management Areas

title: Section 6O.01 Support 13 - General
text:
Section 6O.01 Support 13 - General
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6O. Control Of Traffic Through Traffic Incident Management Areas
Page: 855

The establishment, maintenance, and prompt removal of lane diversions can be effectively managed by interagency planning that includes representatives of highway and public safety agencies.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 6O. Control Of Traffic Through Traffic Incident Management Areas

title: Section 6O.01 Guidance 14 - General
text:
Section 6O.01 Guidance 14 - General
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6O. Control Of Traffic Through Traffic Incident Management Areas
Page: 855

All traffic control devices needed to set up the TTC at a traffic incident should be available so that they can be readily deployed for all major and intermediate traffic incidents. The TTC should include the proper traffic diversions, tapered lane closures, and upstream warning devices to alert traffic approaching the queue and to encourage early diversion to an appropriate alternative route. Rev. 1

metadata.chapter: Chapter 6O. Control Of Traffic Through Traffic Incident Management Areas

title: Section 6O.01 Guidance 15 - General
text:
Section 6O.01 Guidance 15 - General
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6O. Control Of Traffic Through Traffic Incident Management Areas
Page: 855

Attention should be paid to the upstream end of the traffic queue such that warning is given to road users approaching the back of the queue.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 6O. Control Of Traffic Through Traffic Incident Management Areas

title: Section 6O.01 Guidance 16 - General
text:
Section 6O.01 Guidance 16 - General
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6O. Control Of Traffic Through Traffic Incident Management Areas
Page: 855

If manual traffic control is needed, it should be provided by qualified flaggers or uniformed law enforcement officers.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 6O. Control Of Traffic Through Traffic Incident Management Areas

title: Section 6O.01 Option 17 - General
text:
Section 6O.01 Option 17 - General
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6O. Control Of Traffic Through Traffic Incident Management Areas
Page: 855

If flaggers are used to provide traffic control for an incident management situation, the flaggers may use appropriate traffic control devices that are readily available or that can be brought to the traffic incident scene on short notice.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 6O. Control Of Traffic Through Traffic Incident Management Areas

title: Section 6O.01 Guidance 18 - General
text:
Section 6O.01 Guidance 18 - General
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6O. Control Of Traffic Through Traffic Incident Management Areas
Page: 855

When light sticks or flares are used to establish the initial traffic control at incident scenes, channelizing devices (see Section 6K.01) should be installed as soon thereafter as practical.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 6O. Control Of Traffic Through Traffic Incident Management Areas

title: Section 6O.01 Option 19 - General
text:
Section 6O.01 Option 19 - General
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6O. Control Of Traffic Through Traffic Incident Management Areas
Page: 855

The light sticks or flares may remain in place if they are being used to supplement the channelizing devices.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 6O. Control Of Traffic Through Traffic Incident Management Areas

title: Section 6O.01 Guidance 20 - General
text:
Section 6O.01 Guidance 20 - General
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6O. Control Of Traffic Through Traffic Incident Management Areas
Page: 855

The light sticks, flares, and channelizing devices should be removed after the incident is terminated.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 6O. Control Of Traffic Through Traffic Incident Management Areas

title: Section 6O.02 Support 1 - Major Traffic Incidents
text:
Section 6O.02 Support 1 - Major Traffic Incidents
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6O. Control Of Traffic Through Traffic Incident Management Areas
Page: 855

Major traffic incidents are typically traffic incidents involving hazardous materials, fatal traffic crashes involving numerous vehicles, and other natural or man-made disasters. These traffic incidents typically involve closing all or part of a roadway facility for a period exceeding 2 hours.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 6O. Control Of Traffic Through Traffic Incident Management Areas

title: Section 6O.02 Guidance 2 - Major Traffic Incidents
text:
Section 6O.02 Guidance 2 - Major Traffic Incidents
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6O. Control Of Traffic Through Traffic Incident Management Areas
Page: 856

If the traffic incident is anticipated to last more than 24 hours, applicable procedures and devices set forth in other Chapters of Part 6 should be used. December 2025

metadata.chapter: Chapter 6O. Control Of Traffic Through Traffic Incident Management Areas

title: Section 6O.02 Support 3 - Major Traffic Incidents
text:
Section 6O.02 Support 3 - Major Traffic Incidents
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6O. Control Of Traffic Through Traffic Incident Management Areas
Page: 856

A road closure can be caused by a traffic incident such as a road user crash that blocks the traveled way. Road users are usually diverted through lane shifts or detoured around the traffic incident and back to the original roadway. A combination of traffic engineering and enforcement preparations is needed to determine the detour route, and to install, maintain, or operate, and then to remove the necessary traffic control devices when the detour is terminated. Large trucks are a significant concern in such a detour, especially when detouring them from a controlled-access roadway onto local or arterial streets.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 6O. Control Of Traffic Through Traffic Incident Management Areas

title: Section 6O.02 Support 4 - Major Traffic Incidents
text:
Section 6O.02 Support 4 - Major Traffic Incidents
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6O. Control Of Traffic Through Traffic Incident Management Areas
Page: 856

During traffic incidents, large trucks might need to follow a route separate from that of automobiles because of bridge, weight, clearance, or geometric restrictions. Also, vehicles carrying hazardous material might need to follow a different route from other vehicles.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 6O. Control Of Traffic Through Traffic Incident Management Areas

title: Section 6O.02 Support 5 - Major Traffic Incidents
text:
Section 6O.02 Support 5 - Major Traffic Incidents
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6O. Control Of Traffic Through Traffic Incident Management Areas
Page: 856

Some traffic incidents such as hazardous material spills might require closure of an entire highway. Through road users must have adequate guidance around the traffic incident. Maintaining good public relations is desirable. The cooperation of the news media in publicizing the existence of, and reasons for, traffic incident management areas and their TTC can be of great assistance in keeping road users and the general public well informed.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 6O. Control Of Traffic Through Traffic Incident Management Areas

title: Section 6O.03 Support 1 - Intermediate Traffic Incidents
text:
Section 6O.03 Support 1 - Intermediate Traffic Incidents
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6O. Control Of Traffic Through Traffic Incident Management Areas
Page: 856

Intermediate traffic incidents typically affect travel lanes for a time period of 30 minutes to 2 hours, and usually require traffic control on the scene to divert road users past the blockage. Full roadway closures might be needed for short periods during traffic incident clearance to allow traffic incident responders to accomplish their tasks.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 6O. Control Of Traffic Through Traffic Incident Management Areas

title: Section 6O.04 Support 1 - Minor Traffic Incidents
text:
Section 6O.04 Support 1 - Minor Traffic Incidents
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6O. Control Of Traffic Through Traffic Incident Management Areas
Page: 856

Minor traffic incidents are typically disabled vehicles and minor crashes that result in lane closures of less than 30 minutes. On-scene responders are typically law enforcement and towing companies, and occasionally highway agency service patrol vehicles.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 6O. Control Of Traffic Through Traffic Incident Management Areas

title: Section 6O.04 Support 2 - Minor Traffic Incidents
text:
Section 6O.04 Support 2 - Minor Traffic Incidents
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6O. Control Of Traffic Through Traffic Incident Management Areas
Page: 856

Diversion of traffic into other lanes is often not needed or is needed only briefly. It is not generally possible or practical to set up a lane closure with traffic control devices for a minor traffic incident. Traffic control is the responsibility of on-scene responders.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 6O. Control Of Traffic Through Traffic Incident Management Areas

title: Section 6O.04 Guidance 3 - Minor Traffic Incidents
text:
Section 6O.04 Guidance 3 - Minor Traffic Incidents
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6O. Control Of Traffic Through Traffic Incident Management Areas
Page: 856

When a minor traffic incident blocks a travel lane, the vehicles involved in the incident should be moved from the blocked lane to the shoulder as quickly as possible.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 6O. Control Of Traffic Through Traffic Incident Management Areas

title: Section 6O.05 Support 1 - Use of Emergency-Vehicle Lighting
text:
Section 6O.05 Support 1 - Use of Emergency-Vehicle Lighting
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6O. Control Of Traffic Through Traffic Incident Management Areas
Page: 856

The use of emergency-vehicle lighting (such as high-intensity rotating, flashing, oscillating, or strobe lights) is essential, especially in the initial stages of a traffic incident, for the safety of emergency responders and persons involved in the traffic incident, as well as road users approaching the traffic incident. Emergency-vehicle lighting, however, provides warning only and provides no effective traffic control. The use of too many lights at an incident scene can be distracting and can create confusion for approaching road users, especially at night. Road users approaching the traffic incident from the opposite direction on a divided facility are often distracted by emergency- vehicle lighting and slow their vehicles to look at the traffic incident posing a hazard to themselves and others traveling in their direction.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 6O. Control Of Traffic Through Traffic Incident Management Areas

title: Section 6O.05 Support 2 - Use of Emergency-Vehicle Lighting
text:
Section 6O.05 Support 2 - Use of Emergency-Vehicle Lighting
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6O. Control Of Traffic Through Traffic Incident Management Areas
Page: 856

The use of emergency-vehicle lighting can be reduced if good traffic control has been established at a traffic incident scene. This is especially true for major traffic incidents that might involve a number of emergency vehicles. If good traffic control is established through placement of advance warning signs and traffic control devices to divert or detour traffic, then public safety agencies can perform their tasks on scene with minimal emergency-vehicle lighting.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 6O. Control Of Traffic Through Traffic Incident Management Areas

title: Section 6O.05 Guidance 3 - Use of Emergency-Vehicle Lighting
text:
Section 6O.05 Guidance 3 - Use of Emergency-Vehicle Lighting
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6O. Control Of Traffic Through Traffic Incident Management Areas
Page: 856

Public safety agencies should examine their policies on the use of emergency-vehicle lighting, especially after a traffic incident scene is secured, with the intent of reducing the use of this lighting as much as possible while not endangering those at the scene. Special consideration should be given to reducing or extinguishing forward facing emergency-vehicle lighting, especially on divided roadways, to reduce distractions to oncoming road users.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 6O. Control Of Traffic Through Traffic Incident Management Areas

title: Section 6O.05 Guidance 4 - Use of Emergency-Vehicle Lighting
text:
Section 6O.05 Guidance 4 - Use of Emergency-Vehicle Lighting
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6O. Control Of Traffic Through Traffic Incident Management Areas
Page: 857

Because the glare from floodlights or vehicle headlights can impair the nighttime vision of approaching road users, any floodlights or vehicle headlights that are not needed for illumination, or to provide notice to other road users of an incident response vehicle being in an unexpected location, should be turned off at night.

metadata.chapter: Chapter 6O. Control Of Traffic Through Traffic Incident Management Areas

title: Section 6P.01 Support 1 - Typical Applications
text:
Section 6P.01 Support 1 - Typical Applications
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6P. Typical Applications
Page: 857

Chapter 6N contains discussions of typical TTC activities. Section 6A.02 contains discussions on development of TTC plans for the various activities. This Chapter presents typical applications for a variety of situations commonly encountered. While not every situation is addressed, the information illustrated can generally be adapted to a broad range of conditions. In many instances, an appropriate TTC plan is achieved by combining features from various typical applications. For example, work at an intersection might present a near-side TTC zone for one street and a far-side TTC zone for the other street. These treatments are found in two different typical applications, while a third typical application shows how to handle pedestrian crosswalk closures.

title: Section 6P.01 Support 2 - Typical Applications
text:
Section 6P.01 Support 2 - Typical Applications
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6P. Typical Applications
Page: 857

In general, the procedures illustrated represent minimum solutions for the situations depicted. Except for the notes (which are clearly classified using headings as being Standard, Guidance, Option, or Support), the information presented in the typical applications can generally be regarded as Guidance.

title: Section 6P.01 Option 3 - Typical Applications
text:
Section 6P.01 Option 3 - Typical Applications
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6P. Typical Applications
Page: 857

TTC plans may deviate from the typical applications described in this Chapter to allow for conditions and requirements of a particular site or jurisdiction.

title: Section 6P.01 Option 4 - Typical Applications
text:
Section 6P.01 Option 4 - Typical Applications
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6P. Typical Applications
Page: 857

Other devices may be added to supplement the devices and device spacing may be adjusted to provide additional reaction time or delineation. Fewer devices may be used based on field conditions.

title: Section 6P.01 Support 5 - Typical Applications
text:
Section 6P.01 Support 5 - Typical Applications
Part: Part 6 Temporary Traffic Control
Chapter: Chapter 6P. Typical Applications
Page: 857

Figures and tables found throughout Part 6 provide information for the development of TTC plans.

title: Section 7A.02 Guidance 1 - School Route Plans and School Crossings
text:
Section 7A.02 Guidance 1 - School Route Plans and School Crossings
Part: Part 7 Traffic Control For School Areas
Chapter: Chapter 7A. General
Page: 969

A school route plan for each school serving elementary to high school students should be prepared in order to develop uniformity in the use of school area traffic controls and to serve as the basis for a school traffic control plan for each school.

metadata.section_title: School Route Plans and School Crossings
metadata.part: Part 7 Traffic Control For School Areas

title: Section 7A.02 Guidance 2 - School Route Plans and School Crossings
text:
Section 7A.02 Guidance 2 - School Route Plans and School Crossings
Part: Part 7 Traffic Control For School Areas
Chapter: Chapter 7A. General
Page: 970

The school route plan, developed in a systematic manner by the school, law enforcement, and traffic officials responsible for school pedestrian safety, should consist of a map (see Figure 7A-1) showing streets, the school, existing traffic controls, established school walk routes, and established school crossings. Figure 7A-1. Example of School Route Plan Map

metadata.section_title: School Route Plans and School Crossings
metadata.part: Part 7 Traffic Control For School Areas

title: Section 7A.02 Guidance 3 - School Route Plans and School Crossings
text:
Section 7A.02 Guidance 3 - School Route Plans and School Crossings
Part: Part 7 Traffic Control For School Areas
Chapter: Chapter 7A. General
Page: 970

Bicycle use as a mode of transportation, as applicable, should also be considered if students biking to and from school are not allowed to use the sidewalks along the pedestrian route.

metadata.section_title: School Route Plans and School Crossings
metadata.part: Part 7 Traffic Control For School Areas

title: Section 7A.02 Guidance 4 - School Route Plans and School Crossings
text:
Section 7A.02 Guidance 4 - School Route Plans and School Crossings
Part: Part 7 Traffic Control For School Areas
Chapter: Chapter 7A. General
Page: 970

The type(s) of school area traffic control devices used, either warning or regulatory, should be related to the volume and speed of vehicular traffic, street width, and the number and age of the students using the crossing.

metadata.section_title: School Route Plans and School Crossings
metadata.part: Part 7 Traffic Control For School Areas

title: Section 7A.02 Guidance 5 - School Route Plans and School Crossings
text:
Section 7A.02 Guidance 5 - School Route Plans and School Crossings
Part: Part 7 Traffic Control For School Areas
Chapter: Chapter 7A. General
Page: 970

School area traffic control devices should be included in a school traffic control plan.

metadata.section_title: School Route Plans and School Crossings
metadata.part: Part 7 Traffic Control For School Areas

title: Section 7A.02 Support 6 - School Route Plans and School Crossings
text:
Section 7A.02 Support 6 - School Route Plans and School Crossings
Part: Part 7 Traffic Control For School Areas
Chapter: Chapter 7A. General
Page: 970

To establish a safer route to and from school for schoolchildren, the application of planning criterion for school walk routes might make it necessary for children to walk an indirect route to an established school crossing located where there is existing traffic control and to avoid the use of a direct crossing where there is no existing traffic control.

metadata.section_title: School Route Plans and School Crossings
metadata.part: Part 7 Traffic Control For School Areas

title: Section 7A.02 Support 7 - School Route Plans and School Crossings
text:
Section 7A.02 Support 7 - School Route Plans and School Crossings
Part: Part 7 Traffic Control For School Areas
Chapter: Chapter 7A. General
Page: 970

The frequency of gaps in the traffic stream that are sufficient for student crossing is different at each crossing location. When the delay between the occurrences of adequate gaps becomes excessive, students might become impatient and endanger themselves by attempting to cross the street during an inadequate gap. In these instances, the creation of sufficient gaps needs to be considered to accommodate the crossing demand.

metadata.section_title: School Route Plans and School Crossings
metadata.part: Part 7 Traffic Control For School Areas

title: Section 7A.02 Guidance 8 - School Route Plans and School Crossings
text:
Section 7A.02 Guidance 8 - School Route Plans and School Crossings
Part: Part 7 Traffic Control For School Areas
Chapter: Chapter 7A. General
Page: 970

School walk routes should be planned to take advantage of existing traffic controls.

metadata.section_title: School Route Plans and School Crossings
metadata.part: Part 7 Traffic Control For School Areas

title: Section 7A.02 Guidance 9 - School Route Plans and School Crossings
text:
Section 7A.02 Guidance 9 - School Route Plans and School Crossings
Part: Part 7 Traffic Control For School Areas
Chapter: Chapter 7A. General
Page: 970

The following factors should be considered when determining the feasibility of requiring children to walk a longer distance to a crossing with existing traffic control: A. The availability of adequate sidewalks or other pedestrian walkways to and from the location with existing control, B. The number of students using the crossing, C. The age levels of the students using the crossing, and D. The total extra walking distance.

metadata.section_title: School Route Plans and School Crossings
metadata.part: Part 7 Traffic Control For School Areas

text:
Section 7A.02 Support 10 - School Route Plans and School Crossings
Part: Part 7 Traffic Control For School Areas
Chapter: Chapter 7A. General
Page: 971

A School Crossing signal warrant is provided in Section 4C.06.

metadata.part: Part 7 Traffic Control For School Areas

text:
Section 7B.01 Standard 1 - Design of School Signs
Part: Part 7 Traffic Control For School Areas
Chapter: Chapter 7B. Signs

Except as provided in Section 2A.07, the sizes of signs and plaques to be used on conventional roadways in school areas shall be as shown in Table 7B-1.

Section 7B.01 Standard 2 - Design of School Signs
Part: Part 7 Traffic Control For School Areas
Chapter: Chapter 7B. Signs
Page: 971

The sizes in the Oversized column in Table 7B-1 shall be used on expressways in school areas.

title: Section 7B.01 Guidance 3 - Design of School Signs
text:
Section 7B.01 Guidance 3 - Design of School Signs
Part: Part 7 Traffic Control For School Areas
Chapter: Chapter 7B. Signs
Page: 972

The sizes in the Oversized column should be used on roadways that have four or more lanes with posted speed limits of 40 mph or higher. Table 7B-1. metadata.part: Part 7 Traffic Control For School Areas

title: Section 7B.01 Option 4 - Design of School Signs
text:
Section 7B.01 Option 4 - Design of School Signs
Part: Part 7 Traffic Control For School Areas
Chapter: Chapter 7B. Signs
Page: 972

Signs and plaques larger than those shown in Table 7B-1 may be used (see Section 2A.07).

metadata.part: Part 7 Traffic Control For School Areas

title: Section 7B.01 Standard 5 - Design of School Signs
text:
Section 7B.01 Standard 5 - Design of School Signs
Part: Part 7 Traffic Control For School Areas
Chapter: Chapter 7B. Signs
Page: 972

School warning signs, including the “SCHOOL” portion of the School Speed Limit (S5-1) sign and including any supplemental plaques used in association with these warning signs, shall have a fluorescent yellow-green background with a black legend and border unless otherwise provided in this Manual for a specific sign.

metadata.part: Part 7 Traffic Control For School Areas

title: Section 7B.01 Standard 6 - Design of School Signs
text:
Section 7B.01 Standard 6 - Design of School Signs
Part: Part 7 Traffic Control For School Areas
Chapter: Chapter 7B. Signs
Page: 972

The signs used for school area traffic control shall be retroreflective or illuminated.

metadata.part: Part 7 Traffic Control For School Areas

title: Section 7B.01 Support 7 - Design of School Signs
text:
Section 7B.01 Support 7 - Design of School Signs
Part: Part 7 Traffic Control For School Areas
Chapter: Chapter 7B. Signs
Page: 972

Sections 2A.13 and 2A.14 contain provisions regarding the installation, placement, and location of signs.

metadata.part: Part 7 Traffic Control For School Areas

title: Section 7B.02 Support 1 - School Area Signs and Plaques
text:
Section 7B.02 Support 1 - School Area Signs and Plaques
Part: Part 7 Traffic Control For School Areas
Chapter: Chapter 7B. Signs
Page: 972

Many state and local jurisdictions find it beneficial to advise road users that they are approaching a school that is adjacent to a highway, where additional care is needed, even though no school crossing is involved and the speed limit remains unchanged. Additionally, some jurisdictions designate school zones that have a unique legal standing in that fines for speeding or other traffic violations within designated school zones are increased or special enforcement techniques such as photo radar systems are used. It is important and sometimes legally necessary to mark the beginning and end points of these designated school zones so that the road user is given proper notice.

metadata.part: Part 7 Traffic Control For School Areas

title: Section 7B.02 Support 2 - School Area Signs and Plaques
text:
Section 7B.02 Support 2 - School Area Signs and Plaques
Part: Part 7 Traffic Control For School Areas
Chapter: Chapter 7B. Signs
Page: 972

The School (S1-1) sign (see Figure 7B-1) has the following four applications: A. School Area - the S1-1 sign can be used to warn road users that they are approaching a school area that might include school buildings or grounds, a school crossing, or school related activity adjacent to the highway. B. School Zone - the S1-1 sign can be used to identify the location of the beginning of a designated school zone. C. School Advance Crossing - if combined with an AHEAD (W16-9P) plaque or an XX FEET (W16-2P or W16-2aP) plaque to comprise the School Advance Crossing assembly (see Figure 7B-1), the S1-1 sign can be used to warn road users that they are approaching a crossing where schoolchildren cross the roadway (see Section 7B.03). D. School Crossing - if combined with a diagonal downward-pointing arrow (W16-7P) plaque to comprise the School Crossing assembly (see Figure 7B-1), the S1-1 sign can be used to warn approaching road users of the location of a crossing where schoolchildren cross the roadway (see Section 7B.03).

metadata.part: Part 7 Traffic Control For School Areas

title: Section 7B.02 Option 3 - School Area Signs and Plaques
text:
Section 7B.02 Option 3 - School Area Signs and Plaques
Part: Part 7 Traffic Control For School Areas
Chapter: Chapter 7B. Signs
Page: 972

If a school area or school zone is located on a cross street in close proximity to the intersection, a School (S1-1) sign with a supplemental arrow (W16-5P or W16-6P) plaque (see Figure 7B-1) may be installed on each approach of the street or highway to warn road users making a turn onto the cross street that they will encounter a school area soon after making the turn.

metadata.part: Part 7 Traffic Control For School Areas

title: Section 7B.02 Standard 4 - School Area Signs and Plaques
text:
Section 7B.02 Standard 4 - School Area Signs and Plaques
Part: Part 7 Traffic Control For School Areas
Chapter: Chapter 7B. Signs
Page: 972

If a school zone has been designated under State or local statute, a School (S1-1) sign (see Figure 7B-1) shall be installed to identify the beginning point(s) of the designated school zone (see Figure 7B-2).

metadata.part: Part 7 Traffic Control For School Areas

title: Section 7B.02 Option 5 - School Area Signs and Plaques
text:
Section 7B.02 Option 5 - School Area Signs and Plaques
Part: Part 7 Traffic Control For School Areas
Chapter: Chapter 7B. Signs
Page: 972

A School Zone (S1-1) sign may be supplemented with a SCHOOL (S4-3P) plaque (see Figure 7B-1).

metadata.part: Part 7 Traffic Control For School Areas

title: Section 7B.02 Option 6 - School Area Signs and Plaques
text:
Section 7B.02 Option 6 - School Area Signs and Plaques
Part: Part 7 Traffic Control For School Areas
Chapter: Chapter 7B. Signs
Page: 972

A School Zone (S1-1) sign may be supplemented with an ALL YEAR (S4-7P) plaque (see Figure 7B-1) if the school operates on a 12-month schedule.

metadata.part: Part 7 Traffic Control For School Areas

title: Section 7B.02 Option 7 - School Area Signs and Plaques
text:
Section 7B.02 Option 7 - School Area Signs and Plaques
Part: Part 7 Traffic Control For School Areas
Chapter: Chapter 7B. Signs
Page: 976

The downstream end of a designated school zone may be identified with an END SCHOOL ZONE (S5-2) sign (see Figures 7B-1 and 7B-2). MUTCD 11th Edition - Revision 1 Figure 7B-1. Signs in School Areas and at School Crossings (Sheet 1 of 2) A - School area signs School Speed Limit Assembly School Speed Limit When Flashing Sign School Advance Crossing Assembly School Zone Sign School Crossing Assembly Rev. 1 If used, the assembly or sign with WHEN FLASHING legend shall be accompanied by a flashing yellow Speed Limit Sign Beacon (see Section 4S.04). December 2025 Figure 7B-1. Signs in School Areas and at School Crossings (Sheet 2 of 2) B - Signs in advance of the school crossing In-Street Use C - In-street signs at the school crossing D - Overhead signs at the school crossing Notes: 1. The use of the STATE LAW legend is optional on the R1-6 series and R1-9 series signs *Reduced size signs for in-street use (see ): Section 7B.03 S1-1 12 x 12 inches S4-3P 12 x 4 inches W16-7P 12 x 6 inches W16-9P 12 x 6 inches (see Section 7B.03). 2. The use of the SCHOOL plaque above the R1-6 and R1-6a signs is optional. 3. Signs are shown in proportion to their designated sizes unless otherwise noted. Figure 7B-2. Example of Signing for a School Zone with a School Speed Limit and a School Crossing Note: The use of a School Advance Crossing Assembly is optional within a signed school zone (see Section 7B.03) MUTCD 11th Edition - Revision 1

metadata.part: Part 7 Traffic Control For School Areas

title: Section 7B.03 Standard 1 - School Crossing Signs
text:
Section 7B.03 Standard 1 - School Crossing Signs
Part: Part 7 Traffic Control For School Areas
Chapter: Chapter 7B. Signs
Page: 976

The School Advance Crossing assembly (see Figure 7B-1) shall consist of a School (S1-1) sign supplemented with an AHEAD (W16-9P) plaque or an XX FEET (W16-2P or W16-2aP) plaque.

metadata.part: Part 7 Traffic Control For School Areas

title: Section 7B.03 Standard 2 - School Crossing Signs
text:
Section 7B.03 Standard 2 - School Crossing Signs
Part: Part 7 Traffic Control For School Areas
Chapter: Chapter 7B. Signs
Page: 976

Except as provided in Paragraph 3 of this Section, a School Advance Crossing assembly shall be used in advance (see Table 2C-3 for advance placement guidelines) of the first School Crossing assembly that is encountered in each direction as traffic approaches a school crosswalk (see Figure 7B-3).

metadata.part: Part 7 Traffic Control For School Areas

title: Section 7B.03 Option 3 - School Crossing Signs
text:
Section 7B.03 Option 3 - School Crossing Signs
Part: Part 7 Traffic Control For School Areas
Chapter: Chapter 7B. Signs
Page: 976

The School Advance Crossing assembly may be omitted (see Figure 7B-2) where a School Zone (S1-1) sign (see Section 7B.02) is installed to identify the beginning of a school zone in advance of the School Crossing assembly.

metadata.part: Part 7 Traffic Control For School Areas

title: Section 7B.03 Option 4 - School Crossing Signs
text:
Section 7B.03 Option 4 - School Crossing Signs
Part: Part 7 Traffic Control For School Areas
Chapter: Chapter 7B. Signs
Page: 976

If a school crosswalk is located on a cross street in close proximity to an intersection, a School Advance Crossing assembly with a supplemental arrow (W16-5P or W16-6P) plaque may be installed on each approach of the street or highway to warn road users making a turn onto the cross street that they will encounter a school crosswalk soon after making the turn (see Figure 7B-3).

metadata.part: Part 7 Traffic Control For School Areas

title: Section 7B.03 Option 5 - School Crossing Signs
text:
Section 7B.03 Option 5 - School Crossing Signs
Part: Part 7 Traffic Control For School Areas
Chapter: Chapter 7B. Signs
Page: 976

A 12-inch reduced size in-street School (S1-1) sign (see Figure 7B-1), installed in compliance with the mounting height and special mounting support requirements for an In-Street Pedestrian Crossing (R1-6 or R1-6a) sign (see Section 2B.20), may be used in advance of a school crossing to supplement the post-mounted school warning signs. A 12 x 6-inch reduced size AHEAD (W16-9P) plaque (see Figure 7B-1) may be mounted below the reduced size in-street School (S1-1) sign.

metadata.part: Part 7 Traffic Control For School Areas

title: Section 7B.03 Standard 6 - School Crossing Signs
text:
Section 7B.03 Standard 6 - School Crossing Signs
Part: Part 7 Traffic Control For School Areas
Chapter: Chapter 7B. Signs
Page: 976

If used, the School Crossing assembly (see Figure 7B-1) shall be installed at the school crossing (see Figures 7B-2 and 7B-3), or as close to it as possible, and shall consist of a School (S1-1) sign supplemented with a diagonal downward-pointing arrow (W16-7P) plaque (see Section 2C.63) to show the location of the crossing.

metadata.part: Part 7 Traffic Control For School Areas

title: Section 7B.03 Standard 7 - School Crossing Signs
text:
Section 7B.03 Standard 7 - School Crossing Signs
Part: Part 7 Traffic Control For School Areas
Chapter: Chapter 7B. Signs
Page: 976

The School Crossing assembly shall not be used at crossings other than those adjacent to schools and those on established school pedestrian routes.

metadata.part: Part 7 Traffic Control For School Areas

title: Section 7B.03 Standard 8 - School Crossing Signs
text:
Section 7B.03 Standard 8 - School Crossing Signs
Part: Part 7 Traffic Control For School Areas
Chapter: Chapter 7B. Signs
Page: 976

The School Crossing assembly shall not be installed on an approach controlled by a STOP or a YIELD sign except as provided in Paragraphs 9 and 10 of this Section.

metadata.part: Part 7 Traffic Control For School Areas

title: Section 7B.03 Option 9 - School Crossing Signs
text:
Section 7B.03 Option 9 - School Crossing Signs
Part: Part 7 Traffic Control For School Areas
Chapter: Chapter 7B. Signs
Page: 976

The School Crossing assembly may be installed on an approach to a circular intersection controlled by a YIELD sign where the crosswalk is at least 20 feet in advance of the yield point at the entrance to a circulatory roadway.

metadata.part: Part 7 Traffic Control For School Areas

title: Section 7B.03 Option 10 - School Crossing Signs
text:
Section 7B.03 Option 10 - School Crossing Signs
Part: Part 7 Traffic Control For School Areas
Chapter: Chapter 7B. Signs
Page: 976

At a signalized or stop-controlled intersection the School Crossing assembly may be installed on an approach to a channelized right turn lane controlled by a YIELD sign where the crosswalk is at least 20 feet in advance of the yield point.

metadata.part: Part 7 Traffic Control For School Areas

title: Section 7B.03 Option 11 - School Crossing Signs
text:
Section 7B.03 Option 11 - School Crossing Signs
Part: Part 7 Traffic Control For School Areas
Chapter: Chapter 7B. Signs
Page: 976

A Yield Here To (Stop Here For) School Crossing (R1-5a or R1-5c) sign (see Figure 7B-1) may be used, in accordance with the provisions of Section 2B.19, in advance of a marked crosswalk that crosses an uncontrolled multi-lane approach within school zones. Rev. 1

metadata.part: Part 7 Traffic Control For School Areas

title: Section 7B.03 Option 12 - School Crossing Signs
text:
Section 7B.03 Option 12 - School Crossing Signs
Part: Part 7 Traffic Control For School Areas
Chapter: Chapter 7B. Signs
Page: 976

The In-Street Pedestrian Crossing (R1-6 or R1-6a) sign (see Section 2B.20 and Figure 7B-1) or the In-Street School Crossing (R1-6b or R1-6c) sign (see Figure 7B-1) may be used at school crossings on approaches that are not controlled by a traffic control signal, a pedestrian hybrid beacon, or emergency-vehicle hybrid beacon. If used at a school crossing, a 12 x 4-inch SCHOOL (S4-3P) plaque (see Figure 7B-1) may be mounted above the sign. The STATE LAW legend on the R1-6 series signs may be omitted.

metadata.part: Part 7 Traffic Control For School Areas

title: Section 7B.03 Option 13 - School Crossing Signs
text:
Section 7B.03 Option 13 - School Crossing Signs
Part: Part 7 Traffic Control For School Areas
Chapter: Chapter 7B. Signs
Page: 976

The In-Street Pedestrian Crossing (R1-6 or R1-6a) sign or In-Street School Crossing (R1-6b or R1-6c) sign may be used at intersections or midblock crossings with flashing beacons.

metadata.part: Part 7 Traffic Control For School Areas

title: Section 7B.03 Option 14 - School Crossing Signs
text:
Section 7B.03 Option 14 - School Crossing Signs
Part: Part 7 Traffic Control For School Areas
Chapter: Chapter 7B. Signs
Page: 976

The Overhead School Crossing (R1-9b or R1-9c) sign (see Figure 7B-1) may be used at school crossings on approaches that are not controlled by a traffic control signal, pedestrian hybrid beacon, or an emergency-vehicle hybrid beacon. The STATE LAW legend on the R1-9 series signs may be omitted.

metadata.part: Part 7 Traffic Control For School Areas

title: Section 7B.03 Standard 15 - School Crossing Signs
text:
Section 7B.03 Standard 15 - School Crossing Signs
Part: Part 7 Traffic Control For School Areas
Chapter: Chapter 7B. Signs
Page: 978

When used at an uncontrolled crossing, the In-Street or Overhead Pedestrian Crossing sign shall be used only as a supplement to a School Crossing assembly with a diagonal downward-pointing arrow (W16-7P) plaque at the crosswalk location. December 2025 Figure 7B-3. Example of Signing for a School Crossing Outside of a School Zone

metadata.part: Part 7 Traffic Control For School Areas

title: Section 7B.03 Option 16 - School Crossing Signs
text:
Section 7B.03 Option 16 - School Crossing Signs
Part: Part 7 Traffic Control For School Areas
Chapter: Chapter 7B. Signs
Page: 978

A 12-inch reduced size in-street School (S1-1) sign (see Figure 7B-1) may be used instead of the In-Street Pedestrian Crossing (R1-6 or R1-6a) or the In-Street School Crossing (R1-6b or R1-6c) sign at a school crossing on approaches that are not controlled by a traffic control signal, pedestrian hybrid beacon, or an emergency-vehicle hybrid beacon. A 12 x 6-inch reduced size diagonal downward-pointing arrow (W16-7P) plaque (see Figure 7B-1) may be mounted below the reduced size in-street School (S1-1) sign.

metadata.part: Part 7 Traffic Control For School Areas

title: Section 7B.03 Standard 17 - School Crossing Signs
text:
Section 7B.03 Standard 17 - School Crossing Signs
Part: Part 7 Traffic Control For School Areas
Chapter: Chapter 7B. Signs
Page: 978

If an In-Street Pedestrian Crossing sign, an In-Street School Crossing sign, or a reduced size in-street School (S1-1) sign is placed in the roadway, the sign support shall comply with the mounting height and special mounting support requirements for an In-Street Pedestrian Crossing (R1-6 or R1-6a) sign (see Section 2B.20).

metadata.part: Part 7 Traffic Control For School Areas

title: Section 7B.03 Standard 18 - School Crossing Signs
text:
Section 7B.03 Standard 18 - School Crossing Signs
Part: Part 7 Traffic Control For School Areas
Chapter: Chapter 7B. Signs
Page: 978

The In-Street Pedestrian Crossing sign, the In-Street School Crossing sign, the Overhead Pedestrian Crossing sign, and the reduced size in-street School (S1-1) sign shall not be used on approaches that are controlled by a traffic control signal, pedestrian hybrid beacon, or an emergency-vehicle hybrid beacon.

metadata.part: Part 7 Traffic Control For School Areas

title: Section 7B.04 Guidance 1 - School Bus Stop Signs
text:
Section 7B.04 Guidance 1 - School Bus Stop Signs
Part: Part 7 Traffic Control For School Areas
Chapter: Chapter 7B. Signs
Page: 978

The School Bus Stop Ahead (S3-1) sign (see Figure 7B-1) should be installed in advance of locations where a school bus, when stopped to pick up or discharge passengers, is not visible to road users for an adequate distance and where there is no opportunity to relocate the school bus stop to provide adequate sight distance.

metadata.part: Part 7 Traffic Control For School Areas

title: Section 7B.04 Option 2 - School Bus Stop Signs
text:
Section 7B.04 Option 2 - School Bus Stop Signs
Part: Part 7 Traffic Control For School Areas
Chapter: Chapter 7B. Signs
Page: 978

The SCHOOL BUS TURN AHEAD (S3-2) sign (see Figure 7B-1) may be installed in advance of locations where a school bus turns around on a roadway at a location not visible to approaching road users for a distance as determined by the “0” column under Condition B of Table 2C-3, and where there is no opportunity to relocate the school bus turn around to provide the distance provided in Table 2C-3.

metadata.part: Part 7 Traffic Control For School Areas

title: Section 7B.05 Standard 1 - School Speed Limit Signs and Plaques
text:
Section 7B.05 Standard 1 - School Speed Limit Signs and Plaques
Part: Part 7 Traffic Control For School Areas
Chapter: Chapter 7B. Signs
Page: 978

A School Speed Limit assembly (see Figure 7B-1) or a School Speed Limit When Flashing (S5-1) sign (see Figure 7B-1) shall be used to indicate the speed limit where a reduced school speed limit zone has been established based upon an engineering study or where a reduced school speed limit is specified for such areas by statute. The School Speed Limit assembly or School Speed Limit When Flashing sign shall be placed at or as near as practicable to the point where the reduced school speed limit zone begins (see Figures 7B-2 and 7B-4).

metadata.section_title: School Speed Limit Signs and Plaques
metadata.part: Part 7 Traffic Control For School Areas

title: Section 7B.05 Standard 2 - School Speed Limit Signs and Plaques
text:
Section 7B.05 Standard 2 - School Speed Limit Signs and Plaques
Part: Part 7 Traffic Control For School Areas
Chapter: Chapter 7B. Signs
Page: 978

If a reduced school speed limit zone has been established, a School (S1-1) sign shall be installed in advance (see Table 2C-3 for advance placement guidelines) of the first School Speed Limit sign assembly or S5-1 sign that is encountered in each direction as traffic approaches the reduced school speed limit zone (see Figures 7B-2 and 7B-4).

metadata.section_title: School Speed Limit Signs and Plaques
metadata.part: Part 7 Traffic Control For School Areas

title: Section 7B.05 Standard 3 - School Speed Limit Signs and Plaques
text:
Section 7B.05 Standard 3 - School Speed Limit Signs and Plaques
Part: Part 7 Traffic Control For School Areas
Chapter: Chapter 7B. Signs
Page: 978

Except as provided in Paragraph 4 of this Section, the downstream end of an authorized and posted reduced school speed limit zone shall be identified with an END SCHOOL SPEED LIMIT (S5-3) sign (see Figures 7B-1, 7B-2, and 7B-4).

metadata.section_title: School Speed Limit Signs and Plaques
metadata.part: Part 7 Traffic Control For School Areas

title: Section 7B.05 Option 4 - School Speed Limit Signs and Plaques
text:
Section 7B.05 Option 4 - School Speed Limit Signs and Plaques
Part: Part 7 Traffic Control For School Areas
Chapter: Chapter 7B. Signs
Page: 978

If a reduced school speed limit zone ends at the same point as a designated school zone (see Section 7B.02), an END SCHOOL ZONE (S5-2) sign may be used instead of an END SCHOOL SPEED LIMIT (S5-3) sign. A standard Speed Limit sign showing the speed limit for the section of highway that is downstream from the authorized and posted reduced school speed limit zone may be mounted on the same post above the END SCHOOL SPEED LIMIT (S5-3) sign or the END SCHOOL ZONE (S5-2) sign.

metadata.section_title: School Speed Limit Signs and Plaques
metadata.part: Part 7 Traffic Control For School Areas

title: Section 7B.05 Guidance 5 - School Speed Limit Signs and Plaques
text:
Section 7B.05 Guidance 5 - School Speed Limit Signs and Plaques
Part: Part 7 Traffic Control For School Areas
Chapter: Chapter 7B. Signs
Page: 978

The beginning point of a reduced school speed limit zone should be at least 200 feet in advance of the school grounds or a school crossing; however, this 200-foot distance should be increased if the reduced school speed limit is 30 mph or higher. The maximum beginning point of a reduced school speed limit zone should not be greater than 500 feet in advance of the school grounds or a school crossing.

metadata.section_title: School Speed Limit Signs and Plaques
metadata.part: Part 7 Traffic Control For School Areas

title: Section 7B.05 Standard 6 - School Speed Limit Signs and Plaques
text:
Section 7B.05 Standard 6 - School Speed Limit Signs and Plaques
Part: Part 7 Traffic Control For School Areas
Chapter: Chapter 7B. Signs
Page: 980

The School Speed Limit assembly shall be either a static sign assembly, a blank-out sign, or a changeable message sign (see Chapter 2L). MUTCD 11th Edition - Revision 1 Figure 7B-4. Example of Signing for a School Zone with a School Speed Limit and Higher Fines Only for Speeding Rev. 1 Rev. 1 December 2025

metadata.section_title: School Speed Limit Signs and Plaques
metadata.part: Part 7 Traffic Control For School Areas

title: Section 7B.05 Standard 7 - School Speed Limit Signs and Plaques
text:
Section 7B.05 Standard 7 - School Speed Limit Signs and Plaques
Part: Part 7 Traffic Control For School Areas
Chapter: Chapter 7B. Signs
Page: 980

The static School Speed Limit assembly shall consist of a top plaque (S4-3P) with the legend SCHOOL, a Speed Limit (R2-1) sign, and a bottom plaque (S4-1P, S4-2P, S4-4P, or S4-6P) indicating the specific periods of the day and/or days of the week that the special school speed limit is in effect (see Figure 7B-1).

metadata.section_title: School Speed Limit Signs and Plaques
metadata.part: Part 7 Traffic Control For School Areas

title: Section 7B.05 Standard 8 - School Speed Limit Signs and Plaques
text:
Section 7B.05 Standard 8 - School Speed Limit Signs and Plaques
Part: Part 7 Traffic Control For School Areas
Chapter: Chapter 7B. Signs
Page: 980

When a School Speed Limit When Flashing (S5-1) sign or a Speed Limit (R2-1) sign with a supplemental WHEN FLASHING (S4-4P) plaque is used, a Speed Limit Sign Beacon (see Section 4S.04) shall be used to identify the periods that the school speed limit is in effect.

metadata.section_title: School Speed Limit Signs and Plaques
metadata.part: Part 7 Traffic Control For School Areas

title: Section 7B.05 Standard 9 - School Speed Limit Signs and Plaques
text:
Section 7B.05 Standard 9 - School Speed Limit Signs and Plaques
Part: Part 7 Traffic Control For School Areas
Chapter: Chapter 7B. Signs
Page: 980

Fluorescent yellow-green pixels shall be used when the “SCHOOL” message is displayed on a changeable message sign for a school speed limit.

metadata.section_title: School Speed Limit Signs and Plaques
metadata.part: Part 7 Traffic Control For School Areas

title: Section 7B.05 Option 10 - School Speed Limit Signs and Plaques
text:
Section 7B.05 Option 10 - School Speed Limit Signs and Plaques
Part: Part 7 Traffic Control For School Areas
Chapter: Chapter 7B. Signs
Page: 980

Changeable message signs may use blank-out messages or other methods in order to display the school speed limit only during the periods it applies.

metadata.section_title: School Speed Limit Signs and Plaques
metadata.part: Part 7 Traffic Control For School Areas

title: Section 7B.05 Option 11 - School Speed Limit Signs and Plaques
text:
Section 7B.05 Option 11 - School Speed Limit Signs and Plaques
Part: Part 7 Traffic Control For School Areas
Chapter: Chapter 7B. Signs
Page: 980

A Vehicle Speed Feedback (W13-20aP) plaque that displays the speed of approaching drivers (see Sections 2B.21 and 2C.13), that is part of a School Speed Limit assembly or a School Speed Limit When Flashing (S5-1) sign, may be used in a school speed limit zone.

metadata.section_title: School Speed Limit Signs and Plaques
metadata.part: Part 7 Traffic Control For School Areas

title: Section 7B.05 Guidance 12 - School Speed Limit Signs and Plaques
text:
Section 7B.05 Guidance 12 - School Speed Limit Signs and Plaques
Part: Part 7 Traffic Control For School Areas
Chapter: Chapter 7B. Signs
Page: 980

If used, the Vehicle Speed Feedback (W13-20aP) plaque should only be used during the time period when the school speed limit is in effect.

metadata.section_title: School Speed Limit Signs and Plaques
metadata.part: Part 7 Traffic Control For School Areas

title: Section 7B.05 Guidance 13 - School Speed Limit Signs and Plaques
text:
Section 7B.05 Guidance 13 - School Speed Limit Signs and Plaques
Part: Part 7 Traffic Control For School Areas
Chapter: Chapter 7B. Signs
Page: 980

A Reduced School Speed Limit Ahead (S4-5or S4-5a) sign (see Figure 7B-1) should be used to inform road users of a reduced speed zone where the speed limit is being reduced by more than 10 mph, or where engineering judgment indicates that advance notice would be appropriate.

metadata.section_title: School Speed Limit Signs and Plaques
